### C.4 Proof of Theorem 3.1: Pooling dominates linear aggregation

Here we prove that the oracle pooled estimators $\hat{\theta}_{\textnormal{AIPW}}^{*}$ and $\hat{\theta}_{\textnormal{EPL}}^{*}$ dominate the best linearly aggregated estimators $\hat{\theta}_{\textnormal{AIPW}}^{*,(\mathrm{LA})}$ and $\hat{\theta}_{\textnormal{EPL}}^{*,(\mathrm{LA})}$ for estimating $\theta_{0,\textnormal{ATE}}$ and $\theta_{0,\textnormal{PL}}$ , respectively. For $\theta_{0.\textnormal{PL}}$ , Theorem 3.1 generalizes to nonstationary batches as described in Appendix A. But for $\theta_{0,\textnormal{ATE}}$ , the Theorem does not necessarily hold under the nonstationarities of Appendix A. For example, suppose that $T=2$ , $P_{1}^{X}$ is uniform on $(0,1)$ , and $P_{2}^{X}$ is the distribution with density $2x$ on $(0,1)$ with respect to Lebesgue measure. Let $v_{0}(z,x)=x$ and suppose $e_{1}(x)=e_{2}(x)=\kappa_{1}=1/2$ for each $x\in\mathcal{X}$ . Then $V_{0,\textnormal{AIPW}}=7/3>V^{(\mathrm{LA})}_{\textnormal{AIPW}}=16/7$ . We can however generalize the ATE result to the case of a multivariate outcome variable, i.e., $Y(1),Y(0)\in\real^{q}$ , where the conditional mean and variance functions $m_{0}(\cdot)$ and $v_{0}(\cdot)$ take values in q and $\mathbb{S}_{+}^{q}$ , respectively.

We begin by showing the result for ATE estimation. We have $V^{(\mathrm{LA})}_{\textnormal{AIPW}}=\left(\sum_{t=1}^{T}\kappa_{t}V_{t,\textnormal{AIPW}}^{-1}\right)^{-1}$ where we compute

$$ V_{t,\textnormal{AIPW}}=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{v_{0}(1,X)}{e_{t}(X)}+\frac{v_{0}(0,X)}{1-e_{t}(X)}+(\tau_{0}(X)-\theta_{0})^{\otimes 2}\right],\quad t=1,\ldots,T $$

by applying Corollary 3.1 to the observations in each single batch $t\in\{1,\ldots,T\}$ . Letting

$$ \displaystyle h(e) \displaystyle=\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{v_{0}(1,X)}{e(X)}+\frac{v_{0}(0,X)}{1-e(X)}+(\tau_{0}(X)-\theta_{0})^{\otimes 2}\right]\right)^{-1} \displaystyle=\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{v_{0}(1,X)(1-e(X))+v_{0}(0,X)e(X)}{e(X)(1-e(X))}+(\tau_{0}(X)-\theta_{0})^{\otimes 2}\right]\right)^{-1} $$

for each $e\in\mathcal{F}_{\gamma}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\Bigl(V^{(\mathrm{LA})}_{\textnormal{AIPW}}\Bigr)^{-1} \displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\kappa_{t}\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{v_{0}(1,X)}{e_{t}(X)}+\frac{v_{0}(0,X)}{1-e_{t}(X)}+(\tau_{0}(X)-\theta_{0})^{\otimes 2}\right]\right)^{-1} \displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\kappa_{t}h(e_{t}),\quad\text{versus} \displaystyle V_{0,\textnormal{AIPW}}^{-1} \displaystyle=\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{v_{0}(1,X)}{e_{0}(X)}+\frac{v_{0}(0,X)}{1-e_{0}(X)}+(\tau_{0}(X)-\theta_{0})^{\otimes 2}\right]\right)^{-1} \displaystyle=h(e_{0}). $$

Thus, to prove the desired result, it suffices to show $h(\cdot)$ is a concave (matrix-valued) function on $\mathcal{F}_{\gamma}$ . To that end, fix $e_{1},e_{2}\in\mathcal{F}_{\gamma}$ and $\lambda\in(0,1)$ . It suffices to show that $g(\lambda)=h(e_{1}+\lambda(e_{2}-e_{1}))$ is concave on $[0,1]$ , i.e., that $g(\lambda)\succcurlyeq\lambda g(e_{2})+(1-\lambda)g(e_{1})$ for each $\lambda\in[0,1]$ . Because $g(\cdot)$ is continuous on $[0,1]$ , we need only show that $g^{\prime\prime}(\lambda)\preccurlyeq 0$ for each $\lambda\in(0,1)$ . Letting $e_{\lambda}=e_{1}+\lambda(e_{2}-e_{1})$ and $V_{\lambda}=h(e_{\lambda})^{-1}$ , we obtain

$$ \displaystyle g^{\prime\prime}(\lambda)=2h(e_{\lambda})[B_{\lambda}h(e_{\lambda})B_{\lambda}-C_{\lambda}]h(e_{\lambda}) $$

for

$$ \displaystyle B_{\lambda} \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[(e_{2}(X)-e_{1}(X))\left(\frac{v_{0}(0,X)}{(1-e_{\lambda}(X))^{2}}-\frac{v_{0}(1,X)}{(e_{\lambda}(X))^{2}}\right)\right],\quad\text{and} \displaystyle C_{\lambda} \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[(e_{2}(X)-e_{1}(X))^{2}\left(\frac{v_{0}(1,X)}{(e_{\lambda}(X))^{3}}+\frac{v_{0}(0,X)}{(1-e_{\lambda}(X))^{3}}\right)\right]. $$

To get this, we reversed the order of differentiation and expectation, which is justified by the regularity conditions in Assumption 3.1.

Since $h(e_{\lambda})$ is symmetric and appears on the left and right in (57), it suffices to show that $B_{\lambda}h(e_{\lambda})B_{\lambda}\preccurlyeq C_{\lambda}$ . For this we note that for $\tilde{Z}$ conditionally independent of $(Y(0),Y(1))$ given $X$ with $\tilde{Z}\mid X\sim\textnormal{Bern}(e_{\lambda}(X))$ , we have $h(e_{\lambda})=(\textnormal{Cov}(b_{\lambda}))^{-1}$ , $B_{\lambda}=\textnormal{Cov}(c_{\lambda},b_{\lambda})=B_{\lambda}^{\prime}$ , and $C_{\lambda}=\textnormal{Cov}(c_{\lambda})$ where

$$ \displaystyle b_{\lambda} \displaystyle=\frac{(1-\tilde{Z})(Y(0)-m_{0}(0,X))}{1-e_{\lambda}(X)}-\frac{\tilde{Z}(Y(1)-m_{0}(1,X))}{e_{\lambda}(X)}-(\tau_{0}(X)-\theta_{0}) \displaystyle c_{\lambda} \displaystyle=(e_{2}(X)-e_{1}(X))\biggl(\frac{\tilde{Z}(Y(1)-m_{0}(1,X))}{(e_{\lambda}(X))^{2}}+\frac{(1-\tilde{Z})(Y(0)-m_{0}(0,X))}{(1-e_{\lambda}(X))^{2}}\biggr) $$

are mean zero random vectors in d. Applying Lemma B.6 completes the proof for ATE.

Now we consider the partially linear model, allowing for the generalizations in Appendix A, as discussed above. We have $V_{\textnormal{EPL}}^{(\mathrm{LA})}=\bigl(\sum_{t=1}^{T}\kappa_{t}V_{t,\textnormal{EPL}}^{-1}\bigr)^{-1}$ where

$$ \displaystyle V_{t,\textnormal{EPL}}=\biggl(\mathbb{E}_{t}\left[\frac{e_{t}(X)(1-e_{t}(X))}{v_{0}(0,X)e_{t}(X)+v_{0}(1,X)(1-e_{t}(X))}\psi(X)\psi(X)^{\top}\right]\biggr)^{-1} $$

by applying Corollary 3.2 to the observations in each single batch $t\in\{1,\ldots,T\}$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\bigl(V^{(\mathrm{LA})}_{\textnormal{EPL}}\bigr)^{-1} \displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\kappa_{t}V_{t,\textnormal{EPL}}^{-1} \displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{t}\left[\kappa_{t}\frac{e_{t}(X)(1-e_{t}(X))}{v_{0}(0,X)e_{t}(X)+v_{0}(1,X)(1-e_{t}(X))}\psi(X)\psi(X)^{\top}\right] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{0}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\kappa_{t}\frac{\mathrm{d}P_{t}^{X}}{\mathrm{d}P_{0}^{X}}(X)\frac{e_{t}(X)(1-e_{t}(X))}{v_{0}(0,X)e_{t}(X)+v_{0}(1,X)(1-e_{t}(X))}\psi(X)\psi(X)^{\top}\right] \displaystyle\preccurlyeq\mathbb{E}_{0}\left[\frac{e_{0}(X)(1-e_{0}(X))}{v_{0}(0,X)e_{0}(X)+v_{0}(1,X)(1-e_{0}(X))}\psi(X)\psi(X)^{\top}\right] \displaystyle=(V_{0,\textnormal{EPL}})^{-1} $$

where the inequality follows from the fact that for each $x\in\mathcal{X}$ , we have $\sum_{t=1}^{T}\kappa_{t}{\mathrm{d}P_{t}^{X}}/{\mathrm{d}P_{0}^{X}}(x)=1$ and the map

$$ e\mapsto\frac{e(1-e)}{v(0,x)e+v(1,x)(1-e)}\psi(x)\psi(x)^{\top} $$

is concave on $e\in[0,1]$ .

### C.5 Proof of Theorem 4.1: CLT for feasible $\hat{\theta}$ in a CSBAE

Here we prove the CLT for the feasible estimator $\hat{\theta}$ in a CSBAE. It holds under the nonstationarity conditions described in Appendix A.

We begin by constructing the non-adaptive batch experiment in the statement of the theorem. Define the counterfactual treatment indicators via

$$ \tilde{Z}_{ti}=\bm{1}(U_{ti}\leqslant e_{t}(X_{ti})),\quad t=1,\ldots,T,\quad i=1,\ldots,N_{t} $$

for $U_{ti}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{iid}}}{{\sim}}\mathbb{U}(0,1)$ . Then the observations in the counterfactual non-adaptive batch experiment are the vectors $\tilde{W}_{ti}=(\tilde{Y}_{ti},X_{ti},\tilde{Z}_{ti})$ , where

$$ \tilde{Y}_{ti}=Y_{ti}(\tilde{Z}_{it})=\tilde{Z}_{it}Y_{ti}(1)+(1-\tilde{Z}_{it})Y_{ti}(0). $$

The corresponding oracle estimator $\hat{\theta}^{*}$ from (11) is then

$$ \displaystyle\hat{\theta}^{*} \displaystyle=-\biggl(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}s_{a}(\tilde{W}_{ti};\nu_{0},e_{0,N})\biggr)^{-1}\biggl(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}s_{b}(\tilde{W}_{ti};\nu_{0},e_{0,N})\biggr). $$

Because $(\nu_{0},e_{0,N})\in\mathcal{T}_{N}$ , conditions 1, 2, and 3 of Proposition 3.1 are satisfied for this counterfactual non-adaptive batch experiment by equations (22), (23), and (25) along with condition (a) of Assumption 4.1. Hence the oracle CLT $\sqrt{n}(\hat{\theta}^{*}-\theta_{0})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{d\,\,}}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathcal{N}(0,V_{0})$ holds with $V_{0}$ as in the conclusion of Proposition 3.1.

It remains to show that

$$ \hat{\theta}=\hat{\theta}^{*}+o_{p}(N^{-1/2}) $$

where

$$ \displaystyle\hat{\theta}=-\biggl(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}s_{a}(W_{ti};\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})\biggr)^{-1}\biggl(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}s_{b}(W_{ti};\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})\biggr) $$

as in (18). To do so, we show that the following intermediate quantity

$$ \tilde{\theta}=-\biggl(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}s_{a}(\tilde{W}_{ti};\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})\biggr)^{-1}\biggl(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}s_{b}(\tilde{W}_{ti};\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})\biggr) $$

satisfies both $\tilde{\theta}=\hat{\theta}^{*}+o_{p}(N^{-1/2})$ and $\hat{\theta}=\tilde{\theta}+o_{p}(N^{-1/2})$ .

#### C.5.1 Showing that $\tilde{\theta}=\hat{\theta}^{*}+o_{p}(N^{-1/2})$

We first show $\tilde{\theta}=\hat{\theta}^{*}+o_{p}(N^{-1/2})$ . By score linearity (4), we can write

$$ N^{1/2}(\tilde{\theta}-\hat{\theta}^{*})=N^{1/2}(\tilde{\theta}-\theta_{0})-N^{1/2}(\hat{\theta}^{*}-\theta_{0})=A_{1}B_{1}+A_{2}B_{2} $$

where

$$ \displaystyle A_{1} \displaystyle=\biggl(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}s_{a}(\tilde{W}_{ti};\nu_{0},e_{0,N})\biggr)^{-1}-\biggl(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}s_{a}(\tilde{W}_{ti};\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})\biggr)^{-1}, \displaystyle B_{1} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}s(\tilde{W}_{ti};\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N}), \displaystyle A_{2} \displaystyle=\biggl(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}s_{a}(\tilde{W}_{ti};\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})\biggr)^{-1}\quad\text{and} \displaystyle B_{2} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}[s(\tilde{W}_{ti};\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})-s(\tilde{W}_{ti};\theta_{0},\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})]. $$

We will prove that $A_{1}=o_{p}(1)$ , $B_{1}=O_{p}(1)$ , $A_{2}=O_{p}(1)$ , and $B_{2}=o_{p}(1)$ .

To show $A_{1}=o_{p}(1)$ , for each fold $k\in\{1,\ldots,K\}$ let $N_{k}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}n_{t,k}=N/K+O(1)$ be the total number of observations in fold $k$ across all batches $t=1,\ldots,T$ . Also define the quantity

$$ \tilde{A}_{1}^{(k)}=\frac{1}{N_{k}}\sum_{(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}[s_{a}(\tilde{W}_{ti};\nu_{0},e_{0,N})-s_{a}(\tilde{W}_{ti};\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})]=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{n_{t,k}}{N_{k}}\tilde{A}_{1,t}^{(k)} $$

where

$$ \tilde{A}_{1,t}^{(k)}=\frac{1}{n_{t,k}}\sum_{i:(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}s_{a}(\tilde{W}_{ti};\nu_{0},e_{0,N})-s_{a}(\tilde{W}_{ti};\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)}). $$

For each $k=1,\ldots,K$ , let $\mathcal{E}_{N,k}$ be the event that $(\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})\in\mathcal{T}_{N}$ . This $\mathcal{E}_{N,k}$ is $\mathcal{S}^{(-k)}$ measurable and $\textnormal{Pr}(\mathcal{E}_{N,k})\rightarrow 1$ as $N\rightarrow\infty$ by assumption. Then for all sufficiently large $N$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\phantom{=}\,\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|\tilde{A}_{1,t}^{(k)}\bm{1}(\mathcal{E}_{N,k})\|\mid\mathcal{S}^{(-k)}\bigr] \displaystyle\leqslant\bm{1}(\mathcal{E}_{N,k})\biggl(\frac{1}{n_{t,k}}\sum_{i:(t,i)\in I_{j}}\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|s_{a}(\tilde{W}_{ti};\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})-s_{a}(\tilde{W}_{ti};\nu_{0},e_{0,N})\|\mid\mathcal{S}^{(-k)}\bigr]\biggr) \displaystyle\leqslant\sup_{(\nu,e)\in\mathcal{T}_{N}}\mathbb{E}_{t}\bigl[\|s_{a}(W;\nu,e)-s_{a}(W;\nu_{0},e_{0,N})\|\bigr] \displaystyle\leqslant\kappa_{t}^{-1}\sup_{(\nu,e)\in\mathcal{T}_{N}}\mathbb{E}_{0}\bigl[\|s_{a}(W;\nu,e)-s_{a}(W;\nu_{0},e_{0})\|\bigr]+\kappa_{t}^{-1}\mathbb{E}_{0}[\|s_{a}(W;\nu_{0},e_{0,N})-s_{a}(W;\nu_{0},e_{0})\|] \displaystyle\leqslant 2\kappa_{t}^{-1}\delta_{N} $$

by equation (22). The second inequality above uses the fact that $\hat{\nu}^{(-k)}$ , $\hat{e}^{(-k)}$ are nonrandom given $\mathcal{S}^{(-k)}$ , but the vectors $\tilde{W}_{ti}$ in fold $k$ are independent of $\mathcal{S}^{(-k)}$ and i.i.d. from $P_{t}$ ; the third inequality follows because

$$ \frac{\mathrm{d}P_{t}}{\mathrm{d}P_{0}}(w)\leqslant\kappa_{t}^{-1} $$

for all $w$ by the definitions of $P_{t}$ and $P_{0}$ . Then $\tilde{A}_{1,t}^{(k)}=o_{p}(1)$ by Lemma B.1. This immediately shows $\tilde{A}_{1}^{(k)}=o_{p}(1)$ for all folds $k=1,\ldots,K$ and so

$$ \tilde{A}_{1}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{N_{k}}{N}\tilde{A}_{1}^{(k)}=o_{p}(1), $$

too. Now recall the identity

$$ \|A^{-1}-B^{-1}\|=\|A^{-1}(A-B)B^{-1}\|\leqslant\|A^{-1}\|\|A-B\|\|B^{-1}\| $$

for any invertible square matrices $A,B$ of the same size. By (52) we know that

$$ \frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}s_{a}(\tilde{W}_{ti};\nu_{0},e_{0,N})=\mathbb{E}_{0}[s_{a}(W;\nu_{0},e_{0})]+o_{p}(1) $$

and hence

$$ \displaystyle\biggl(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}s_{a}(\tilde{W}_{ti};\nu_{0},e_{0,N})\biggr)^{-1}\quad\text{and}\quad\biggl(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}s_{a}(\tilde{W}_{ti};\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})\biggr)^{-1} $$

are both $O_{p}(1)$ . The preceding display along with (59) and (60) show $A_{1}=o_{p}(1)$ .

Equations (59) and (61) immediately imply that $A_{2}=O_{p}(1)$ , while (53) implies that $B_{1}=O_{p}(1)$ . It remains to show $B_{2}=o_{p}(1)$ . To that end we consider the quantity

$$ \displaystyle B_{2}^{(k)} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N_{k}}}\sum_{(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}s(\tilde{W}_{ti};\theta_{0},\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})-s(\tilde{W}_{ti};\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N}) \displaystyle=\bar{B}_{2}^{(k)}+\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sqrt{\frac{n_{t,k}}{N_{k}}}\tilde{B}_{2,t}^{(k)} $$

where for each $t=1,\ldots,T$

$$ \displaystyle\bar{B}_{2}^{(k)} \displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sqrt{\frac{n_{t,k}}{N_{k}}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n_{t,k}}}\sum_{i:(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\mathbb{E}[s(\tilde{W}_{ti};\theta_{0},\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})-s(\tilde{W}_{ti};\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})\mid\mathcal{S}^{(-k)}],\quad\text{and} \displaystyle\tilde{B}_{2,t}^{(k)} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n_{t,k}}}\sum_{i:(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}s(\tilde{W}_{ti};\theta_{0},\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})-s(\tilde{W}_{ti};\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N}) \displaystyle\phantom{=}-\mathbb{E}[s(\tilde{W}_{ti};\theta_{0},\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})-s(\tilde{W}_{ti};\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})\mid\mathcal{S}^{(-k)}]. $$

To see that $\bar{B}_{2}^{(k)}=o_{p}(1)$ , we write

$$ \displaystyle\bar{B}_{2}^{(k)} \displaystyle=N_{k}^{1/2}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{n_{t,k}}{N_{k}}\int s(w;\theta_{0},\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})-s(w;\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})\mathrm{d}P_{t}(w) \displaystyle=N_{k}^{1/2}\int s(w;\theta_{0},\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})-s(w;\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})\mathrm{d}P_{0,N}(w) \displaystyle\phantom{=}+N_{k}^{1/2}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(\frac{n_{t,k}}{N_{k}}-\frac{N_{t}}{N}\right)\int s(w;\theta_{0},\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})-s(w;\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})\mathrm{d}P_{t}(w). $$

Now

$$ f_{N}^{(k)}(\lambda)=\int s(w;\theta_{0},\nu_{0}+\lambda(\hat{\nu}^{(-k)}-\nu_{0}),e_{0,N}+\lambda(\hat{e}^{(-k)}-e_{0,N}))-s(w;\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})\mathrm{d}P_{0,N}(w) $$

is twice continuously differentiable on $[0,1]$ by regularity. Hence by Taylor’s theorem

$$ \|f_{N}^{(k)}(1)-f_{N}^{(k)}(0)-f_{N}^{(k)\prime}(0)\|\leqslant\frac{1}{2}\sup_{\lambda\in(0,1)}\|f_{N}^{(k)\prime\prime}(\lambda)\|. $$

By (21) we know that

$$ \displaystyle\sup_{\lambda\in(0,1)}\|f_{N}^{(k)\prime\prime}(\lambda)\|\bm{1}(\mathcal{E}_{N,k}) \displaystyle\leqslant\sup_{\lambda\in(0,1)}\sup_{(\nu,e)\in\mathcal{T}_{N}}\bigg\|\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial\lambda^{2}}\mathbb{E}_{0,N}[s(W;\theta_{0},\nu_{0}+\lambda(\nu-\nu_{0}),e_{0,N}+\lambda(e-e_{0,N}))]\bigg\| \displaystyle\leqslant N^{-1/2}\delta_{N}. $$

With $f_{N}^{(k)}(0)=0$ , by (20) and (62) we conclude that that

$$ \|f_{N}^{(k)}(1)\|\bm{1}(\mathcal{E}_{N,K})\leqslant\frac{3}{2}N^{-1/2}\delta_{N}. $$

Recalling that $\textnormal{Pr}(\mathcal{E}_{N,k})\rightarrow 1$ , we have $\|f_{N}^{(k)}(1)\|=o_{p}(N^{-1/2})$ and

$$ \bigg\|N_{k}^{1/2}\int s(w;\theta_{0},\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})-s(w;\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})\,\mathrm{d}P_{0,N}(w)\bigg\|=N_{k}^{1/2}\|f_{N}^{(k)}(1)\|=o_{p}(1). $$

Using $N_{t}/N\to\kappa_{t}$ from (3) we have

$$ \displaystyle\phantom{=}\,\bigg\|N_{k}^{1/2}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(\frac{n_{t,k}}{N_{k}}-\frac{N_{t}}{N}\right)\int s(w;\theta_{0},\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})-s(w;\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})\,\mathrm{d}P_{t}(w)\bigg\| \displaystyle\leqslant N_{k}^{1/2}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\bigg|\frac{n_{t,k}}{N_{k}}-\frac{N_{t}}{N}\bigg|\cdot\frac{N}{N_{t}}\|f_{N}^{(k)}(1)\| \displaystyle=o_{p}(1) $$

as

$$ \frac{\mathrm{d}P_{t}}{\mathrm{d}P_{0,N}}(w)\leqslant\frac{N}{N_{t}},\quad t=1,\ldots,T,\quad w\in\mathcal{W}. $$

Thus we have shown $\bar{B}_{2}^{(k)}=o_{p}(1)$ . Finally, for each batch $t=1,\ldots,T$ , the quantity $\tilde{B}_{2,t}^{(k)}$ is a sum of $n_{t,k}$ random variables that are i.i.d. and mean 0 conditional on $\mathcal{S}^{(-k)}$ . Thus by Lemma B.7, we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|\tilde{B}_{2,t}^{(k)}\|^{2}\mid\mathcal{S}^{(-k)}\bigr] \displaystyle=\sum_{i:(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\frac{1}{n_{t,k}}\bar{\mathbb{E}}\bigl[\|r_{ti}^{(k)}\|^{2}\bigr] \displaystyle\leqslant\sum_{i:(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\frac{1}{n_{t,k}}\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|s(W_{ti};\theta_{0},\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})-s(W_{ti};\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})\|^{2}\mid\mathcal{S}^{(-k)}\bigr] $$

where for each $i$ such that $(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}$ we’ve defined

$$ \displaystyle\begin{split}r_{ti}^{(k)}&=s(W_{ti};\theta_{0},\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})-s(\tilde{W}_{ti};\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})\\
&\phantom{=}\,-\mathbb{E}[s(\tilde{W}_{ti};\theta_{0},\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})-s(\tilde{W}_{ti};\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})\mid\mathcal{S}^{(-k)}]\end{split} $$

and used the basic variance inequality

$$ \mathbb{E}\bigl[\|X-\mathbb{E}[X\mid\mathcal{S}]\|^{2}\bigr]\leqslant\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|X\|^{2}\mid\mathcal{S}\bigr] $$

for any random vector $X$ and $\sigma$ -algebra $\mathcal{S}$ . Hence by (58), Minkowski’s inequality, and then (23), we have

$$ \displaystyle\bigl(\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|\tilde{B}_{2,t}^{(k)}\|^{2}\mid\mathcal{S}^{(-k)}\bigr]\bigr)^{1/2}\bm{1}(\mathcal{E}_{N,k}) \displaystyle\leqslant\sup_{(\nu,e)\in\mathcal{T}_{N}}\bigl(\mathbb{E}_{t}\bigl[\|s(W;\theta_{0},\nu,e)-s(W;\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})\|^{2}\bigr]\bigr)^{1/2} \displaystyle\leqslant\kappa_{t}^{-1/2}\sup_{(\nu,e)\in\mathcal{T}_{N}}\bigl(\mathbb{E}_{0,N}\bigl[\|s(W;\theta_{0},\nu,e)-s(W;\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0})\|^{2}\bigr]\bigr)^{1/2} \displaystyle\phantom{=}\,+\kappa_{t}^{-1/2}\bigl(\mathbb{E}_{0,N}\bigl[\|s(W;\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})-s(W;\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0})\|^{2}\bigr]\bigr)^{1/2} \displaystyle\leqslant 2\kappa_{t}^{-1/2}\delta_{N}. $$

Thus $\tilde{B}_{2,t}^{(k)}=o_{p}(1)$ by Lemma B.1. With

$$ -B_{2}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sqrt{\frac{N_{k}}{N}}B_{2}^{(k)}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sqrt{\frac{N_{k}}{N}}\biggl(\bar{B}_{2}^{(k)}+\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sqrt{\frac{n_{t,k}}{N_{k}}}\tilde{B}_{2,t}^{(k)}\biggr) $$

we conclude that $B_{2}=o_{p}(1)$ , as desired. This establishes that $\hat{\theta}^{*}=\tilde{\theta}+o_{p}(N^{-1/2})$ .

#### C.5.2 Showing that $\hat{\theta}=\hat{\theta}^{*}+o_{p}(N^{-1/2})$

To establish that $\hat{\theta}=\tilde{\theta}+o_{p}(N^{-1/2})$ , similar to above we write

$$ N^{1/2}(\hat{\theta}-\tilde{\theta})=N^{1/2}(\hat{\theta}-\theta_{0})-N^{1/2}(\tilde{\theta}-\theta_{0})=A_{3}B_{3}+A_{4}B_{4} $$

where

$$ \displaystyle A_{3} \displaystyle=\biggl(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}s_{a}(\tilde{W}_{ti};\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})\biggr)^{-1}-\biggl(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}s_{a}(W_{ti};\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})\biggr)^{-1}, \displaystyle B_{3} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}s(\tilde{W}_{ti};\theta_{0},\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)}), \displaystyle A_{4} \displaystyle=\biggl(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}s_{a}(W_{ti};\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})\biggr)^{-1},\quad\text{and} \displaystyle B_{4} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}[s(\tilde{W}_{ti};\theta_{0},\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})-s(W_{ti};\theta_{0},\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})]. $$

We will show that $A_{3}=o_{p}(1)$ , $B_{3}=O_{p}(1)$ , $A_{4}=O_{p}(1)$ , and $B_{4}=o_{p}(1)$ . First we define

$$ \tilde{A}_{3}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{N_{k}}{N}\tilde{A}_{3}^{(k)} $$

where the term $\tilde{A}_{3}^{(k)}$ for each fold is decomposed into a sum over batches $t=1,\ldots,T$ :

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{A}_{3}^{(k)} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{N_{k}}\sum_{(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}[s_{a}(\tilde{W}_{ti};\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})-s_{a}(W_{ti};\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})] \displaystyle=\frac{1}{N_{k}}\sum_{(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}(\tilde{Z}_{ti}-Z_{ti})(s_{a}(W_{ti}(1);\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})-s_{a}(W_{ti}(0);\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})) \displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{n_{t,k}}{N_{k}}\tilde{A}_{3,t}^{(k)}. $$

Here

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{A}_{3,t}^{(k)} \displaystyle:=\frac{1}{n_{t,k}}\sum_{i:(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}(\tilde{Z}_{ti}-Z_{ti})(s_{a}(W_{ti}(1);\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})-s_{a}(W_{ti}(0);\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})) $$

satisfies

$$ \displaystyle\|\tilde{A}_{3,t}^{(k)}\| \displaystyle\leqslant\frac{1}{n_{t,k}}\sum_{i:(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\bm{1}(Z_{ti}\neq\tilde{Z}_{ti})\cdot\|s_{a}(W_{ti}(1);\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})-s_{a}(W_{ti}(0);\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})\| \displaystyle\leqslant\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_{t,k}}\sum_{i:(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\|s_{a}(W_{ti}(1);\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})-s_{a}(W_{ti}(0);\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})\|^{2}} \displaystyle\phantom{=}\,\cdot\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_{t,k}}\sum_{i:(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\bm{1}(Z_{ti}\neq\tilde{Z}_{ti})} $$

by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. Recalling the $\sigma$ -algebra $\mathcal{S}_{t}^{X,(k)}$ in the definition of a CSBAE (Definition 4.1), we have

$$ \textnormal{Pr}(Z_{ti}\neq\tilde{Z}_{ti}\mid\mathcal{S}_{t}^{X,(k)})=|\hat{e}_{t}^{(k)}(X_{ti})-e_{t}(X_{ti})| $$

and so by (17)

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\biggl[\frac{1}{n_{t,k}}\sum_{i:(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\bm{1}(Z_{ti}\neq\tilde{Z}_{ti})\Bigm|\mathcal{S}_{t}^{X,(k)}\biggr] \displaystyle=\frac{1}{n_{t,k}}\sum_{i:(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}|\hat{e}_{t}^{(k)}(X_{ti})-e_{t}(X_{ti})| \displaystyle\leqslant\|\hat{e}_{t}^{(k)}-e_{t}\|_{2,P_{N,t}^{X,(k)}} \displaystyle=o_{p}(1). $$

Hence

$$ \sqrt{\frac{1}{n_{t,k}}\sum_{i:(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\bm{1}(Z_{ti}\neq\tilde{Z}_{ti})}=o_{p}(1) $$

by Lemma B.1. Next, for $z=0,1$ and $(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}$ , by Jensen’s inequality and (58) we have

$$ \displaystyle\left(\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|s_{a}(W_{ti}(z);\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})\|^{2}\bm{1}(\mathcal{E}_{N,k})\mid\mathcal{S}^{(-k)}\bigr]\right)^{q/2} \displaystyle\leqslant\sup_{(\nu,e)\in\mathcal{T}_{N}}(\mathbb{E}_{t}\bigl[\|s_{a}(W(z);\nu,e)\|^{2}\bigr])^{q/2} \displaystyle\leqslant\kappa_{t}^{-1}\sup_{(\nu,e)\in\mathcal{T}_{N}}\mathbb{E}_{0}[\|s_{a}(W(z);\nu,e)\|^{q}] \displaystyle\leqslant\kappa_{t}^{-1}C^{q} $$

by (25). By Markov’s inequality, for each batch $t=1,\ldots,T$ and fold $k=1,\ldots,K$ ,

$$ \sqrt{\frac{1}{n_{t,k}}\sum_{i:(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\|s_{a}(W_{ti}(z);\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})\|^{2}}=O_{p}(1) $$

holds for $z=0,1$ . Applying Minkowski’s inequality with the $L^{2}_{P_{N,t}^{X}}$ norm shows

$$ \sqrt{\frac{1}{n_{t,k}}\sum_{i:(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\|s_{a}(W_{ti}(1);\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})-s_{a}(W_{ti}(0);\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})\|^{2}}=O_{p}(1). $$

We conclude $\tilde{A}_{3,t}^{(k)}=o_{p}(1)$ , hence $\tilde{A}_{3}^{(k)}=o_{p}(1)$ and $\tilde{A}_{3}=o_{p}(1)$ as well. Now we recall

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}s_{a}(\tilde{W}_{ti};\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}s_{a}(\tilde{W}_{ti};\nu_{0},e_{0,N})+o_{p}(1)\text{\quad(by~\eqref{eq:A_1_tilde})} \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{0}[s_{a}(W;\nu_{0},e_{0})]+o_{p}(1)\text{\quad(by~\eqref{eq:oracle_s_a_lln_folds})}. $$

Then

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}s_{a}(W_{ti};\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}s_{a}(\tilde{W}_{ti};\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})-\tilde{A}_{3} \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{0}[s_{a}(W;\nu_{0},e_{0})]+o_{p}(1) $$

as well. Thus we have both

$$ \displaystyle\biggl(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}s_{a}(\tilde{W}_{ti};\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})\biggr)^{-1} \displaystyle=(\mathbb{E}_{0}[s_{a}(W;\nu_{0},e_{0})])^{-1}+o_{p}(1),\quad\text{and} \displaystyle\biggl(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}s_{a}(W_{ti};\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})\biggr)^{-1} \displaystyle=(\mathbb{E}_{0}[s_{a}(W;\nu_{0},e_{0})])^{-1}+o_{p}(1). $$

Subtracting these two equations gives $A_{3}=o_{p}(1)$ .

Next, equation (66) immediately provides $A_{4}=O_{p}(1)$ , while $B_{3}=B_{1}-B_{2}=O_{p}(1)$ as shown above. Thus it only remains to show that $B_{4}=o_{p}(1)$ . We write

$$ B_{4}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sqrt{\frac{N_{k}}{N}}\Bigl(B_{4}^{(k),1}+B_{4}^{(k),2}+B_{4}^{(k),3}\Bigr) $$

where

$$ \displaystyle B_{4}^{(k),1} \displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sqrt{\frac{n_{t,k}}{N_{k}}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n_{t,k}}}\sum_{i:(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}(\tilde{Z}_{ti}-Z_{ti})\bigl(s(W_{ti}(1);\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})-s(W_{ti}(0);\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})\bigr), \displaystyle B_{4}^{(k),2} \displaystyle=N_{k}^{1/2}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{n_{t,k}}{N_{k}}\frac{1}{n_{t,k}}\sum_{i:(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}(\tilde{Z}_{ti}-Z_{ti})\mathbb{E}[s(W_{ti}(1);\theta_{0},\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})-s(W_{ti}(1);\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})\mid\mathcal{S}^{(-k)},X_{ti}] \displaystyle\phantom{=}\,-N_{k}^{1/2}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{n_{t,k}}{N_{k}}\frac{1}{n_{t,k}}\sum_{i:(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}(\tilde{Z}_{ti}-Z_{ti})\mathbb{E}[s(W_{ti}(0);\theta_{0},\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})-s(W_{ti}(0);\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})\mid\mathcal{S}^{(-k)},X_{ti}] \displaystyle B_{4}^{(k),3} \displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sqrt{\frac{n_{t,k}}{N_{k}}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n_{t,k}}}\sum_{i:(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}(\tilde{Z}_{ti}-Z_{ti})\bigl(s(W_{ti}(1);\theta_{0},\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})-s(W_{ti}(0);\theta_{0},\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})\bigr) \displaystyle-B_{4}^{(k),1}-B_{4}^{(k),2}. $$

It suffices to prove that for each $k=1,\ldots,K$ , the terms $B_{4}^{(k),1}$ , $B_{4}^{(k),2}$ , and $B_{4}^{(k),3}$ are all asymptotically negligible. First, we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E} \displaystyle\left[(\tilde{Z}_{ti}-Z_{ti})(s(W_{ti}(1);\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})-s(W_{ti}(0);\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N}))\mid\mathcal{S}_{t}^{X,(k)}\right] \displaystyle=(e_{t}(X_{ti})-\hat{e}_{t}^{(k)}(X_{ti}))\mathbb{E}[s(W_{ti}(1);\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})-s(W_{ti}(0);\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})\mid\mathcal{S}_{t}^{X,(k)}] \displaystyle=(e_{t}(X_{ti})-\hat{e}_{t}^{(k)}(X_{ti}))\mathbb{E}[s(W_{ti}(1);\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})-s(W_{ti}(0);\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})\mid X_{ti}] \displaystyle=0. $$

We briefly justify each of the equalities in the preceding display:

- • The first equality holds because given $\mathcal{S}_{t}^{X,(k)}$ , the only randomness in $(Z_{ti},\tilde{Z}_{ti})$ for any $(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}$ is in $U_{ti}$ , which is independent of $(W_{ti}(0),W_{ti}(1))$ , $\mathcal{S}^{(-k)}$ , and $\mathcal{S}_{t}^{X,(k)}$ ; hence

$$ \begin{split}(Z_{ti},\tilde{Z}_{ti})&\perp\!\!\!\perp(W_{ti}(0),W_{ti}(1))\mid\mathcal{S}_{t}^{X,(k)}\quad\text{ and }\\ (Z_{ti},\tilde{Z}_{ti})&\perp\!\!\!\perp(W_{ti}(0),W_{ti}(1))\mid\mathcal{S}^{(-k)},\mathcal{S}_{t}^{X,(k)}.\end{split} $$

(67)

- • The second equality holds because the vectors $\{S_{ti},1\leqslant t\leqslant T,1\leqslant i\leqslant N_{t}\}$ are mutually independent (Assumption A.1).

- • The third equality follows directly from (19).

For batches $t=1,\ldots,T$ , the vectors $\{(\tilde{Z}_{ti},Z_{ti},W_{ti}(1),W_{ti}(0)),1\leqslant i\leqslant N_{t}\}$ are conditionally independent given $\mathcal{S}_{t}^{X,(k)}$ . Defining

$$ \mathcal{I}_{4,t}^{(k)}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n_{t,k}}}\sum_{i:(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}(\tilde{Z}_{ti}-Z_{ti})(s(W_{ti}(1);\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})-s(W_{ti}(0);\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})) $$

and letting $p$ be the real solution to $p^{-1}+2q^{-1}=1$ , we apply Lemma B.7 and Holder’s inequality to get

$$ \displaystyle\phantom{=}\,\mathbb{E}[\|\mathcal{I}_{4,t}^{(k)}\|^{2}\mid\mathcal{S}_{t}^{X,(k)}] \displaystyle=\frac{1}{n_{t,k}}\sum_{i:(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\mathbb{E}[(\tilde{Z}_{ti}-Z_{ti})^{2}\|s(W_{ti}(1);\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})-s(W_{ti}(0);\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})\|^{2}\mid\mathcal{S}_{t}^{X,(k)}] \displaystyle=\frac{1}{n_{t,k}}\sum_{i:(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}|\hat{e}_{t}^{(k)}(X_{ti})-e_{t}(X_{ti})|\mathbb{E}\big[\|s(W_{ti}(1);\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})-s(W_{ti}(0);\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})\|^{2}\mid\mathcal{S}_{t}^{X,(k)}\big] $$

using the conditional independence in (67) once again. Then

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\|\mathcal{I}_{4,t}^{(k)}\|^{2}\mid\mathcal{S}_{t}^{X,(k)}] \displaystyle\leqslant\biggl(\frac{1}{n_{t,k}}\sum_{i:(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}|\hat{e}_{t}^{(k)}(X_{ti})-e_{t}(X_{ti})|^{p}\biggr)^{1/p} \displaystyle\cdot\biggl(\frac{1}{n_{t,k}}\sum_{i:(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\left(\mathbb{E}[\|s(W_{ti}(1);\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})-s(W_{ti}(0);\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})\|^{2}\mid\mathcal{S}_{t}^{X,(k)}]\right)^{q/2}\biggr)^{2/q}. $$

We can assume WLOG that $q<4$ so that $p>2$ . Then with $0\leqslant|\hat{e}_{t}^{(j)}(x)-e_{t}(x)|\leqslant 1$ for all $x$ , we conclude

$$ \frac{1}{n_{t,k}}\sum_{i:(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\big|\hat{e}_{t}^{(k)}(X_{ti})-e_{t}(X_{ti})\big|^{p}\leqslant\frac{1}{n_{t,k}}\sum_{i:(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\bigl(\hat{e}_{t}^{(k)}(X_{ti})-e_{t}(X_{ti})\bigr)^{2}=o_{p}(1) $$

by (17). Next, from Jensen’s inequality

$$ \displaystyle\phantom{=}\,\frac{1}{n_{t,k}}\sum_{i:(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\left(\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|s(W_{ti}(1);\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})-s(W_{ti}(0);\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})\|^{2}\mid\mathcal{S}_{t}^{X,(k)}\bigr]\right)^{q/2} \displaystyle\leqslant\frac{1}{n_{t,k}}\sum_{i:(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\mathbb{E}\left[\|s(W_{ti}(1);\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})-s(W_{ti}(0);\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})\|^{q}\mid\mathcal{S}_{t}^{X,(k)}\right] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{t}\bigl[\|s(W(1);\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})-s(W(0);\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})\|^{q}\mid X\bigr]. $$

But by Minkowski’s inequality, (58), and (25), we see

$$ \displaystyle\phantom{=}\ \bigl(\mathbb{E}_{t}[\|s(W(1);\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})-s(W(0);\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})\|^{q}]\bigr)^{1/q} \displaystyle\leqslant\bigl(\mathbb{E}_{t}[\|s(W(1);\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})\|^{q}])^{1/q}+(\mathbb{E}_{t}[\|s(W(0);\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})\|^{q}]\bigr)^{1/q} \displaystyle\leqslant\kappa_{t}^{-1/q}[(\mathbb{E}_{0}[\|s(W(1);\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})\|^{q}])^{1/q}+(\mathbb{E}_{0}[\|s(W(0);\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})\|^{q}])^{1/q}] \displaystyle\leqslant 2C\kappa_{t}^{-1/q}. $$

We conclude by Markov’s inequality that

$$ \frac{1}{n_{t,k}}\sum_{i:(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\left(\mathbb{E}[\|s(W_{ti}(1);\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})-s(W_{ti}(0);\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})\|^{2}\mid\mathcal{S}_{t}^{X,(k)}]\right)^{q/2}=O_{p}(1). $$

Along with (68) we can conclude that $\mathcal{I}_{4,t}^{(k)}=o_{p}(1)$ by Lemma B.1. Then also

$$ B_{4}^{(k),1}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sqrt{\frac{n_{t,k}}{N_{k}}}\mathcal{I}_{4,t}^{(k)}=o_{p}(1) $$

Next, for $z=0,1$ define

$$ B_{4}^{(k),2}(z)=N_{k}^{1/2}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{n_{t,k}}{N_{k}}\frac{1}{n_{t,k}}\sum_{i:(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}(\tilde{Z}_{ti}-Z_{ti})\mathbb{E}\bigl[s(W_{ti}(z);\theta_{0},\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})-s(W_{ti}(z);\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})\mid\mathcal{S}^{(-k)},X_{ti}\bigr] $$

so that $B_{4}^{(k),2}=B_{4}^{(k),2}(1)-B_{4}^{(k),2}(0)$ . Then by the triangle inequality $\|B_{4}^{(k),2}(z)\|$ is no larger than

$$ N_{k}^{1/2}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{n_{t,k}}{N_{k}}\frac{1}{n_{t,k}}\sum_{i:(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}|\tilde{Z}_{ti}-Z_{ti}|\cdot\|\mathbb{E}[s(W_{ti}(z);\theta_{0},\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})-s(W_{ti}(z);\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})\mid\mathcal{S}^{(-k)},X_{ti}]\|. $$

Taking conditional expectations of both sides yields

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|B_{4}^{(k),2}(z)\|\mid\mathcal{S}^{(-k)},\mathcal{S}_{t}^{X,(k)}\bigr] \displaystyle\leqslant N_{k}^{1/2}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{n_{t,k}}{N_{k}}\frac{1}{n_{t,k}}\sum_{i:(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\bigl|\hat{e}_{t}^{(k)}(X_{ti})-e_{t}(X_{ti})\bigr| \displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\times\bigl\|\mathbb{E}[s(W_{ti}(z);\theta_{0},\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})-s(W_{ti}(z);\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})\mid\mathcal{S}^{(-k)},X_{ti}]\bigr\| \displaystyle\leqslant N_{k}^{1/2}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\frac{n_{t,k}}{N_{k}}\cdot S_{t}^{(-k)}(z)\cdot\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_{t,k}}\sum_{i:(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}(\hat{e}_{t}^{(k)}(X_{ti})-e_{t}(X_{ti}))^{2}} $$

by Cauchy-Schwarz. We have by (17) that

$$ \sqrt{\frac{1}{n_{t,k}}\sum_{i:(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}(\hat{e}_{t}^{(k)}(X_{ti})-e_{t}(X_{ti}))^{2}}=O_{p}(N^{-1/4}), $$

Then by equation (26), we get $B_{4}^{(k),2}(z)=o_{p}(1)$ for $z=0,1$ , and so $B_{4}^{(k),2}=o_{p}(1)$ as well.

Finally, we write

$$ B_{4}^{(k),3}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sqrt{\frac{n_{t,k}}{N_{k}}}B_{4,t}^{(k),3} $$

for

$$ \displaystyle B_{4,t}^{(k),3} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n_{t,k}}}\sum_{i:(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}(\tilde{Z}_{ti}-Z_{ti})\Delta_{ti}^{(-k)}, \displaystyle\Delta_{ti}^{(-k)} \displaystyle=(s(W_{ti}(1);\theta_{0},\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})-s(W_{ti}(0);\theta_{0},\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})) \displaystyle\phantom{=}\ -(s(W_{ti}(1);\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})-s(W_{ti}(0);\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})) \displaystyle\phantom{=}\ -\mathbb{E}[s(W_{ti}(1);\theta_{0},\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})-s(W_{ti}(0);\theta_{0},\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})\mid\mathcal{S}^{(-k)},X_{ti}] \displaystyle\phantom{=}\ -\mathbb{E}[s(W_{ti}(1);\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0})-s(W_{ti}(0);\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0})\mid\mathcal{S}^{(-k)},X_{ti}]. $$

For each $(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}$ , we have

$$ (W_{ti}(0),W_{ti}(1))\perp\!\!\!\perp\mathcal{S}_{t}^{X,(k)}\mid\mathcal{S}^{(-k)},X_{ti} $$

since given $\mathcal{S}^{(-k)}$ and $X_{ti}$ , the only remaining randomness in $(W_{ti}(0),W_{ti}(1))$ is in the potential outcomes $(Y_{ti}(0),Y_{ti}(1))$ . These are independent of both $\mathcal{S}^{(-k)}$ and $\{X_{tj}\mid j\neq i\}$ , the covariates of the other subjects in batch $t$ . Thus $\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{ti}^{(-k)}\mid\mathcal{S}^{(-k)},\mathcal{S}_{t}^{X,(k)}]=0$ , and by (67) we have

$$ \mathbb{E}[B_{4,t}^{(k),3}\mid\mathcal{S}^{(-k)},\mathcal{S}_{t}^{X,(k)}]=0. $$

Then applying Lemma B.7 and equations (67) and (65),

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\|B_{4,t}^{(k),3}\|^{2}\mid\mathcal{S}^{(-k)},\mathcal{S}_{t}^{X,(k)}] \displaystyle=\frac{1}{n_{t,k}}\sum_{i:(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\mathbb{E}[(\tilde{Z}_{ti}-Z_{ti})^{2}\|\Delta_{ti}^{(-k)}\|^{2}\mid\mathcal{S}^{(-k)},\mathcal{S}_{t}^{X,(k)}] \displaystyle=\frac{1}{n_{t,k}}\sum_{i:(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}|\hat{e}_{t}^{(k)}(X_{ti})-e_{t}(X_{ti})|\mathbb{E}[\|\Delta_{ti}^{(-k)}\|^{2}\mid\mathcal{S}^{(-k)},\mathcal{S}_{t}^{X,(k)}] \displaystyle\leqslant\frac{1}{n_{t,k}}\sum_{i:(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}|\hat{e}_{t}^{(k)}(X_{ti})-e_{t}(X_{ti})|\mathbb{E}[\|\tilde{\Delta}_{ti}^{(-k)}\|^{2}\mid\mathcal{S}^{(-k)},\mathcal{S}_{t}^{X,(k)}] \displaystyle\leqslant\biggl(\frac{1}{n_{t,k}}\sum_{i:(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}|\hat{e}_{t}^{(k)}(X_{ti})-e_{t}(X_{ti})|^{p}\biggr)^{1/p}\Gamma_{t}^{(k)} $$

by Holder’s inequality, where $p$ is as above for

$$ \displaystyle\Gamma_{t}^{(k)} \displaystyle=\biggl(\frac{1}{n_{t,k}}\sum_{i:(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}(\mathbb{E}[\|\tilde{\Delta}_{ti}^{(-k)}\|^{2}\mid\mathcal{S}^{(-k)},\mathcal{S}_{t}^{X,(k)}])^{q/2}\biggr)^{2/q},\quad\text{with} \displaystyle\tilde{\Delta}_{ti}^{(-k)} \displaystyle=(s(W_{ti}(1);\theta_{0},\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})-s(W_{ti}(0);\theta_{0},\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})) \displaystyle\phantom{=}\ -(s(W_{ti}(1);\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})-s(W_{ti}(0);\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})). $$

By Jensen’s inequality

$$ (\Gamma_{t}^{(k)})^{q/2}\leqslant\frac{1}{n_{t,k}}\sum_{i:(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|\tilde{\Delta}_{ti}^{(-k)}\|^{q}\mid\mathcal{S}^{(-k)},\mathcal{S}_{t}^{X,(k)}\bigr]. $$

Taking conditional expectations, we get

$$ \mathbb{E}\bigl[(\Gamma_{t}^{(k)})^{q/2}\mid\mathcal{S}^{(-k)}\bigr]=\frac{1}{n_{t,k}}\sum_{i:(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|\tilde{\Delta}_{ti}^{(-k)}\|^{q}\mid\mathcal{S}^{(-k)}\bigr]. $$

Then

$$ \displaystyle\phantom{=}\ \left(\mathbb{E}[(\Gamma_{t}^{(k)})^{q/2}\mid\mathcal{S}^{(-k)}]\right)^{1/q}\bm{1}(\mathcal{E}_{N,k}) \displaystyle\leqslant\sup_{(\nu,e)\in\mathcal{T}_{N}}\left(\mathbb{E}_{t}[\|(s(W(1);\theta_{0},\nu,e)-s(W(0);\theta_{0},\nu,e))-(s(W(1);\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})-s(W(0);\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N}))\|^{q}]\right)^{1/q} \displaystyle\leqslant\sup_{(\nu,e)\in\mathcal{T}_{N}}\sum_{z\in\{0,1\}}(\mathbb{E}_{t}[\|s(W(z);\theta_{0},\nu,e)\|^{q}])^{1/q}+(\mathbb{E}_{t}[\|s(W(z);\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0,N})\|^{q}])^{1/q} \displaystyle\leqslant 4C\kappa_{t}^{-1/q} $$

by (58) and moment boundedness. We conclude that $\mathbb{E}[(\Gamma_{t}^{(k)})^{q/2}\mid\mathcal{S}^{(-k)}]\bm{1}(\mathcal{E}_{N,k})$ is uniformly bounded. Recalling that $\textnormal{Pr}(\mathcal{E}_{N,k})\rightarrow 1$ , Markov’s inequality then ensures $\Gamma_{t}^{(k)}=O_{p}(1)$ . In view of (68), we then have $\mathbb{E}[\|B_{4,t}^{(k),3}\|^{2}\mid\mathcal{S}^{(-k)},\mathcal{S}_{t}^{X,(k)}]=o_{p}(1)$ . This implies $B_{4,t}^{(k),3}=o_{p}(1)$ by Lemma B.1, and hence $B_{4}^{(k),3}=o_{p}(1)$ . This establishes that $\hat{\theta}=\tilde{\theta}+o_{p}(N^{-1/2})$ and completes the proof.

### C.6 Proof of Corollary 4.1: CLT for feasible $\hat{\theta}_{\textnormal{AIPW}}$ in a CSBAE

Corollary 4.1, which shows the feasible estimator $\hat{\theta}_{\textnormal{AIPW}}$ satisfies a CLT for estimating $\hat{\theta}_{0,\textnormal{ATE}}$ in a CSBAE, holds under the numbered generalizations at the end of Appendix A, subject to the additional requirement that the mean functions are stationary, as in our generalization of Corollary 3.1 to nonstationary batches. We prove this more general result. The proof of our generalized Corollary 3.1 shows that Assumption A.2 is satisfied under the moment bounds in Assumption 3.1 with $\theta_{0}=\theta_{0,\textnormal{ATE}}$ , $s(\cdot)=s_{\textnormal{AIPW}}(\cdot)$ , $\nu_{0}=\nu_{0,\textnormal{AIPW}}\in\mathcal{N}=\mathcal{N}_{\textnormal{AIPW}}$ , and any $\gamma\in(0,1/2)$ . It remains to show that the further conditions of Assumption 4.1, namely (a), (b), (c) and equations (20) through (25), are satisfied. Then Corollary 4.1 follows by Theorem 4.1.

Invertibility of $\mathbb{E}_{0}[\theta_{0}(W;\nu_{0},e_{0})]$ and existence of $\mathbb{E}_{0}[s(W;\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0})^{2}]$ follow from Assumption 3.1, as shown in the proof of Corollary 3.1.

Fix $\lambda\in[0,1]$ and $(\nu,e)\in\mathcal{T}=\mathcal{N}\times\mathcal{F}_{\gamma}$ , where $\nu(\cdot)=(m(0,\cdot),m(1,\cdot))$ . Consider

$$ \displaystyle f_{N}(\lambda) \displaystyle:=s(W;\theta_{0},\nu_{0}+\lambda(\nu-\nu_{0}),e_{0,N}+\lambda(e-e_{0,N})) \displaystyle=m_{\lambda}(1,X)-m_{\lambda}(0,X)+\frac{Z(Y-m_{\lambda}(1,X))}{e_{\lambda,N}(x)}-\frac{(1-Z)(Y-m_{\lambda}(0,X))}{1-e_{\lambda,N}(x)} $$

where $m_{\lambda}(z,x):=m_{0}(z,x)+\lambda(m(z,x)-m_{0}(z,x))$ and $e_{\lambda,N}(x):=e_{0,N}(x)+\lambda(e(x)-e_{0,N}(x))$ . Taking two derivatives with respect to $\lambda$ we get

$$ \displaystyle f_{N}^{\prime}(\lambda) \displaystyle=(m(1,X)-m_{0}(1,X))-(m(0,X)-m_{0}(0,X)) \displaystyle\phantom{=}\ +Z\left(\frac{m_{0}(1,X)-m(1,X)}{e_{\lambda,N}(X)}-\frac{(Y-m_{\lambda}(1,X))(e(X)-e_{0,N}(X))}{e_{\lambda,N}(X)^{2}}\right) \displaystyle\phantom{=}\ -(1-Z)\left(\frac{m_{0}(0,X)-m(0,X)}{1-e_{\lambda,N}(X)}-\frac{(Y-m_{\lambda}(0,X))(e_{0,N}(X)-e(X))}{(1-e_{\lambda,N}(X))^{2}}\right),\quad\text{and} \displaystyle f_{N}^{\prime\prime}(\lambda) \displaystyle=2Z\left(\frac{(Y-m_{\lambda}(1,X))(e(X)-e_{0,N}(X))^{2}}{e_{\lambda,N}(X)^{3}}-\frac{(m_{0}(1,X)-m(1,X))(e(X)-e_{0,N}(X))}{e_{\lambda,N}(X)^{2}}\right) \displaystyle\phantom{=}\ +2(1-Z)\left(\frac{m_{0}(0,X)-m(0,X)(e_{0,N}(X)-e(X))}{(1-e_{\lambda,N}(X))^{2}}-\frac{(Y-m_{\lambda}(0,X))(e_{0,N}(X)-e(X))^{2}}{(1-e_{\lambda,N}(X))^{3}}\right). $$

We now show that $f_{N}(\cdot)$ , $f_{N}^{\prime}(\cdot)$ , and $f_{N}^{\prime\prime}(\cdot)$ are upper bounded by an integrable random variable on an open interval containing $[0,1]$ , so that by the Leibniz rule, we can swap both first and second derivatives with expectations to conclude the function $\lambda\mapsto\mathbb{E}_{0,N}[s(W;\theta_{0},\nu_{0}+\lambda(\nu-\nu_{0}),e_{0,N}+\lambda(e-e_{0,N}))]$ has second derivative $\mathbb{E}_{0,N}[f_{N}^{\prime\prime}(\lambda)]$ for $\lambda\in[0,1]$ . Note $e_{\lambda,N}\in\mathcal{F}_{\gamma}$ . Then by repeated application of the triangle inequality, we see that for sufficiently small $\epsilon>0$ , we must have

$$ \displaystyle\sup_{\lambda\in(-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)}|f_{N}(\lambda)| \displaystyle\leqslant 2(|m(1,X)|+|m_{0}(1,X)|+|m(0,X)|+|m_{0}(0,X)|) \displaystyle+2\gamma^{-1}(|Y(1)|+|Y(0)|+|m(1,X)|+|m_{0}(1,X)|+|m(0,X)|+|m_{0}(0,X)|) \displaystyle\sup_{\lambda\in(-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)}|f_{N}^{\prime}(\lambda)| \displaystyle\leqslant 2(|m(1,X)|+|m_{0}(1,X)|+|m(0,X)|+|m_{0}(0,X)|) \displaystyle+2\gamma^{-2}(|Y(1)|+|Y(0)|+|m(1,X)|+|m_{0}(1,X)|+|m(0,X)|+|m_{0}(0,X)|) \displaystyle\sup_{\lambda\in(-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)}|f_{N}^{\prime\prime}(\lambda)| \displaystyle\leqslant 2\gamma^{-3}(|Y(1)|+|Y(0)|+|m(1,X)|+|m_{0}(1,X)|+|m(0,X)|+|m_{0}(0,X)|). $$

The right-hand sides above are clearly integrable under $P_{0,N}$ . Hence, the mapping $\lambda\mapsto\mathbb{E}_{0,N}[s(W;\theta_{0},\nu_{0}+\lambda(\nu-\nu_{0}),e_{0,N}+\lambda(e-e_{0,N}))]$ is indeed twice differentiable with second derivative $\mathbb{E}_{0,N}[f_{N}^{\prime\prime}(\lambda)]$ for $\lambda\in[0,1]$ . This second derivative is continuous for such $\lambda$ by continuity of $f_{N}^{\prime\prime}(\cdot)$ and dominated convergence.

Fix $e\in\mathcal{F}_{\gamma}$ . By stationarity of the mean functions $m_{0}(z,\cdot)$ , $z=0,1$ , for each $t=1,\ldots,T$ , $i=1,\ldots,N_{t}$ we have (letting $\nu_{0}=\nu_{0,\textnormal{AIPW}}$ for brevity)

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[s(W_{ti}(1);\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e)\mid X_{ti}] \displaystyle=m_{0}(1,X)-m_{0}(0,X)-\theta_{0}+\mathbb{E}_{t}\left[\frac{Y(1)-m_{0}(1,X)}{e(X)}\Bigm|X\right] \displaystyle=m_{0}(1,X)-m_{0}(0,X)-\theta_{0}+(e(X))^{-1}\mathbb{E}_{t}[Y(1)-m_{0}(1,X)\!\mid\!X] \displaystyle=m_{0}(1,X)-m_{0}(0,X)-\theta_{0} $$

and similarly

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[s(W_{ti}(0);\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e)\mid X_{ti}] \displaystyle=m_{0}(1,X)-m_{0}(0,X)-\theta_{0}-\mathbb{E}_{t}\left[\frac{Y(0)-m_{0}(0,X)}{1-e(X)}\Bigm|X\right] \displaystyle=m_{0}(1,X)-m_{0}(0,X)-\theta_{0}-(1-e(X))^{-1}\mathbb{E}_{t}[Y(0)-m_{0}(0,X)\!\mid\!X] \displaystyle=m_{0}(1,X)-m_{0}(0,X)-\theta_{0}. $$

Subtracting shows (19).

It remains to show that the out-of-fold estimators $(\hat{m}^{(-k)}(0,\cdot),\hat{m}^{(-k)}(1,\cdot),\hat{e}^{(-k)})$ lie in some set $\mathcal{T}_{N}$ with high probability for all sufficiently large $N$ , where this set $\mathcal{T}_{N}$ satisfies equations (20) through (25). To construct this $\mathcal{T}_{N}$ , we see that by the rate conditions on the nuisance estimators along with equation (54), there exists a sequence $\tilde{\delta}_{N}\downarrow 0$ so that $\|e_{0,N}-e_{0}\|_{2,P_{0}^{X}}\leqslant\tilde{\delta}_{N}$ for all $N$ . Furthermore, with probability approaching 1 as $N\rightarrow\infty$ , these four conditions hold for $z=0,1$ and all folds $k=1,\ldots,K$ :

$$ \displaystyle\|\hat{m}^{(-k)}(z,\cdot)-m_{0}(z,\cdot)\|_{2,P_{0}^{X}}+\|\hat{e}^{(-k)}-e_{0,N}\|_{2,P_{0}^{X}} \displaystyle\leqslant\tilde{\delta}_{N}, \displaystyle\|\hat{m}^{(-k)}(z,\cdot)\|_{2,P_{0}^{X}}\times\|\hat{e}^{(-k)}-e_{0,N}\|_{2,P_{0}^{X}} \displaystyle\leqslant N^{-1/2}\tilde{\delta}_{N}, \displaystyle\|\hat{m}^{(-k)}(z,\cdot)-m_{0}(z,\cdot)\|_{q,P_{0}^{X}} \displaystyle\leqslant C, \displaystyle\hat{e}^{(-k)}(\cdot) \displaystyle\in\mathcal{F}_{\gamma}. $$

We then define $\mathcal{T}_{N}$ be the set of functions $(m(0,\cdot),m(1,\cdot),e(\cdot))$ in $\mathcal{T}=\mathcal{N}_{\textnormal{AIPW}}\times\mathcal{E}$ obeying these conditions:

$$ \displaystyle\|m(z,\cdot)-m_{0}(z,\cdot)\|_{2,P_{0}^{X}}+\|e-e_{0,N}\|_{2,P_{0}^{X}} \displaystyle\leqslant\tilde{\delta}_{N}, \displaystyle\|m(z,\cdot)\|_{2,P_{0}^{X}}\times\|e-e_{0,N}\|_{2,P_{0}^{X}} \displaystyle\leqslant N^{-1/2}\tilde{\delta}_{N}, \displaystyle\|m(z,\cdot)-m_{0}(z,\cdot)\|_{q,P_{0}^{X}} \displaystyle\leqslant C, \displaystyle e(\cdot) \displaystyle\in\mathcal{F}_{\gamma}. $$

By construction, for all $k=1,\ldots,K$ we have $\textnormal{Pr}((\hat{m}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})\in\mathcal{T}_{N})\rightarrow 1$ as $N\rightarrow\infty$ .

For the remainder of the proof, we take $N$ large enough so that $1/2\leqslant{\mathrm{d}P_{0,N}^{X}}/{\mathrm{d}P_{0}^{X}}\leqslant 2$ . For such $N$ , $\|f\|_{2,P_{0,N}^{X}}\leqslant\sqrt{2}\|f\|_{2,P_{0}^{X}}$ holds for all $f\in L^{2}(P_{0}^{X})$ . We will show equations (20) through (23) hold for a sequence $\delta_{N}$ that is some constant multiple of $\tilde{\delta}_{N}$ .

Fix $(\nu,e)\in\mathcal{T}_{N}$ . By the calculations and notation above in the proof of condition (b) and interchanging differentiation with expectation, we can verify using unconfoundedness that

$$ \frac{\partial}{\partial\lambda}\mathbb{E}_{0,N}[s(W;\theta_{0},\nu_{0},\lambda(\nu-\nu_{0}),e_{0,N}+\lambda(e-e_{0,N})]\Big|_{\lambda=0}=\mathbb{E}_{0,N}[f_{N}^{\prime}(0)]=0 $$

so the left-hand side of the Neyman orthogonality condition (20) is 0. The full calculation is shown in the proof of Theorem 5.1 of Chernozhukov et al., (2018).

Once again, we fix $(\nu,e)\in\mathcal{T}_{N}$ and recall the calculations and notations in the proof of condition (b) above. We see that

$$ \displaystyle\Big|\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial\lambda^{2}}\mathbb{E}_{0,N}[s(W;\theta_{0},\nu_{0},\lambda(\nu-\nu_{0}),e_{0,N}+\lambda(e-e_{0,N})]\Big|=\bigl|\mathbb{E}_{0,N}[f_{N}^{\prime\prime}(\lambda)]\bigr| $$

and hence

$$ \displaystyle\bigl|\mathbb{E}_{0,N}[f_{N}^{\prime\prime}(\lambda)]\bigr| \displaystyle\leqslant\frac{2}{\gamma^{3}}\Bigl(\bigl|\mathbb{E}_{0,N}[(Y(1)-m_{\lambda}(1,X))(e(X)-e_{0,N}(X))^{2}]\bigr| \displaystyle\phantom{=}\ +\bigl|\mathbb{E}_{0,N}[(Y(0)-m_{\lambda}(0,X))(e_{0,N}(X)-e(X))^{2}]\bigr|\Bigr) \displaystyle\phantom{=}\ +\frac{2}{\gamma^{2}}\Bigl(|\mathbb{E}_{0,N}[(m_{0}(1,X)-m(1,X))(e(X)-e_{0}(X))]| \displaystyle\phantom{=}\ +\bigl|\mathbb{E}_{0,N}[(m_{0}(0,X)-m(0,X))(e(X)-e_{0}(X))]\bigr|\Bigr). $$

### C.7 Proof of Corollary 4.2: CLT for feasible $\hat{\theta}_{\textnormal{EPL}}$ in a CSBAE

Corollary 4.2, which shows the feasible estimator $\hat{\theta}_{\textnormal{EPL}}$ satisfies a CLT for estimating $\theta_{0,\textnormal{PL}}$ in a CSBAE, holds under the numbered generalizations at the end of Appendix A, subject to the additional requirement that the mean and variance functions are stationary across batches, as in Appendix C.3. We prove this more general result using the same structure as the proof of Corollary 4.1 in Appendix C.6.

The proof of Corollary 3.2 in Appendix C.3 shows that Assumption A.2 is satisfied with $\theta_{0}=\theta_{0,\textnormal{PL}}$ , $s(\cdot)=s(\cdot)_{\textnormal{EPL}}$ , $\nu_{0}=\nu_{0,\textnormal{EPL}}\in\mathcal{N}=\mathcal{N}_{\textnormal{EPL}}$ , and $\gamma=0$ . Then it suffices to show the remaining conditions of Assumption 4.1 to complete the proof, in view of Theorem 4.1. Throughout the remainder of this proof we let $C_{0}$ be a generic positive finite constant; possibly depending on $c$ and $C$ in Assumption 3.2; different appearances of $C_{0}$ may correspond to different constants.

Invertibility of $\mathbb{E}_{0}[s_{a}(W;\nu_{0},e_{0})]$ and existence of $\mathbb{E}_{0}[\|s(W;\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0})\|^{2}]$ follow from Assumption 3.2, as shown in the proof of Corollary 3.2.

Fix $(\nu,e)\in\mathcal{T}$ . Recall that the weight function in our estimator $\hat{\theta}_{\textnormal{EPL}}$ is $w(X,\nu,e)=(v(0,x)e(x)+v(1,x)(1-e(x)))^{-1}$ . We compute

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{0,N} \displaystyle[s(W;\theta_{0},\nu_{0}+\lambda(\nu-\nu_{0}),e_{0,N}+\lambda(e-e_{0,N}))] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{0,N}[w(X;\nu_{\lambda},e_{\lambda,N})(Z-e_{\lambda,N}(X))(Y-m_{\lambda}(0,X)-Z\psi(X)^{\top}\theta_{0})\psi(X)] \displaystyle=\lambda\mathbb{E}_{0,N}[w(X;\nu_{\lambda},e_{\lambda,N})(Z-e_{\lambda,N}(X))(m_{0}(0,X)-m(0,X))\psi(X)] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{0,N}[f_{N}(\lambda)] $$

where the last two equalities follow by conditioning on $(X,Z)$ then just $X$ , and we have defined

$$ \displaystyle\nu_{\lambda}(\cdot) \displaystyle=\nu_{0}(\cdot)+\lambda(\nu(\cdot)-\nu_{0}(\cdot)), \displaystyle e_{\lambda,N}(\cdot) \displaystyle=e_{0,N}(\cdot)+\lambda(e(\cdot)-e_{0,N}(\cdot))\quad\text{and} \displaystyle f_{N}(\lambda) \displaystyle=\lambda^{2}w(X;\nu_{\lambda},e_{\lambda,N})(e_{0,N}(X)-e(X))(m_{0}(0,X)-m(0,X))\psi(X) \displaystyle=\lambda^{2}w(X;\nu_{\lambda},e_{\lambda,N})g_{N}(X) $$

for $g_{N}(X)=(e_{0,N}(X)-e(X))(m_{0}(0,X)-m(0,X))\psi(X)$ . We compute

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\partial}{\partial\lambda}w(X;\nu_{\lambda},e_{\lambda,N}) \displaystyle=-w^{2}(X;\nu_{\lambda},e_{\lambda,N})\Delta_{N}(\lambda,X) \displaystyle\frac{\partial}{\partial\lambda}w^{2}(X;\nu_{\lambda},e_{\lambda,N}) \displaystyle=-2w^{3}(X;\nu_{\lambda},e_{\lambda,N})\Delta_{N}(\lambda,X) $$

where

$$ \displaystyle\Delta_{N}(\lambda,X) \displaystyle=\frac{\partial}{\partial\lambda}\bigl(v_{\lambda}(0,X)e_{\lambda,N}(X)+v_{\lambda}(1,X)(1-e_{\lambda,N}(X))\bigr) \displaystyle=(1-e_{\lambda}(X))(v(1,X)-v_{0}(1,X))+e_{\lambda}(X)(v(0,X)-v_{0}(0,X))\quad\text{and} \displaystyle\phantom{=}\ +(e(X)-e_{0,N}(X))(v_{\lambda}(0,X)-v_{\lambda}(1,X)) $$

Then

$$ \displaystyle f_{N}^{\prime}(\lambda) \displaystyle=(-\lambda^{2}\Delta_{N}(\lambda,X)w^{2}(X;\nu_{\lambda},e_{\lambda,N})+2\lambda w(X;\nu_{\lambda},e_{\lambda,N}))g_{N}(X) \displaystyle f_{N}^{\prime\prime}(\lambda) \displaystyle=(2\lambda^{2}(\Delta_{N}(\lambda,X))^{2}w^{3}(X;\nu_{\lambda},e_{\lambda,N})-\lambda^{2}\Delta_{N}^{(2)}(\lambda,X)w^{2}(X;\nu_{\lambda},e_{\lambda,N}))g_{N}(X) \displaystyle+(2w(X;\nu_{\lambda},e_{\lambda,N})-4\lambda\Delta_{N}(\lambda,X)w^{2}(X;\nu_{\lambda},e_{\lambda,N}))g_{N}(X) $$

where

$$ \displaystyle\Delta_{N}^{(2)}(\lambda,X) \displaystyle=\frac{\partial}{\partial\lambda}\Delta_{N}(\lambda,X) \displaystyle=2(e(X)-e_{0,N}(X))(v(0,X)-v_{0}(0,X)+v_{0}(1,X)-v(1,X)) $$

We conclude that for sufficiently small $\epsilon>0$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\sup_{\lambda\in(-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)}|\Delta_{N}(\lambda,X)| \displaystyle\leqslant\sup_{\lambda\in(-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)}|1-e_{\lambda}(X))||v(1,X)-v_{0}(1,X)|+|e_{\lambda}(X)||v(0,X)-v_{0}(0,X)| \displaystyle\phantom{=}\ +\sup_{\lambda\in(-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)}|e(X)-e_{0,N}(X)||v_{\lambda}(0,X)-v_{\lambda}(1,X)| \displaystyle\leqslant C_{0}\quad\text{and} \displaystyle\sup_{\lambda\in(-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)}|\Delta_{N}^{(2)}(\lambda,X)| \displaystyle\leqslant C_{0}. $$

Taking $\epsilon$ smaller if necessary, we can ensure

$$ \sup_{\lambda\in(-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)}w(X;\nu_{\lambda},e_{\lambda,N})=\sup_{\lambda\in(-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)}(v_{\lambda}(0,X)e_{\lambda,N}(X)+v_{\lambda}(1,X)(1-e_{\lambda,N}(X)))^{-1}<2c^{-1} $$

and then

$$ \displaystyle\sup_{\lambda\in(-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)}\|f_{N}(\lambda)\| \displaystyle\leqslant C_{0}\|g_{n}(X)\|\leqslant C_{0}C|e_{0,N}(X)-e(X)||m_{0}(0,X)-m(0,X)| \displaystyle\sup_{\lambda\in(-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)}\|f_{N}^{\prime}(\lambda)\| \displaystyle\leqslant C_{0}\|g_{n}(X)\|\leqslant C_{0}C|e_{0,N}(X)-e(X)||m_{0}(0,X)-m(0,X)| \displaystyle\sup_{\lambda\in(-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)}\|f_{N}^{\prime\prime}(\lambda)\| \displaystyle\leqslant K\|g_{n}(X)\|\leqslant C_{0}C|e_{0,N}(X)-e(X)||m_{0}(0,X)-m(0,X)| $$

$$ \displaystyle\phantom{=}\ s(W;\theta_{0},\nu,e)-s(W;\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0}) \displaystyle=[w(X;\nu,e)(Z-e(X))-w(X;\nu_{0},e_{0})(Z-e_{0}(X))][Y-m_{0}(0,X)-Z\psi(X)^{\top}\theta_{0}]\psi(X) \displaystyle\phantom{=}\ +w(X;\nu,e)(Z-e(X))(m_{0}(0,X)-m(0,X))\psi(X) $$

so that

$$ \displaystyle\phantom{=}\ \,\mathbb{E}_{0}\bigl[\|s(W;\theta_{0},\nu,e)-s(W;\theta_{0},\nu_{0},e_{0})\|^{2}\bigr]^{1/2} \displaystyle\leqslant C\Bigl(\mathbb{E}_{0}\bigl[\bigl(w(X;\nu,e)(Z-e(X))-w(X;\nu_{0},e_{0})(Z-e_{0}(X))\bigr)^{2}\bigl(Y-m_{0}(0,X)-Z\psi(X)^{\top}\theta_{0}\bigr)^{2}\bigr]\Bigr)^{1/2} \displaystyle\phantom{=}\ +C\bigl(\mathbb{E}_{0}\bigl[(w(X;\nu,e)(Z-e(X)))^{2}(m_{0}(0,X)-m(0,X))^{2}\bigr]\bigr)^{1/2}. $$

By conditioning on $(X,Z)$ we see that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{0} \displaystyle\bigl[|w(X;\nu,e)(Z-e(X))-w(X;\nu_{0},e_{0})(Z-e_{0}(X))|^{2}|Y-m_{0}(0,X)-Z\psi(X)^{\top}\theta_{0}|^{2}\bigr]^{1/2} \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{0}\bigl[v_{0}(Z,X)|w(X;\nu,e)(Z-e(X))-w(X;\nu_{0},e_{0})(Z-e_{0}(X))|^{2}\bigr]^{1/2} \displaystyle\leqslant C^{1/2}\mathbb{E}_{0}\bigl[|w(X;\nu,e)(Z-e(X))-w(X;\nu_{0},e_{0})(Z-e_{0}(X))|^{2}\bigr]^{1/2}. $$

Now we write

$$ \displaystyle\bigl| \displaystyle w(X;\nu,e)(Z-e(X))-w(X;\nu_{0},e_{0})(Z-e_{0}(X))\bigr| \displaystyle\leqslant|w(X;\nu,e)-w(X;\nu_{0},e_{0})||Z-e(X)|+|w(X;\nu_{0},e_{0})||e_{0}(X)-e(X)| \displaystyle\leqslant c^{-2}(|v(0,X)-v_{0}(0,X)|+|v(1,X)-v_{0}(1,X)|+2C|e(X)-e_{0}(X)|)+c^{-1}|e_{0}(X)-e(X)| $$

so that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{0} \displaystyle\bigl[|w(X;\nu,e)(Z-e(X))-w(X;\nu_{0},e_{0})(Z-e_{0}(X))|^{2}|Y-m_{0}(0,X)-Z\psi(X)^{\top}\theta_{0}|^{2}\bigr]^{1/2} \displaystyle\leqslant C^{1/2}\bigl[c^{-2}(\|v(0,\cdot)-v_{0}(0,\cdot)\|_{2,P_{0}^{X}}+\|v(1,\cdot)-v_{0}(1,\cdot)\|_{2,P_{0}^{X}}+2C\|e-e_{0}\|_{2,P_{0}^{X}})+c^{-1}\|e-e_{0}\|_{2,P_{0}^{X}}\bigr] \displaystyle\leqslant C_{0}\tilde{\delta}_{N} $$

With $(\nu,e)\in\mathcal{T}_{N}$ arbitrary and

$$ \mathbb{E}_{0}\bigl[|w(X;\nu,e)(Z-e(X))|^{2}|m_{0}(0,X)-m(0,X)|^{2}\bigr]^{1/2}\leqslant c^{-1}\|m(0,\cdot)-m_{0}(0,\cdot)\|_{2,P_{0}^{X}}\leqslant C_{0}\tilde{\delta}_{N} $$

we have shown (23).

Fix $(\nu,e)\in\mathcal{T}_{N}$ . For $z=0,1$ we have

$$ \sup_{z\in\{0,1\}}\|s_{a}(W(z);\nu,e)\|^{q}=\sup_{z\in\{0,1\}}\|w(X;\nu,e)z(z-e(X))\psi(X)\psi(X)^{\top}\|^{q}\leqslant\left(\frac{C^{2}}{c}\right)^{q} $$

which immediately shows that

$$ \mathbb{E}_{0}\bigl[\|s_{a}(W(z);\nu,e)\|^{q}\bigr]^{1/q}\leqslant C_{0}. $$

For any $(\nu,e)\in\mathcal{T}_{N}$ we have

$$ \mathbb{E}_{0}\bigl[\|s(W(z);\theta_{0},\nu,e)\|^{q}\bigr]^{1/q}\leqslant\frac{C}{c}\mathbb{E}\bigl[|Y(z)-m(0,X)-z\psi(X)^{\top}\theta_{0}|^{q}\bigr]^{1/q}\leqslant C_{0} $$

since

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{0} \displaystyle\bigl[|Y(z)-m(0,X)-z\psi(X)^{\top}\theta_{0}|^{q}\bigr]^{1/q} \displaystyle\leqslant\mathbb{E}_{0}\bigl[|Y(z)|^{q}\bigr]^{1/q}+\mathbb{E}_{0}\bigl[|m(0,X)|^{q}\bigr]^{1/q}+\mathbb{E}_{0}\bigl[|m(1,X)|^{q}\bigr]^{1/q}. $$

We have $(\mathbb{E}_{0}[|Y(z)|^{q}])^{1/q}\leqslant C_{0}$ by Assumption 3.2, hence for $z=0,1$

$$ \displaystyle(\mathbb{E}_{0}[|m(z,X)|^{q}])^{1/q} \displaystyle\leqslant(\mathbb{E}_{0}[|m_{0}(z,X)|^{q}])^{1/q}+\|m(z,\cdot)-m_{0}(z,\cdot)\|_{q,P_{0}^{X}} \displaystyle\leqslant(\mathbb{E}_{0}[|Y(z)|^{q}])^{1/q}+\|m(z,\cdot)-m_{0}(z,\cdot)\|_{q,P_{0}^{X}} \displaystyle\leqslant C_{0} $$

which shows (25).

Fix a fold $k\in\{1,\ldots,K\}$ . For each $z=0,1$ and $(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}$ we have

$$ \displaystyle s \displaystyle(W_{ti}(z);\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})-s(W_{ti}(z);\nu_{0},e_{0,N}) \displaystyle=\bigl[w(X_{ti};\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})(z-\hat{e}^{(-k)}(X_{ti}))-w(X_{ti};\nu_{0},e_{0,N})(z-e_{0,N}(X_{ti}))\bigr] \displaystyle\phantom{=}\times[Y_{ti}(z)-m_{0}(0,X_{ti})-z\psi(X_{ti})^{\top}\theta_{0}]\psi(X_{ti}) \displaystyle\phantom{=}+w(X_{ti};\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})(z-\hat{e}^{(-k)}(X_{ti}))(m_{0}(0,X_{ti})-\hat{m}^{(-k)}(0,X_{ti}))\psi(X_{ti}). $$

Taking the conditional expectation given $\mathcal{S}^{(-k)},X_{ti}$ gives

$$ \displaystyle\Big\|\mathbb{E} \displaystyle\bigl[s(W_{ti}(z);\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})-s(W_{ti}(z);\nu_{0},e_{0,N})\!\mid\!\mathcal{S}^{(-k)},X_{ti}\bigr]\Big\|^{2} \displaystyle=w^{2}(X_{ti};\hat{\nu}^{(-k)},\hat{e}^{(-k)})(z-\hat{e}^{(-k)}(X_{ti}))^{2}(\hat{m}^{(-k)}(0,X_{ti})-m_{0}(0,X_{ti}))^{2}\|\psi(X_{ti})\|^{2} \displaystyle\leqslant\frac{C^{2}}{c^{2}}(\hat{m}^{(-k)}(0,X_{ti})-m_{0}(0,X_{ti}))^{2} $$

and so

$$ S_{t}^{(-k)}(z)\leqslant C_{0}\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_{t,k}}\sum_{(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}(\hat{m}^{(-k)}(0,X_{ti})-m_{0}(0,X_{ti}))^{2}}=o_{p}(N^{-1/4}) $$

in view of conditional Markov’s inequality, as

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\biggl[\frac{1}{n_{t,k}}\sum_{(t,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}(\hat{m}^{(-k)}(0,X_{ti})-m_{0}(0,X_{ti}))^{2}\Bigm|\mathcal{S}^{(-k)}\biggr] \displaystyle=\|\hat{m}^{(-k)}(0,\cdot)-m_{0}(0,\cdot)\|_{2,P_{t}^{X}} \displaystyle\leqslant\kappa_{t}^{-1}\|\hat{m}^{(-k)}(0,\cdot)-m_{0}(0,\cdot)\|_{2,P_{0}^{X}} \displaystyle=o_{p}(N^{-1/4}) $$

by assumption.

Having shown all conditions of Assumption 4.1, we can apply Theorem 4.1 to complete the proof of Corollary 4.2.

### C.8 Proof of Lemma 5.1

Here we show that the information functions $\Psi_{d}(\cdot)$ and $\Psi_{a}(\cdot)$ for D-optimality and A-optimality, respectively, both satisfy conditions (a) through (d) of Assumption 5.2. That both $\Psi_{d}(\cdot)$ and $\Psi_{a}(\cdot)$ are continuous, concave, and non-decreasing on $\mathbb{S}_{+}^{p}$ is well known.

If $M$ is singular then $\Psi_{d}(M)=\Psi_{a}(M)=-\infty$ ; however if $M\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^{p}$ then $\Psi_{d}(M)$ and $\Psi_{a}(M)$ are finite. Thus condition (a) holds with $\Psi_{0}=-\infty$ .

Next, we recall that for $M\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^{p}$ , we have $\nabla\Psi_{d}(M)=M^{-1}$ and $\nabla\Psi_{a}(M)=M^{-2}$ . Now we fix $0<k<K$ and $A,B\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^{p}$ such that $KI\succcurlyeq A\succcurlyeq kI$ and $KI\succcurlyeq B\succcurlyeq kI$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\|\nabla\Psi_{d}(A)-\nabla\Psi_{d}(B)\| \displaystyle=\|A^{-1}-B^{-1}\|=\|A^{-1}(B-A)B^{-1}\| \displaystyle\leqslant\|A^{-1}\|\|B^{-1}\|\|B-A\|\leqslant k^{-2}\|A-B\|\quad\text{and} \displaystyle\|\nabla\Psi_{a}(A)-\nabla\Psi_{a}(B)\| \displaystyle=\|A^{-2}-B^{-2}\|=\|A^{-2}(B^{2}-A^{2})B^{-2}\| \displaystyle\leqslant\|A^{-2}\|\|B^{-2}\|(\|B\|\|B-A\|+\|B-A\|\|A\|) \displaystyle\leqslant Kk^{-4}\|A-B\| $$

which shows condition (b).

We also have $K^{-1}I\preccurlyeq\nabla\Psi_{d}(A)\preccurlyeq k^{-1}I$ and $K^{-2}I\preccurlyeq\nabla\Psi_{a}(A)\preccurlyeq k^{-2}I$ . Therefore condition (c) holds.

Finally fix $\tilde{\Psi}_{0}>-\infty$ , and suppose $0\preccurlyeq A\preccurlyeq KI$ with $\Psi_{d}(A)\geqslant\tilde{\Psi}_{0}$ . Letting $\lambda_{1}\geqslant\ldots\geqslant\lambda_{p}$ be the eigenvalues of $A$ , we have $\lambda_{j}\leqslant K$ for all $j$ and so

$$ (p-1)\log(K)+\lambda_{p}\geqslant\Psi_{d}(A)=\sum_{j=1}^{p}\log\lambda_{j}\geqslant\tilde{\Psi}_{0} $$

so that $\lambda_{p}\geqslant\exp(\tilde{\Psi}_{0}-(p-1)\log K)>0$ , showing condition (d) for $\Psi_{d}(\cdot)$ . Similarly if $\Psi_{a}(A)\geqslant\tilde{\Psi}_{0}$ then

$$ -\frac{p-1}{K}-\lambda_{p}^{-1}\geqslant\Psi_{a}(A)=-\sum_{j=1}^{p}\lambda_{j}^{-1}\geqslant\tilde{\Psi}_{0} $$

which implies $-\tilde{\Psi}_{0}-(p-1)/K\geqslant\lambda_{p}^{-1}>0$ . Therefore $\lambda_{p}\geqslant(-\tilde{\Psi}_{0}-{(p-1)}/{K})^{-1}>0$ , showing condition (d) for $\Psi_{a}(\cdot)$ as well.

### C.9 Proof of Lemma 5.2: Convergence of generic concave maximization routine

Here we prove Lemma 5.2 about the convergence rates of our generic concave maximization routine.

#### Proof.

Let $\tilde{\delta}=\delta/2$ , with $\delta<0$ as in Assumption 5.1. We will repeatedly use the fact that since $[\tilde{\delta},1-\tilde{\delta}]\times\mathcal{W}\subseteq\real^{r+1}$ is compact, Assumption 5.1 implies that $f=f(\cdot,\cdot)$ and all of its partial derivatives up to second order are uniformly bounded above in norm on that set. Then WLOG we can make $C$ from Assumption 5.1 larger so that

$$ \sup_{(k,w)\in[\tilde{\delta},1-\tilde{\delta}]\times\mathcal{W}}\|h(k,w)\|\leqslant C,\quad\forall h=h(\cdot,\cdot)\in\{f,f^{\prime},f^{\prime\prime},f_{w},f_{ww},f_{w}^{\prime}\} $$

where $f_{w}=f_{w}(\cdot,\cdot)$ , $f_{ww}=f_{ww}(\cdot,\cdot)$ , and $f_{w}^{\prime}=f_{w}^{\prime}(\cdot,\cdot)$ are tensors with $f_{w}$ the partial derivative of $f$ with respect to the second argument, $f_{ww}$ the second partial derivative of $f$ with respect to the second argument, and $f_{w}^{\prime}$ the partial derivative of $f^{\prime}$ with respect to the second argument.

First, we show the existence of $e^{*}(\cdot)$ satisfying (27). For each propensity $e=e(\cdot)\in\mathcal{E}$ define $\phi(e)=\Psi(M(e))$ and $\hat{\phi}_{n}(e)=\Psi(\hat{M}_{n}(e))$ where

$$ M(e)=\int_{\mathcal{X}}f(e(x),\eta(x))\mathrm{d}P(x)\quad\text{and}\quad\hat{M}_{n}(e)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f(e(X_{i}),\hat{\eta}(X_{i})). $$

For any $e_{1}=e_{1}(\cdot),e_{2}=e_{2}(\cdot)\in\mathcal{E}$ and $\lambda\in[0,1]$ we have

$$ \displaystyle M(\lambda e_{1}+(1-\lambda)e_{2}) \displaystyle=\int_{\mathcal{X}}f\bigl(\lambda e_{1}(x)+(1-\lambda)e_{2}(x),\eta(x)\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}P(x) \displaystyle\succcurlyeq\int_{\mathcal{X}}\bigl(\lambda f(e_{1}(x),\eta(x))+(1-\lambda)f(e_{2}(x),\eta(x))\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}P(x) \displaystyle=\lambda M(e_{1})+(1-\lambda)M(e_{2}) $$

where the matrix inequality follows from the fact that the function $u\mapsto f(u,\eta(x))$ is a concave matrix-valued function on $[0,1]$ since its second derivative is globally negative semidefinite by (29). Thus $M=M(\cdot)$ is also a concave matrix-valued function on $\mathcal{E}$ . In fact, $M$ is also Lipschitz continuous in the sense that

$$ \displaystyle\|M(e_{1})-M(e_{2})\| \displaystyle\leqslant\int_{\mathcal{X}}\|f(e_{1}(x),\eta(x))-f(e_{2}(x),\eta(x))\|\,\mathrm{d}P(x) \displaystyle\leqslant C\int_{\mathcal{X}}|e_{1}(x)-e_{2}(x)|\,\mathrm{d}P(x) \displaystyle\leqslant C\|e_{1}-e_{2}\|_{2,P},\quad\forall e_{1},e_{2}\in\mathcal{E} $$

where the second inequality uses (71) with $h=f^{\prime}$ and Taylor’s theorem with the Lagrange form of the remainder. With the information function $\Psi=\Psi(\cdot)$ continuous, concave, and increasing in the semidefinite ordering by Assumption 5.2, we conclude that $\phi=\phi(\cdot)$ is continuous and concave on $\mathcal{E}$ (e.g., by Section 3.6 of Boyd and Vandenberghe, (2004)).

We now consider an extension $\bar{\phi}=\bar{\phi}(\cdot)$ of $\phi$ to $L^{2}(P)$ ,

$$ \bar{\phi}(e)=\begin{cases}\phi(e),&e\in\mathcal{E}\\
-\infty,&\text{ otherwise.}\end{cases} $$

Since $\phi(\cdot)$ is continuous and concave on $\mathcal{E}$ , it is straightforward to show that the extension $\bar{\phi}$ is concave and upper semicontinuous on $L^{2}(P)$ ; the latter means that $\bar{\phi}(e_{0})=\limsup_{e\rightarrow e_{0}}\bar{\phi}(e)$ for all $e_{0}=e_{0}(\cdot)\in L^{2}(P)$ . The function $\bar{\phi}$ is also “proper” in that it never equals $+\infty$ . Since $\mathcal{F}_{*}$ is a closed, bounded, and convex subset of the Hilbert space $L^{2}(P)$ , by Proposition 1.88 and Theorem 2.11 of Barbu and Precupanu, (2012) we conclude $\bar{\phi}(\cdot)$ , and hence $\phi(\cdot)$ , attains its maximum on $\mathcal{F}_{*}$ . This shows the existence of $e^{*}=\argmax_{e\in\mathcal{F}}\phi(e)$ . We will show uniqueness ( $P$ -almost surely) later.

Next, note that compactness of $F_{n}\subseteq\real^{n}$ and continuity of the map $(e_{1},\ldots,e_{n})\mapsto\Psi\left(n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f(e_{i},\hat{\eta}(X_{i}))\right)$ , which follows from continuity of the information function $\Psi$ and of $e\mapsto f(e,\hat{\eta}(x))$ on $[0,1]$ for each $x\in\mathcal{X}$ , ensure the existence of a vector $(\hat{e}_{1},\ldots,\hat{e}_{n})$ satisfying (31). This shows the second claim of Lemma 5.2. Then condition 2 of Assumption 5.1 ensures that there exists a propensity $\hat{e}=\hat{e}(\cdot)\in\mathcal{E}$ with $\hat{e}(X_{i})=\hat{e}_{i}$ for all $i=1,\ldots,n$ . So all that remains is to show that any such propensity $\hat{e}(\cdot)$ satisfies the rate conditions $\|\hat{e}-e^{*}\|_{2,P_{n}}+\|\hat{e}-e^{*}\|_{2,P}=O_{p}(n^{-1/4}+\alpha_{n})$ , along with uniqueness of $e^{*}(\cdot)$ satisfying (27) ( $P$ -almost surely).

We have now established existence of $e^{*}(\cdot)$ , $\hat{e}_{1},\dots,\hat{e}_{n}$ and $\hat{e}(\cdot)$ . It remains to show the desired convergence rates of $\hat{e}(\cdot)$ to $e^{*}(\cdot)$ in $L^{2}$ under both $P$ and $\hat{P}_{n}$ . Before proceeding further, we list a few useful facts. By (71) with $h=f$ and recalling that the Frobenius norm of a matrix upper bounds its spectral norm, we have

$$ M(e)\preccurlyeq CI\quad\text{ and }\quad\hat{M}_{n}(e)\preccurlyeq CI,\quad\forall e\in\mathcal{E}. $$

Next, we claim that

$$ M(e^{*})\succcurlyeq k^{*}I $$

for some $k^{*}>0$ . To see this, note that $\Psi(M(e^{*}))=\phi(e^{*})\geqslant\phi(e_{0})=\Psi(M(e_{0}))>\Psi_{0}$ by Assumption 5.2(a) and condition 3 of Assumption 5.1. Then Assumption 5.2(d) shows that the $k_{*}>0$ we need exists.

Now, we define the function class

$$ \mathcal{F}_{n}=\biggl\{e\in\mathcal{E}\Bigm|m_{L}\leqslant\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}e(X_{i})\leqslant m_{H}\biggr\}. $$

This class contains any propensity $\hat{e}(\cdot)$ derived as above by solving (31) and interpolating within the base propensity class $\mathcal{E}$ .

We complete the proof by the following 4 steps:

- 1. This means there exist nonrandom positive constants $c_{0}$ , $r_{0}$ , and $k_{0}$ such that $\displaystyle c_{0}\min\bigl(r_{0},\|e^{*}-e\|_{2,P}\bigr)\times\|e^{*}-e\|_{2,P}\leqslant\phi(e^{*})-\phi(e),\quad\forall e\in\mathcal{F}_{*}$ (75) and $\displaystyle c_{0}\min\bigl(r_{0},\|\hat{e}-e\|_{2,P_{n}}\bigr)\times\|\hat{e}-e\|_{2,P_{n}}\bm{1}(A_{n})\leqslant(\hat{\phi}_{n}(\hat{e})-\hat{\phi}_{n}(e))\bm{1}(A_{n}),\quad\forall e\in\mathcal{F}_{n}$ (76) where $A_{n}$ is the event that $\hat{M}_{n}(\hat{e})\succcurlyeq k_{0}I$ . - 2. $$ \phi(e^{*})-\phi(\hat{e}_{\mathcal{F}})+\hat{\phi}_{n}(\hat{e})-\hat{\phi}_{n}(e_{n}^{*})=O_{p}(n^{-1/2})+O_{p}(\alpha_{n}). $$

as well. In particular, $\hat{e}$ is mean square consistent for $e^{*}$ both in-sample and out-of-sample.
