$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[h_{1}(R)h(R)] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{h_{1}(R)\mathbb{E}[(Y-m^{*}(R))g(W)\mid R]}{V^{*}(R)}\right] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{(Y-m^{*}(R))g(W)h_{1}(R)}{V^{*}(R)}\right] \displaystyle=0 $$

where the last equality follows since $g\in\mathcal{T}_{1}^{\perp}$ but

$$ \hat{g}(w)=\frac{(y-m^{*}(r))h_{1}(r)}{V^{*}(r)} $$

satisfies $\mathbb{E}[\hat{g}(W)\mid R]=0$ and $\mathbb{E}[Y\hat{g}(W)\mid R]=h_{1}(R)$ so that $\hat{g}\in\mathcal{T}_{1}$ by definition.

### A.3 Proof of Corollary 1

We write $\mathcal{H}_{W}^{0}$ as the direct sum of orthogonal subspaces $\mathcal{T}_{1}\oplus\mathcal{T}_{2}$ where

$$ \mathcal{T}_{1}=\{f\in\mathcal{H}_{W}^{0}\mid\mathbb{E}[f(W)\mid R]=0\},\quad\mathcal{T}_{2}=\mathcal{H}_{R}^{0}. $$

Since the model $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}}$ places no restrictions on the distribution of $R$ , it follows that its semiparametric tangent space $\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{M}}=\bar{\mathcal{T}}_{1}\oplus\mathcal{T}_{2}$ for some $\bar{\mathcal{T}}_{1}\subseteq\mathcal{T}_{1}$ (this is also easy to see directly from the fact that $\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\perp}\subseteq\mathcal{T}_{1}$ by (8)). Conversely, the experimental propensity score being known places no restriction on the conditional distribution of $Y$ given $R$ . Thus, we can write $\tilde{\mathcal{T}}_{\mathcal{M}}=\bar{\mathcal{T}}_{1}\oplus\bar{\mathcal{T}}_{2}$ where $\bar{\mathcal{T}}_{2}$ is the semiparametric tangent space for the model $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{N}}$ on the distribution of $R=(Z,S,X)$ , viewing $Z$ as the outcome and $(S,X)$ the covariates and letting $\mathcal{N}=\{(s,x)\mapsto se^{*}(x)+(1-s)h(x)\mid h\in\mathcal{H}_{X}\}$ so that the restriction that the mapping $(s,x)\mapsto\mathbb{E}[Z\mid S=s,X=x]\in\mathcal{N}$ amounts precisely to the experimental propensity score being known and equal to $e^{*}$ . By (8) we have

$$ \addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:T_{2}{}_{p}erp_{t}ilde}\bar{\mathcal{T}}_{2}^{\perp}=\{(z-e^{*}(x))h(x)\mid h\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{N}}^{\perp}\} $$

where $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{N}}^{\perp}$ is the orthogonal complement of $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{N}}$ in $\mathcal{H}_{SX}$ and $\bar{\mathcal{T}}_{2}^{\perp}$ denotes the orthogonal complement of $\bar{\mathcal{T}}_{2}$ in $\mathcal{T}_{2}=\mathcal{H}_{R}^{0}$ , (not the orthogonal complement in $\mathcal{H}_{W}^{0}$ ). We conclude

$$ \tilde{\mathcal{T}}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\perp}=\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\perp}\oplus\tilde{\mathcal{T}}_{2}^{\perp}. $$

Thus, to prove (24) it suffices to show that

$$ \mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{N}}^{\perp}=\{(s,x)\mapsto sh(x)\mid h\in\mathcal{H}_{X}\}. $$

To that end, we first show that $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{N}}=\{(s,x)\mapsto(1-s)h(x)\mid h\in\mathcal{H}_{X}\}$ . To do so, note that the RHS is a closed subset of $\mathcal{H}_{SX}$ , and that an arbitrary outcome mean function parametric submodel of $\mathcal{N}$ takes the form

$$ m(s,x;\gamma)=se^{*}(x)+(1-s)h(x;\gamma) $$

where $h(x;0)=r^{*}(x)$ . For any $c$ with the same length as $\gamma$ we have

$$ c^{\top}\frac{\partial m(s,x;0)}{\partial\gamma}=(1-s)c^{\top}\frac{\partial h(x;0)}{\partial\gamma} $$

which clearly lies in the set $\{(s,x)\mapsto(1-s)h(x)\mid h\in\mathcal{H}_{X}\}$ . Hence $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{N}}$ is contained inside this set. Conversely, given an arbitrary element $g$ given by $g(s,x)=(1-s)h(x)$ in this set, we can consider the univariate submodels

$$ m_{n}(s,x;\gamma)=se^{*}(x)+(1-s)(q^{*}(x)+\gamma h_{n}(x)) $$

for a sequence of bounded functions $h_{n}\in\mathcal{H}_{X}$ converging in mean square to $h$ . Note the validity of each of these submodels for $\gamma$ in a neighborhood of zero uses the fact that $h_{n}$ is bounded and $\delta<q^{*}(x)<1-\delta$ for all $x$ and some $\delta>0$ . With $\partial m_{n}(s,x;\gamma)/\partial\gamma\Big|_{\gamma=0}$ converging to $g(s,x)$ in mean square, we conclude $g\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{N}}$ , and indeed $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{N}}=\{(s,x)\mapsto(1-s)h(x)\mid h\in\mathcal{H}_{X}\}$ . Given this, it is then straightforward to verify that

$$ \mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{N}}^{\perp}=\{(s,x)\mapsto sh(x)\mid h\in\mathcal{H}_{X}\} $$

upon recalling that $s(1-s)=0$ .

### A.4 Proof of Corollary 2

It suffices to show that $\varphi_{0,\textnormal{rct}}$ is the EIF for $\tau_{\textnormal{rct}}$ in the model $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}_{\mathcal{M}}$ , since $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}_{\mathcal{M}}\subseteq\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}}\subseteq\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{H}_{R}}$ and hence the semiparametric bound for $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}}$ must be sandwiched between the bounds for $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}_{\mathcal{M}}$ and the nonparametric model $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{H}_{R}}$ . To do so, by Theorem 1 it suffices to show that $\varphi_{0,\textnormal{rct}}\in(\tilde{\mathcal{T}}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\perp})^{\perp}=\tilde{\mathcal{T}}_{\mathcal{M}}$ .

Fix an arbitrary element $g\in\tilde{\mathcal{T}}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\perp}$ . By Theorem 2, we can write $g(w)=h(r)(y-m^{*}(r))+s\tilde{h}(x)(z-e^{*}(x))$ for some $h\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\perp}$ and $\tilde{h}\in\mathcal{H}_{X}$ . For each $f\in\mathcal{H}_{R}$ , with $\Delta(z,x,y;\eta)$ as in Proposition 1, we define

$$ \displaystyle\phi(r;f) \displaystyle=h(r)\mathbb{E}[((\rho^{*})^{-1}S\Delta(Z,X,Y;\eta^{*})+f(R))(Y-m^{*}(R))\mid R=r] \displaystyle=h(r)\left(\frac{sz}{\rho^{*}e^{*}}\mathbb{E}[(Y-m_{11}^{*}(X))^{2}\mid R]-\frac{s(1-z)}{\rho^{*}(1-e^{*})}\mathbb{E}[(Y-m_{10}^{*}(X))^{2}\mid R]\right) \displaystyle=h(r)(\rho^{*})^{-1}(c_{1}sz-c_{0}s(1-z)) $$

where $c_{1}=\sigma_{1}^{2}/e^{*}$ and $c_{0}=\sigma_{0}^{2}/(1-e^{*})$ , and the second equality uses the fact that $f(r)\mathbb{E}[Y-m^{*}(R)\mid R]=0$ . Note $\phi(r;f)$ is independent of $f\in\mathcal{H}_{R}$ and by the assumption of the theorem, $r\mapsto(\rho^{*})^{-1}(c_{1}sz-c_{0}s(1-z))\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}}$ . With $h\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\perp}$ we conclude that

$$ \addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:phi}\mathbb{E}[\phi(R;f)]=0,\quad\forall f\in\mathcal{H}_{R}. $$

Next, we note that for any $\bar{g}\in\mathcal{H}_{X}$ we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[S\tilde{h}(X)(Z-e^{*})(\Delta(Z,X,Y;\eta^{*})+\bar{g}(X))\right] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[S\tilde{h}(X)(Z-e^{*})\mathbb{E}(\Delta(Z,X,Y;\eta^{*})\mid S=1,Z,X)\right] \displaystyle+\mathbb{E}[S\tilde{h}(X)\bar{g}(X)\mathbb{E}(Z-e^{*}\mid S=1,X)] \displaystyle=0 $$

Finally, we put together (46) and (47) to show that $\varphi_{0,\textnormal{rct}}$ must be orthogonal to our arbitrary chosen function $g\in\tilde{\mathcal{T}}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\perp}$ . By iterated expectations, defining $f(r)=s(m_{11}^{*}(x)-m_{10}^{*}(x)-\tau_{\textnormal{rct}}^{*})/\rho^{*}$ we compute

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\varphi_{0,rct}(W;\tau_{rct}^{*},\eta^{*})g(W)] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\varphi_{0,\textnormal{rct}}(W;\tau_{\textnormal{rct}}^{*};\eta^{*})(h(R)(Y-m^{*}(R))+S\tilde{h}(X)(Z-e^{*}))] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[h(R)\mathbb{E}(\varphi_{0,\textnormal{rct}}(W;\tau_{\textnormal{rct}}^{*};\eta^{*})(Y-m^{*}(R))\mid R] \displaystyle\quad+(\rho^{*})^{-1}\mathbb{E}[S\tilde{h}(X)(Z-e^{*})(\Delta(Z,X,Y;\eta^{*})+m_{11}^{*}(X)-m_{10}^{*}(X)-\tau_{\textnormal{rct}}^{*})] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\phi(S,Z,X;f)]+0\text{ by~\eqref{eq:h_tilde_iota} with $\bar{g}(X)=m_{11}^{*}(X)-m_{10}^{*}(X)-\tau^{*}_{\textnormal{rct}}$} \displaystyle=0\text{ by~\eqref{eq:phi}}. $$

### A.5 Proof of Lemma 1

As indicated in the main text, here we prove a stronger version of Lemma 1 that is applicable to models of the form $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}_{\mathcal{M}}$ where the experimental propensity score is known, as considered in Corollary 1.

#### Lemma.

Suppose the function $g=g(\cdot;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})$ is any element of the space $\tilde{\mathcal{T}}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\perp}$ for some collection of outcome mean functions $\mathcal{M}\subseteq\mathcal{H}_{R}$ satisfying the conditions of Corollary 1, so that we can write

$$ g(w;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})=(y-m^{*}(r))h_{1}(r;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})+s(z-e^{*}(x))h_{2}(x;\tau^{*},\eta^{*}) $$

where $\eta^{*}$ includes the mean function $m^{*}$ , $h_{1}^{*}(\cdot)=h_{1}(\cdot;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\perp}$ , and $h_{2}^{*}(\cdot)=h_{2}(\cdot;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})\in\mathcal{H}_{X}$ . Then equation (26) holds under the following conditions:

- • (Boundedness) There exists $C<\infty$ for which $V^{*}(r)\leqslant C$ for $P^{*}$ -almost every $r$ and both $\|h_{i}^{*}\|_{\infty,P^{*}}\leqslant C$ and $\left\|\hat{h}_{i}^{(-k)}\right\|_{\infty,P^{*}}\leqslant C$ for $i=1,2$

- • (Approximate tangency) With probability tending to 1, for each $k=1,\ldots,K$ there exists $\hat{R}^{(-k)}=\hat{R}^{(-k)}(\cdot)\in\mathcal{H}_{R}$ depending only on the observations outside fold $k$ such that the function $r\mapsto\hat{m}^{(-k)}(r)-m^{*}(r)-\hat{R}^{(-k)}(r)$ lies in the outcome mean function tangent space $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}}$ , $\|\hat{R}^{(-k)}\|_{2,P^{*}}=o_{p}(1)$ , and the following rate holds:

$$ \addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:R_{h}at_{g}eneralized}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\left|\hat{R}^{(-k)}(R_{i})\right|=o_{p}(N^{-1/2}) $$

(48)

- • (Rate conditions) The following rate conditions hold for all $k=1,\ldots,K$ : – (First order consistency) $\|\hat{m}^{(-k)}-m^{*}\|_{2,P^{*}}+\|\hat{h}_{1}^{(-k)}-h_{1}^{*}\|_{2,P^{*}}+\|\hat{h}_{2}^{(-k)}-h_{2}^{*}\|_{2,P^{*}}=o_{p}(1)$ – (Product rate condition) $\|\hat{m}^{(-k)}-m^{*}\|_{2,P^{*}}\times\|\hat{h}_{1}^{(-k)}-h_{1}^{*}\|_{2,P^{*}}=o_{p}(N^{-1/2})$ .

Lemma 1 follows immediately from the modified Lemma above since $\tilde{\mathcal{T}}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\perp}\supseteq\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\perp}$ , and for any $g\in\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\perp}$ we can apply the modified Lemma with $h_{2}=h_{2}^{(-k)}=0$ .

Writing

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}g\left(W_{i};\hat{\tau}^{(-k)},\hat{\eta}^{(-k)}\right)-g(W_{i};\tau^{*},\eta^{*})=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}{N}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}g\left(W_{i};\hat{\tau}^{(-k)},\hat{\eta}^{(-k)}\right)-g(W_{i};\tau^{*},\eta^{*}) $$

we see it suffices to fix $k\in\{1,\ldots,K\}$ and show

$$ \frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}g\left(W_{i};\hat{\tau}^{(-k)},\hat{\eta}^{(-k)}\right)-g(W_{i};\tau^{*},\eta^{*})=o_{p}(N^{-1/2}). $$

We have

$$ \frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}g\left(W_{i};\hat{\tau}^{(-k)},\hat{\eta}^{(-k)}\right)-g(W_{i};\tau^{*},\eta^{*})=a_{k}+b_{k} $$

where

$$ \displaystyle a_{k} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\left(Y_{i}-\hat{m}^{(-k)}(R_{i})\right)\hat{h}_{1}^{(-k)}(R_{i})-(Y_{i}-m^{*}(R_{i}))h_{1}^{*}(R_{i}) \displaystyle b_{k} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}S_{i}(Z_{i}-e^{*}(X_{i}))\left(\hat{h}_{2}^{(-k)}(X_{i})-h_{2}^{*}(X_{i})\right). $$

We further expand

$$ a_{k}=a_{1k}+a_{2k}+a_{3k} $$

where

$$ \displaystyle a_{1k} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\left(m^{*}(R_{i})-\hat{m}^{(-k)}(R_{i})\right)h_{1}^{*}(R_{i}) \displaystyle a_{2k} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}(Y_{i}-m^{*}(R_{i}))\left(\hat{h}_{1}^{(-k)}(R_{i})-h_{1}^{*}(R_{i})\right) \displaystyle a_{3k} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\left(m^{*}(R_{i})-\hat{m}^{(-k)}(R_{i})\right)\left(\hat{h}_{1}^{(-k)}(R_{i})-h_{1}^{*}(R_{i})\right) $$

First, we show $a_{1k}=o_{p}(N^{-1/2})$ . Note that

$$ \Bigg|\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\hat{R}^{(-k)}(R_{i})h_{1}^{*}(R_{i})\Bigg|\leqslant C\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\left|\hat{R}^{(-k)}(R_{i})\right|=o_{p}(N^{-1/2}) $$

by (48) and the boundedness condition $\|h_{1}^{*}\|_{\infty,P^{*}}\leqslant C$ . Hence $a_{1k}=\tilde{a}_{1k}+o_{p}(N^{-1/2})$ where

$$ \tilde{a}_{1k}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\left(\hat{R}^{(-k)}(R_{i})+m^{*}(R_{i})-\hat{m}^{(-k)}(R_{i})\right)h_{1}^{*}(R_{i}). $$

Furthermore, whenever $\hat{R}^{(-k)}$ exists, we have that

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[\left(\hat{R}^{(-k)}(R_{i})+m^{*}(R_{i})-\hat{m}^{(-k)}(R_{i})\right)h_{1}^{*}(R_{i})\mid\mathcal{F}_{N}^{(-k)}\right]=0 $$

for each $i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}$ ; here $\mathcal{F}_{N}^{(-k)}$ is the $\sigma$ -algebra generated by the observations outside fold $k$ , and the preceding display holds since $\hat{R}^{(-k)}+m^{*}-m^{(-k)}\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}}$ (recall $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}}$ is assumed to be a linear space, hence it is closed under multiplication by negative 1) but $h_{1}^{*}\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\perp}$ . With the summands in $\tilde{a}_{1k}$ i.i.d. across $i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}$ conditional on $\mathcal{F}_{N}^{(-k)}$ , we compute

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\tilde{a}_{1k}^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{N}^{(-k)}\right] \displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}\int\left(\hat{R}^{(-k)}(r)+m^{*}(r)-\hat{m}^{(-k)}(r)\right)^{2}(h_{1}^{*}(r))^{2}dP^{*}(w) \displaystyle\leqslant\frac{C^{2}}{|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}\left\|\hat{R}^{(-k)}+m^{*}-\hat{m}^{(-k)}\right\|_{2,P^{*}}^{2}\text{ by boundedness of $h_{1}^{*}$} \displaystyle=o_{p}(N^{-1}) $$

since $|\mathcal{I}_{k}|^{-1}=O(N^{-1})$ while

$$ \|\hat{R}^{(-k)}+m^{*}-\hat{m}^{(-k)}\|_{2,P^{*}}\leqslant\|\hat{R}^{(-k)}\|_{2,P^{*}}+\|\hat{m}^{(-k)}-m^{*}\|_{2,P^{*}}=o_{p}(1). $$

by Minkowski’s inequality and the rate conditions $\|\hat{R}^{(-k)}\|_{2,P^{*}}=o_{p}(1)$ and $\|\hat{m}^{(-k)}-m^{*}\|_{2,P^{*}}=o_{p}(1)$ . We conclude by Lemma 2 that $\tilde{a}_{1k}=o_{p}(N^{-1/2})$ and hence $a_{1k}=o_{p}(N^{-1/2})$ as well.

Next, we show $a_{2k}=o_{p}(N^{-1/2})$ . Note that $\mathbb{E}\left[Y_{i}-m^{*}(R_{i})\mid\mathcal{F}_{N}^{(-k)},\mathcal{F}_{R}^{(k)}\right]=0$ for all $i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}$ where $\mathcal{F}_{R}^{(k)}$ is the $\sigma$ -algebra generated by $(R_{i})_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}$ . Additionally we have that the collection $\{Y_{i}-m^{*}(R_{i})\}_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}$ is conditionally independent given the $\sigma$ -algebra generated by $\mathcal{F}_{N}^{(-k)}$ and $\mathcal{F}_{R}^{(k)}$ , and that $\hat{h}_{1}^{(-k)}(R_{i})-h_{1}^{*}(R_{i})$ is measurable with respect to this $\sigma$ -algebra. Finally we have $\mathbb{E}\left[(Y_{i}-m^{*}(R_{i}))^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{N}^{(-k)},\mathcal{F}_{R}^{(k)}\right]=V^{*}(R_{i})\leqslant C$ by the boundedness condition. Thus with

$$ \frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\left(\hat{h}_{1}^{(-k)}(R_{i})-h_{1}^{*}(R_{i})\right)^{2}=o_{p}(1) $$

by the rate conditions for the first component and Lemma 4, we conclude by Lemma 5 that $a_{2k}=o_{p}(N^{-1/2})$ .

To show that $a_{3k}=o_{p}(N^{-1/2})$ , simply note that

$$ \displaystyle|a_{3k}| \displaystyle\leqslant\left(\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\left(m^{*}(R_{i})-\hat{m}^{(-k)}(R_{i})\right)^{2}\right)^{1/2}\times\left(\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\left(\hat{h}_{1}^{(-k)}(R_{i})-h_{1}^{*}(R_{i})\right)^{2}\right)^{1/2} \displaystyle=o_{p}(N^{-1/2}) $$

by Cauchy-Schwarz and the product rate condition $\|\hat{m}^{(-k)}-m^{*}\|_{2,P^{*}}\|\hat{h}_{1}^{(-k)}-h_{1}^{*}\|_{2,P^{*}}=o_{p}(N^{-1/2})$ , in view of Lemma 4.

Finally, let $\mathcal{F}_{X}^{(k)}$ be the $\sigma$ -algebra generated by the observations $\{X_{i}\}_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}$ , so that

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[S_{i}(Z_{i}-e^{*}(X_{i}))\mid\mathcal{F}_{N}^{(-k)},\mathcal{F}_{X}^{(k)}\right]=0,\quad\forall i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}. $$

The collection $\{S_{i}(Z_{i}-e^{*}(X_{i}))\}_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}$ is conditionally independent given the $\sigma$ -algebra generated by $\mathcal{F}_{N}^{(-k)}$ and $\mathcal{F}_{X}^{(k)}$ , and $\hat{h}_{2}^{(-k)}(X_{i})-h_{2}^{*}(X_{i})$ is measurable with respect to this $\sigma$ -algebra. Since

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[\left(S_{i}(Z_{i}-e^{*}(X_{i}))\right)^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{N}^{(-k)},\mathcal{F}_{X}^{(k)}\right]\leqslant 1,\quad\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\left(\hat{h}_{2}^{(-k)}(X_{i})-h_{2}^{*}(X_{i})\right)^{2}=o_{p}(1) $$

by the rate conditions for the second component and Lemma 4, we conclude by Lemma 5 that $b_{k}=o_{p}(N^{-1/2})$ .

## Appendix B Additional derivations of efficient influence functions

Here we work through the three-step outline presented following the statement of Theorem 2 in the main text to derive EIF’s in the models $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}_{1}}$ , $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}_{2}}$ , $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}_{3}}$ , and $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}_{4}}$ corresponding to examples 1, 2, 3, and 4.

### B.1 Restricted moment model

In the restricted moment model $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}_{1}}$ of Example 1, under suitable regularity conditions we have by standard $Z$ -estimation theory that the solution to

$$ \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}a(R_{i})(Y_{i}-\mu(R_{i};\beta))=0 $$

is a RAL estimator for $\beta\in\real^{q}$ for any $a\in\mathcal{H}_{R}^{q}$ . The corresponding influence function is

$$ \varphi_{0}(w;\beta^{*},\eta^{*})=\mathbb{E}\left[a(r)D(r;\beta^{*})^{\top}\right]^{-1}a(r)(y-\mu(r;\beta)) $$

where $D(r;b)=\mu_{\beta}(r;b)\equiv\partial\mu(r;\beta)/\partial\beta\Big|_{\beta=b}\in\real^{q}$ (cf. Chapter 5 of Van der Vaart (2000)). In the case that $\mu(r;\beta)=\psi(r)^{\top}\beta$ is a linear model, taking $a(r)=\psi(r)$ gives the ordinary least squares estimator. In any case, we can use $\varphi_{0}$ as above for our initial influence function of an RAL estimator of $\beta$ , which we aim to project via (7) to derive the EIF for $\beta$ in the model $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}_{1}}$ .

To do so, we first compute the semiparametric tangent space $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{1}}$ , similar to the example in Section 2.2. An arbitrary outcome mean function parametric submodel for $\mathcal{M}_{1}$ evidently takes the form

$$ m(r;\gamma)=\mu(r;\alpha(\gamma)) $$

for some smooth $\alpha:\real^{s}\rightarrow\real^{q}$ defined on a neighborhood of $0\in\real^{s}$ with $\alpha(0)=\beta^{*}$ . Then by the chain rule

$$ m_{\gamma}(r;0)=J_{\alpha}(0)^{\top}D(r;\beta^{*}) $$

for $J_{\alpha}(0)\in\real^{q\times s}$ a Jacobian matrix. For any $c_{0}\in\real^{s}$ , $c_{0}^{\top}m_{\gamma}(r;0)$ is of the form $r\mapsto c^{\top}D(r;\beta^{*})$ for some $c\in\real^{q}$ , which is evidently closed. Conversely, any function of this form clearly lies in the span of the derivative of the simple $q$ -dimensional submodel $m(r;\gamma)=\mu(r;\beta^{*}+\gamma)$ . It follows that

$$ \mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{1}}=\{r\mapsto c^{\top}D(r;\beta^{*})\mid c\in\real^{q}\}. $$

We note in passing that for the linear model $\mu(r;\beta)=\psi(r)^{\top}\beta$ we can verify that indeed $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{1}}=\mathcal{M}_{1}$ , as shown by Proposition 2.

To derive the orthogonal complement $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{1}}^{\perp}$ , as suggested in Section 2.3 we solve for the set of functions $h\in\mathcal{H}_{R}$ for which the projection $g=\Pi(h;\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{1}})$ is equal to 0. We have $g(r)=c_{h}^{\top}D(r;\beta^{*})$ where

$$ c_{h}=\argmin_{c\in\real^{q}}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(h(R)-c^{\top}D(R;\beta^{*})\right)^{2}\right] $$

Taking a derivative gives

$$ c_{h}=\left(\mathbb{E}[D(R;\beta^{*})D(R;\beta^{*})^{\top}]\right)^{-1}\mathbb{E}[h(R)D(R;\beta^{*})] $$

so $g=0\iff c_{h}=0\iff\mathbb{E}[h(R)D(R;\beta^{*})=0]$ . It follows that

$$ \mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{1}}^{\perp}=\{h\in\mathcal{H}_{R}\mid\mathbb{E}[h(R)D(R;\beta^{*})]=0\}. $$

and (by Theorem 2) that

$$ \mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{M}_{1}}^{\perp}=\{w\mapsto h(r)(y-\mu(r;\beta^{*}))\mid\mathbb{E}[h(R)D(R;\beta^{*})]=0\}. $$

Finally, we compute the projection $g=\Pi\left(\varphi_{0};\left(\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{M}_{1}}^{\perp}\right)^{q}\right)$ to get the EIF via (7). By definition, $g(w)=(y-\mu(r;\beta^{*}))h_{0}(r)$ where

$$ \displaystyle h_{0} \displaystyle=\argmin_{h\in\mathcal{H}_{R}^{q}:\mathbb{E}[h(R)D(R;\beta^{*})^{\top}]=0}\mathbb{E}\left[(Y-\mu(R;\beta^{*}))^{2}\|A^{-1}a(R)-h(X)\|^{2}\right] \displaystyle A \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[a(R)D(R;\beta^{*})^{\top}]. $$

To compute this projection, we handle the constraint $\mathbb{E}[h(R)D(R;\beta^{*})^{\top}]=0$ by introducing a Lagrange multiplier $\Lambda\in\real^{q\times q}$ . Then we minimize the Lagrangian by conditioning on $R$ and minimizing pointwise:

$$ \displaystyle\argmin_{h\in\mathcal{H}_{R}^{q}}\mathbb{E}\left[(Y-\mu(R;\beta^{*}))^{2}\|A^{-1}a(R)-h(R)\|^{2}\right]-2\textnormal{tr}\left(\Lambda^{\top}\mathbb{E}[h(R)D(R;\beta^{*})^{\top}]\right) \displaystyle\quad=\argmin_{h\in\mathcal{H}_{R}^{q}}\mathbb{E}\left[V^{*}(R)\|h(R)\|^{2}-2\left(V^{*}(R)a(R)^{\top}A^{-1}+D(R;\beta^{*})^{\top}\Lambda^{\top}\right)h(R)\right] $$

Minimizing the argument to the expectation pointwise gives

$$ h_{0}(r)=A^{-1}a(r)+\frac{1}{V^{*}(r)}\Lambda D(r;\beta^{*}) $$

We solve for the Lagrange multiplier $\Lambda$ by plugging the preceding display into the matrix equations $\mathbb{E}[h_{0}(R)D(R;\beta^{*})^{\top}]=0$ , giving

$$ \Lambda=-\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{V^{*}(R)}D(R;\beta^{*})D(R;\beta^{*})^{\top}\right]\right)^{-1}. $$

Then the EIF is

$$ \displaystyle\varphi_{\textnormal{eff}}(w;\beta^{*},\eta^{*}) \displaystyle=\varphi_{0}(w;\beta^{*},\eta^{*})-h_{0}(r)(y-\mu(r;\beta^{*})) \displaystyle=\frac{y-\mu(r;\beta^{*})}{V^{*}(r)}\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{V^{*}(R)}D(R;\beta^{*})D(R;\beta^{*})^{\top}\right]\right)^{-1}D(r;\beta^{*}) $$

which matches equation (4.55) of Tsiatis (2006).

### B.2 Mean-exchangeable controls

We derive EIF’s in the model $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}_{2}}$ . We can use $\varphi_{0,\textnormal{obs}}$ and $\varphi_{0,\textnormal{tgt}}$ as the initial influence functions $\varphi_{0}$ . By Proposition 2, we know $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{2}}=\mathcal{M}_{2}$ . It only remains to compute $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{2}}^{\perp}$ and the projection (7).

As in the derivation of $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{5}}^{\perp}$ in the main text, we characterize $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{2}}^{\perp}$ as the set of all functions $h\in\mathcal{H}_{R}$ for which $g=\Pi(h;\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{2}})=0$ . To that end we write $h(r)=zh_{11}(x)+(1-s)h_{01}(x)+s(1-z)h_{10}(x)$ and

$$ g=zg_{1}(x)+(1-z)g_{0}(x) $$

where

$$ \displaystyle(g_{0},g_{1}) \displaystyle=\argmin_{(f_{0},f_{1})\in\mathcal{H}_{X}^{2}}\mathbb{E}[(h(R)-Zf_{1}(X)-(1-Z)f_{0}(X))^{2}] \displaystyle=\argmin_{(f_{0},f_{1})\in\mathcal{H}_{X}^{2}}\mathbb{E}[Z(h_{11}(X)-f_{1}(X))^{2}] \displaystyle\quad+\mathbb{E}[(1-S)(h_{01}(X)-f_{0}(X))^{2}+S(1-Z)(h_{10}(X)-f_{0}(X))^{2}] \displaystyle=\argmin_{(f_{0},f_{1})\in\mathcal{H}_{X}^{2}}\mathbb{E}[p^{*}(X)e^{*}(X)(h_{11}(X)-f_{1}(X))^{2}+(1-p^{*}(X))(h_{01}(X)-f_{0}(X))^{2}] \displaystyle\quad+\mathbb{E}[p^{*}(X)(1-e^{*}(X))(h_{10}(X)-f_{0}(X))^{2}]. $$

The final equality follows by conditioning on $X$ , and expresses the objective as the expectation of a function of $X$ . Without any restrictions on $f_{0}$ and $f_{1}$ we can perform the minimization by minimizing the argument of the expectation pointwise in $x$ . Writing the first order conditions, we find they are satisfied by $f_{0}=f_{1}=0$ if and only if

$$ \displaystyle p^{*}(x)e^{*}(x)h_{11}(x) \displaystyle=0 \displaystyle p^{*}(x)(1-e^{*}(x))h_{10}(x)+(1-p^{*}(x))h_{00}(x) \displaystyle=0 $$

for all $x\in\mathcal{X}$ . Hence $h\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{2}}^{\perp}$ if and only if $h_{11}(x)=0$ and $h_{10}(x)=-\frac{1-p^{*}(x)}{p^{*}(x)(1-e^{*}(x))}h_{00}(x)$ , with $h_{00}\in\mathcal{H}_{X}$ free to vary. In other words

$$ \mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{2}}^{\perp}=\left\{r\mapsto\left[(1-s)-s(1-z)\frac{1-p^{*}(x)}{p^{*}(x)(1-e^{*}(x))}\right]\zeta(x)\Big|\zeta\in\mathcal{H}_{X}\right\} $$

and so by Theorem 2

$$ \mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{M}_{2}}^{\perp}=\left\{w\mapsto\left[(1-s)-s(1-z)\frac{1-p^{*}(x)}{p^{*}(x)(1-e^{*}(x))}\right]\zeta(x)(y-m^{*}(r))\Big|\zeta\in\mathcal{H}_{X}\right\}. $$

Now we compute the projection $g=\Pi(\varphi_{0};\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{M}_{2}}^{\perp})$ from (7) in terms of $\varphi_{0}$ . We write

$$ g(w)=\left[(1-s)-s(1-z)\frac{1-p^{*}(x)}{p^{*}(x)(1-e^{*}(x))}\right]\zeta(x)(y-m^{*}(r)) $$

where

$$ \zeta=\argmin_{h\in\mathcal{H}_{X}}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\varphi_{0,\textnormal{obs}}(W)-\left[(1-S)-S(1-Z)\frac{1-p^{*}(X)}{p^{*}(X)(1-e^{*}(X))}\right]h(X)(Y-m^{*}(R))\right)^{2}\right]. $$

By our usual approach of rewriting the objective as the expectation of a function of $X$ by iterated expectations and then minimizing the argument of this expectation pointwise, we get

$$ \zeta(x)=\frac{\mathbb{E}\left[\varphi_{0}(W)\left((1-S)-S(1-Z)\frac{1-p^{*}(X)}{p^{*}(X)(1-e^{*}(X))}\right)(Y-m^{*}(R))\mid X=x\right]}{(1-p^{*}(x))V_{00}^{*}(x)+\frac{(1-p^{*}(x))^{2}}{p^{*}(x)(1-e^{*}(x))}V_{10}^{*}(x)} $$

For $\varphi_{0}=\varphi_{0,\textnormal{obs}}$ we observe

$$ \mathbb{E}[\varphi_{0}(W;\tau_{\textnormal{obs}}^{*},\eta^{*})(1-S)(Y-m^{*}(R))\mid X]=0 $$

while

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[-\varphi_{0}(W;\tau_{\textnormal{obs}}^{*},\eta^{*})S(1-Z)\frac{1-p^{*}(X)}{p^{*}(X)(1-e^{*}(X))}(Y-m^{*}(R))\mid X\right]=\frac{(1-p^{*}(X))^{2}V_{10}^{*}(X)}{p^{*}(X)(1-e^{*}(X))(1-\rho^{*})}. $$

Hence

$$ \zeta(x)=\frac{(1-p^{*}(x))V_{10}^{*}(x)}{(1-\rho^{*})[V_{00}^{*}(x)p^{*}(x)(1-e^{*}(x))+V_{10}^{*}(x)(1-p^{*}(x))]} $$

and then the EIF for $\tau_{\textnormal{obs}}$ is

$$ \varphi_{\textnormal{eff}}(w;\tau_{\textnormal{obs}}^{*},\eta^{*})=\varphi_{0,\textnormal{obs}}(w;\tau_{\textnormal{obs}}^{*},\eta^{*})-\left[(1-s)-s(1-z)\frac{1-p^{*}(x)}{p^{*}(x)(1-e^{*}(x))}\right]\zeta(x)(y-m^{*}(z,x)) $$

which after algebraic simplification matches the expression given in Proposition 3 of Li et al. (2023b).

Repeating the calculation in the preceding paragraph with $\varphi_{0}=\varphi_{0,\textnormal{tgt}}$ gives the efficiency bound for $\tau_{\textnormal{tgt}}$ , also given in Proposition 3 of Li et al. (2023b).

### B.3 Parametric confounding bias and CATE

Following our three-step outline, we derive EIF’s in the model $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}_{3}}$ in terms of an arbitrary influence function $\varphi_{0}=\varphi_{0}(\cdot,\tau,\eta)$ for an RAL estimator of some generic pathwise-differentiable estimand $\tau$ . We later specialize to the estimand $\tau_{\textnormal{obs}}$ using $\varphi_{0}=\varphi_{0,\textnormal{obs}}$ , which verifies Theorem 4 of Yang et al. (2024).

We begin by deriving the outcome mean function tangent space $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{3}}$ . The method to do so is similar to that of Appendix B.1. In words, the model $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}_{3}}$ allows the control level ( $z=0$ ) of the outcome mean function to be an arbitrary function of $(s,x)$ . Then given the control level, the treatment level differs by $\mu(x;\beta)$ from the control level when $s=1$ , and by $\mu(x;\beta)+\phi(x;\theta)$ from the control level when $s=0$ . Formalizing this mathematically, this means that an arbitrary outcome mean function parametric submodel of $\mathcal{M}_{3}$ must take the form

$$ \addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:M_{3}{}_{s}ubmodel}m(r;\gamma)=f_{0}(s,x;\gamma_{0})+z[\mu(x;\beta(\gamma_{1}))+(1-s)\phi(x;\theta(\gamma_{2}))] $$

for some smooth mappings $\beta:\real^{s_{1}}\rightarrow\real^{p}$ and $\theta:\real^{s_{2}}\rightarrow\real^{q}$ , where $\gamma=(\gamma_{0}^{\top},\gamma_{1}^{\top},\gamma_{2}^{\top})^{\top}$ and $\gamma_{i}\in\real^{s_{i}}$ , $i=0,1,2$ . Then using the subscript notation for (partial) derivatives from Example 5 in Section 2 of the main text, for arbitrary $c=(c_{0}^{\top},c_{1}^{\top},c_{2}^{\top})^{\top}$ partitioned in the same way as $\gamma$ , we have

$$ c^{\top}m_{\gamma}(r;0)=c_{0}^{\top}f_{0}^{\prime}(s,x;0)+zc_{1}^{\top}J_{\beta}(0)^{\top}D_{\mu}(x;\beta^{*})+z(1-s)c_{2}^{\top}J_{\theta}(0)^{\top}D_{\phi}(x;\theta^{*}) $$

where $J_{\beta}(0)\in\real^{p\times s_{1}}$ and $J_{\theta}(0)\in\real^{q\times s_{2}}$ are the Jacobian matrices for the mappings $\beta$ and $\theta$ at 0, and

$$ D_{\mu}(x;\beta^{*})=\frac{\partial\mu(x;\beta)}{\partial\beta}\Big|_{\beta=\beta^{*}},\quad D_{\phi}(x;\theta^{*})=\frac{\partial\phi(x;\theta)}{\partial\theta}\Big|_{\theta=\theta^{*}}. $$

This is of the form

$$ \addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:S_{M}{}_{3}{}_{f}orm}f(s,x)+z[c_{1}^{\top}D_{\mu}(x;\beta^{*})+(1-s)c_{2}^{\top}D_{\phi}(x;\theta^{*})] $$

for some $f\in\mathcal{H}_{SX}$ , $c_{1}\in\real^{p}$ , $c_{2}\in\real^{q}$ (note we have overloaded the notation for $c_{1}$ and $c_{2}$ ). Conversely, we now show that any function of the form (50), for some $f\in\mathcal{H}_{SX}$ , $c_{1}\in\real^{p}$ , $c_{2}\in\real^{q}$ , lies in $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{3}}$ . To that end, consider the submodel of the form (49) with $s_{0}=1$ , $s_{1}=p$ , $s_{2}=q$ and $f(s,x)=m^{*}(s,0,x)+\gamma_{0}f(s,x)$ , $\beta(\gamma_{1})=\beta^{*}+\gamma_{1}$ , and $\theta(\gamma_{2})=\theta^{*}+\gamma_{2}$ . We observe that our function given by (50) is equivalent to $c^{\top}m_{\gamma}(r;0)$ for $c=(1,c_{1}^{\top},c_{2}^{\top})$ , and thus lies in $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{3}}$ by definition. We conclude that indeed,

$$ \addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:S_{M}{}_{3}}\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{3}}=\{r\mapsto f(s,x)+z[c_{1}^{\top}D_{\mu}(x;\beta^{*})+(1-s)c_{2}^{\top}D_{\phi}(x;\theta^{*})]\mid f\in\mathcal{H}_{SX},c_{1}\in\real^{p},c_{2}\in\real^{q}\}. $$

It remains to compute the orthogonal complement $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{3}}^{\perp}$ and then the projection (7). As in the other examples, we compute $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{3}}^{\perp}$ as the set of all functions $h\in\mathcal{H}_{R}$ for which $g=\Pi(h;\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{3}})=0$ . Given $h$ we write

$$ g(r)=f_{0}(s,x)+z[d_{1}^{\top}D_{\mu}(x;\beta^{*})+(1-s)d_{2}^{\top}D_{\phi}(x;\theta^{*})] $$

where

$$ (f_{0},d_{1},d_{2})=\argmin_{f\in\mathcal{H}_{SX},c_{1}\in\real^{p},c_{2}\in\real^{q}}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(h(R)-f(S,X)-Z[c_{1}^{\top}D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*})+(1-S)c_{2}^{\top}D_{\phi}(X;\theta^{*})]\right)^{2}\right]. $$

As we have seen, we can solve this minimization by rewriting the objective as the expectation of a function of solely $X$ via iterated expectations:

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left(h(R)-f(S,X)-Z[c_{1}^{\top}D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*})+(1-S)c_{2}^{\top}D_{\phi}(X;\theta^{*})]\right)^{2}\right] \displaystyle\quad=\mathbb{E}[p^{*}(X)e^{*}(X)(h_{11}(X)-f(1,X)-c_{1}^{\top}D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*}))^{2}]+\mathbb{E}[p^{*}(X)(1-e^{*}(X))(h_{10}(X)-f(1,X))^{2}] \displaystyle\quad+\mathbb{E}[(1-p^{*}(X))q^{*}(X)(h_{01}(X)-f(0,X)-c_{1}^{\top}D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*})-c_{2}^{\top}D_{\phi}(X;\theta^{*}))^{2}] \displaystyle\quad+\mathbb{E}[(1-p^{*}(X))(1-q^{*}(X))(h_{00}(X)-f(0,X))^{2}] $$

For fixed $c_{1}$ and $c_{2}$ , the minimizer of this objective in $f\in\mathcal{H}_{SX}$ takes the form $f(s,x)=sf(1,x)+(1-s)f(0,x)$ where $f(1,x)$ and $f(0,x)$ globally minimize the argument to the expectation, i.e. they satisfy the first-order conditions

$$ \displaystyle 0 \displaystyle=p^{*}(x)e^{*}(x)(h_{11}(x)-f(1,x)-c_{1}^{\top}D_{\mu}(x;\beta^{*}))+p^{*}(x)(1-e^{*}(x))(h_{10}(x)-f(1,x))^{2} \displaystyle 0 \displaystyle=(1-p^{*}(x))q^{*}(x)(h_{01}(x)-f(0,x)-c_{1}^{\top}D_{\mu}(x;\beta^{*})-c_{2}^{\top}D_{\phi}(X;\theta^{*})) \displaystyle\quad+(1-p^{*}(x))(1-q^{*}(x))(h_{00}(x)-f(0,x)) $$

Conversely for any fixed $f\in\mathcal{S}_{SX}$ , taking the derivative of the objective shows that the minimizers $c_{1}\in\real^{p}$ and $c_{2}\in\real^{q}$ must satisfy the first order conditions

$$ \displaystyle 0 \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[p^{*}(X)e^{*}(X)(h_{11}(X)-f_{1}(X)-c_{1}^{\top}D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*}))D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*})] \displaystyle\quad+\mathbb{E}[(1-p^{*}(X))q^{*}(X)(h_{01}(X)-f(0,X)-c_{1}^{\top}D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*})-c_{2}^{\top}D_{\phi}(X;\theta^{*}))D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*})] \displaystyle 0 \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[(1-p^{*}(X))q^{*}(X)(h_{01}(X)-f(0,X)-c_{1}^{\top}D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*})-c_{2}^{\top}D_{\phi}(X;\theta^{*}))D_{\phi}(X;\theta^{*})] $$

The four first-order conditions are satisfied with $f(0,x)=f(1,x)=0$ and $c_{1}=c_{2}=0$ if and only if

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[[p^{*}(X)e^{*}(X)h_{11}(X)+(1-p^{*}(X))q^{*}(X)h_{01}(X)]D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*})] \displaystyle=0 \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[(1-p^{*}(X))q^{*}(X)h_{01}(X)D_{\phi}(X;\theta^{*})] \displaystyle=0 \displaystyle e^{*}(x)h_{11}(x)+(1-e^{*}(x))h_{10}(x) \displaystyle=0 \displaystyle q^{*}(x)h_{01}(x)+(1-q^{*}(x))h_{00}(x) \displaystyle=0. $$

Thus $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{3}}^{\perp}$ is the set of all functions $h$ satisfying (52), (53), (54), and (55). Recognizing that (54) and (55) determine $h_{00}$ and $h_{10}$ in terms of $h_{11}$ and $h_{01}$ , respectively, which are free to vary other than the moment constraints given by (52) and (53), we can compactly write $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{3}}^{\perp}$ as the set of all mappings

$$ r\mapsto f(s,x)\left[z-(1-z)\left(\frac{se^{*}(x)}{1-e^{*}(x)}+\frac{(1-s)q^{*}(x)}{1-q^{*}(x)}\right)\right] $$

such that $f\in\mathcal{H}_{SX}$ with

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[(p^{*}(X)e^{*}(X)f(1,X)+(1-p^{*}(X))q^{*}(X)f(0,X))D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*})] \displaystyle=0\quad\text{and} \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[(1-p^{*}(X))q^{*}(X)f(1,X)D_{\phi}(X;\theta^{*})] \displaystyle=0. $$

Finally, we compute the projection (7). Given the initial influence function $\varphi_{0}$ , we have by the form of $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{3}}^{\perp}$ derived in the previous paragraph and Theorem 2 that

$$ \pi(\varphi_{0};\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{M}_{3}}^{\perp})=w\mapsto\left(s\Gamma_{1}^{*}(x)+(1-s)\Gamma_{0}^{*}(x)\right)\left(z-(1-z)\left[\frac{se^{*}(x)}{1-e^{*}(x)}+\frac{(1-s)q^{*}(x)}{1-q^{*}(x)}\right]\right)(y-m^{*}(r)) $$

where $\Gamma_{0}^{*}$ and $\Gamma_{1}^{*}$ solve the optimization problem

$$ \displaystyle\min_{\Gamma_{0}\in\mathcal{H}_{X},\Gamma_{1}\in\mathcal{H}_{X}}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\varphi_{0}(W;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})-\left[S\Gamma_{1}(X)+(1-S)\Gamma_{0}(X)\right]\nu^{*}(R)\right)^{2}\right] \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[[p^{*}(X)e^{*}(X)\Gamma_{1}(X)+(1-p^{*}(X))q^{*}(X)\Gamma_{0}(X)]D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*})]=0,\quad\text{and} \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[(1-p^{*}(X))q^{*}(X)\Gamma_{0}(X)D_{\phi}(X;\theta^{*})]=0 $$

with

$$ \nu^{*}(r)=\nu(r;\eta^{*})\text{ for }\nu(r;\eta)=\left[z-(1-z)\left(\frac{se^{*}(x)}{1-e^{*}(x)}+\frac{(1-s)q^{*}(x)}{1-q^{*}(x)}\right)\right](y-m^{*}(r)). $$

Once again, we rewrite the objective by conditioning on $X$ :

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\varphi_{0}(W;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})-\left(S\Gamma_{1}(X)+(1-S)\Gamma_{0}(X)\right)\nu^{*}(R)\right)^{2}\right] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\varphi_{0}(W;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})^{2}\mid X]+\mathbb{E}\left[\Gamma_{1}^{2}(X)p^{*}(X)e^{*}(X)\left(V_{11}^{*}(X)+\frac{e^{*}(X)}{1-e^{*}(X)}V_{10}^{*}(X)\right)\right] \displaystyle\quad+\mathbb{E}\left[\Gamma_{0}^{2}(X)(1-p^{*}(X))q^{*}(X)\left(V_{01}^{*}(X)+\frac{q^{*}(X)}{1-q^{*}(X)}V_{00}^{*}(X)\right)\right]-2\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{J}(X;\Gamma_{0},\Gamma_{1},\eta,\tau,\varphi_{0})] $$

where

$$ \mathcal{J}(x;\Gamma_{0},\Gamma_{1},\eta,\tau,\varphi_{0})=\mathbb{E}\left[\left(S\Gamma_{1}(X)+(1-S)\Gamma_{0}(X)\right)\nu^{*}(R)\varphi_{0}(W;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})\mid X=x\right]. $$

To deal with the two moment constraints, we introduce Lagrange multipliers $\Lambda_{1}\in\real^{p}$ and $\Lambda_{2}\in\real^{q}$ , similar to Appendix B.1. Dropping the constant $\mathbb{E}[\varphi_{0}(W;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})^{2}\mid X=x]$ term from the objective, the Lagrangian is $\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{L}(X)]$ where

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{L}(x) \displaystyle=\Gamma_{1}^{2}(x)p^{*}(x)e^{*}(x)\left(V_{11}^{*}(x)+\frac{e^{*}(x)}{1-e^{*}(x)}V_{10}^{*}(x)\right) \displaystyle\quad+\Gamma_{0}^{2}(x)(1-p^{*}(x))q^{*}(x)\left(V_{01}^{*}(x)+\frac{q^{*}(x)}{1-q^{*}(x)}V_{00}^{*}(x)\right) \displaystyle\quad-2\mathcal{J}(x;\Gamma_{0},\Gamma_{1},\eta^{*},\tau^{*},\varphi_{0}) \displaystyle\quad-2\Lambda_{1}^{\top}[p^{*}(x)e^{*}(x)\Gamma_{1}(x)+(1-p^{*}(x))q^{*}(x)\Gamma_{0}(x)]D_{\mu}(x;\beta^{*}) \displaystyle\quad-2\Lambda_{2}^{\top}[(1-p^{*}(x))q^{*}(x)\Gamma_{0}(x)D_{\phi}(x;\theta^{*})]. $$

We can minimize the Lagrangian over $\Gamma_{0}\in\mathcal{H}_{X}$ and $\Gamma_{1}\in\mathcal{H}_{X}$ by minimizing $\mathcal{L}(x)$ pointwise, giving

$$ \displaystyle\Gamma_{0}^{*}(x) \displaystyle=(1-q^{*}(x))\left(\frac{\Lambda_{1}^{\top}D_{\mu}(x;\beta^{*})+\Lambda_{2}^{\top}D_{\phi}(x;\theta^{*})}{(1-q^{*}(x))V_{01}^{*}(x)+q^{*}(x)V_{00}^{*}(x)}\right) \displaystyle\quad+\frac{(1-q^{*}(x))\mathcal{J}_{0}(x;\eta,\tau,\varphi_{0})}{(1-p^{*}(x))q^{*}(x)[(1-q^{*}(x))V_{01}^{*}(x)+q^{*}(x)V_{00}^{*}(x)]} \displaystyle\Gamma_{1}^{*}(x) \displaystyle=(1-e^{*}(x))\left(\frac{\Lambda_{1}^{\top}D_{\mu}(x;\beta^{*})}{(1-e^{*}(x))V_{11}^{*}(x)+e^{*}(x)V_{10}^{*}(x)}\right) \displaystyle\quad+\frac{(1-e^{*}(x))\mathcal{J}_{1}(x;\eta,\tau,\varphi_{0})}{p^{*}(x)e^{*}(x)[(1-e^{*}(x))V_{11}^{*}(x)+e^{*}(x)V_{10}^{*}(x)]} $$

where the Lagrange multipliers can be solved for by plugging back into the moment constraints and

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{1}(x;\eta,\tau,\varphi_{0}) \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[S\left(Z-(1-Z)\frac{e^{*}(X)}{1-e^{*}(X)}\right)(Y-m^{*}(R))\varphi_{0}(W;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})\mid X=x\right] \displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{0}(x;\eta,\tau,\varphi_{0}) \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[(1-S)\left(Z-(1-Z)\frac{q^{*}(X)}{1-q^{*}(X)}\right)(Y-m^{*}(R))\varphi_{0}(W;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})\mid X=x\right] $$

which come from writing

$$ \mathcal{J}(x;\eta,\tau,\varphi_{0})=\mathcal{J}_{1}(x;\eta,\tau,\varphi_{0})\Gamma_{1}(x)+\mathcal{J}_{1}(x;\eta,\tau,\varphi_{0})\Gamma_{0}(x). $$

This shows that $\Lambda_{1}$ and $\Lambda_{2}$ solve the linear matrix system

$$ \displaystyle A_{\mu\mu}\Lambda_{1}+A_{\mu\phi}\Lambda_{2} \displaystyle=-b_{\mu} \displaystyle A_{\mu\phi}^{\top}+A_{\phi\phi}\Lambda_{2} \displaystyle=-b_{\phi} $$

where

$$ \displaystyle A_{\mu\mu} \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{p^{*}(X)e^{*}(X)(1-e^{*}(X))}{(1-e^{*}(X))V_{11}^{*}(X)+e^{*}(X)V_{10}^{*}(X)}D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*})D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*})^{\top}\right] \displaystyle\quad+\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{(1-p^{*}(X))q^{*}(X)(1-q^{*}(X))}{(1-q^{*}(X))V_{01}^{*}(X)+q^{*}(X)V_{00}^{*}(X)}D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*})D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*})^{\top}\right]\in\real^{p\times p} \displaystyle A_{\mu\phi} \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{(1-p^{*}(X))q^{*}(X)(1-q^{*}(X))}{(1-q^{*}(X))V_{01}^{*}(X)+q^{*}(X)V_{00}^{*}(X)}D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*})D_{\phi}(X;\theta^{*})^{\top}\right]\in\real^{p\times q} \displaystyle A_{\phi\phi} \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{(1-p^{*}(X))q^{*}(X)(1-q^{*}(X))}{(1-q^{*}(X))V_{01}^{*}(X)+q^{*}(X)V_{00}^{*}(X)}D_{\phi}(X;\theta^{*})D_{\phi}(X;\theta^{*})^{\top}\right]\in\real^{q\times q} \displaystyle b_{\mu} \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{(1-e^{*}(X))\mathcal{J}_{1}(X;\eta^{*},\tau^{*},\varphi_{0})}{(1-e^{*}(X))V_{11}^{*}(X)+e^{*}(X)V_{10}^{*}(X)}D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*})\right] \displaystyle\quad+\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{(1-q^{*}(X))\mathcal{J}_{0}(X;\eta^{*},\tau^{*},\varphi_{0})}{(1-q^{*}(X))V_{01}^{*}(X)+q^{*}(X)V_{00}^{*}(X)}D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*})\right]\in\real^{p} \displaystyle b_{\phi} \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{(1-q^{*}(X))\mathcal{J}_{0}(X;\eta^{*},\tau^{*},\varphi_{0})}{(1-q^{*}(X))V_{01}^{*}(X)+q^{*}(X)V_{00}^{*}(X)}D_{\phi}(X;\theta^{*})\right]\in\real^{q}. $$

Taking $\varphi_{0}=\varphi_{0,\textnormal{obs}}$ to give a more explicit EIF for $\tau_{\textnormal{obs}}$ , we can easily compute

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{0}(x;\eta,\tau,\varphi_{0,\textnormal{obs}}) \displaystyle=0, \displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{1}(x;\eta,\tau,\varphi_{0,\textnormal{obs}}) \displaystyle=\frac{1-p^{*}(x)}{1-\rho^{*}}\left(V_{11}^{*}(x)+\frac{e^{*}(x)}{1-e^{*}(x)}V_{10}^{*}(x)\right). $$

Then some of the other expressions simplify:

$$ \displaystyle b_{\phi} \displaystyle=0 \displaystyle b_{\mu} \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1-p^{*}(X)}{1-\rho^{*}}D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*})\right]=\mathbb{E}[D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*})\mid S=0] \displaystyle\Gamma_{0}^{*}(x) \displaystyle=(1-q^{*}(x))\left(\frac{\Lambda_{1}^{\top}D_{\mu}(x;\beta^{*})+\Lambda_{2}^{\top}D_{\phi}(x;\theta^{*})}{(1-q^{*}(x))V_{01}^{*}(x)+q^{*}(x)V_{00}^{*}(x)}\right) \displaystyle\Gamma_{1}^{*}(x) \displaystyle=(1-e^{*}(x))\left(\frac{\Lambda_{1}^{\top}D_{\mu}(x;\beta^{*})}{(1-e^{*}(x))V_{11}^{*}(x)+e^{*}(x)V_{10}^{*}(x)}\right)+\frac{(1-p^{*}(x))}{(1-\rho^{*})p^{*}(x)e^{*}(x)}. $$

Solving the matrix equations for the Lagrange multipliers then gives

$$ \displaystyle\Lambda_{1} \displaystyle=-\left(A_{\mu\mu}-A_{\mu\phi}A_{\phi\phi}^{-1}A_{\mu\phi}^{\top}\right)^{-1}b_{\mu}, \displaystyle\Lambda_{2}=-A_{\phi\phi}^{-1}A_{\mu\mu}^{\top}\Lambda_{1} \displaystyle=A_{\phi\phi}^{-1}A_{\mu\mu}^{\top}\left(A_{\mu\mu}-A_{\mu\phi}A_{\phi\phi}^{-1}A_{\mu\phi}^{\top}\right)^{-1}b_{\mu}. $$

Putting everything together, the EIF for $\tau_{\textnormal{obs}}$ in the model $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}_{3}}$ is given by

$$ \displaystyle\varphi_{\textnormal{eff},\textnormal{obs}}^{(3)}(w;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})=\varphi_{0,\textnormal{obs}}(w;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})- \displaystyle\quad\left(s\Gamma_{1}^{*}(x)+(1-s)\Gamma_{0}^{*}(x)\right)\left(z-(1-z)\left[\frac{se^{*}(x)}{1-e^{*}(x)}+\frac{(1-s)q^{*}(x)}{1-q^{*}(x)}\right]\right)(y-m^{*}(r)) \displaystyle=\frac{1-s}{1-\rho^{*}}(m_{11}^{*}(x)-m_{10}^{*}(x)-\tau_{\textnormal{obs}}^{*})+s\Delta(z,x,y;\eta^{*})\left(\frac{1-p^{*}(x)}{p^{*}(x)(1-\rho^{*})}-e^{*}(x)\Gamma_{1}^{*}(x)\right) \displaystyle\quad-(1-s)\Gamma_{0}^{*}(x)\left(z-(1-z)\frac{q^{*}(x)}{1-q^{*}(x)}\right)(y-m^{*}(r)) $$

where $\Gamma_{0}^{*}$ and $\Gamma_{1}^{*}$ are given by (67) and (68), respectively, for $\Lambda_{1}$ and $\Lambda_{2}$ as in (69) and (70).

We can now verify this matches the result in Theorem 4 of Yang et al. (2024). While that Theorem is stated as giving the efficient score of $\tau_{\textnormal{obs}}$ rather than the efficient influence function of $\tau_{\textnormal{obs}}$ , this is incorrect according to S. Yang (personal communication, April 19, 2025). We correct the theorem below; essentially we must replace the efficient score $s_{\beta}(w;\eta^{*})$ for $\beta$ with the efficient influence function $\varphi_{\beta}(w;\eta^{*})$ for $\beta$ .

#### Theorem (Theorem 4, Yang et al. (2024), corrected).

Suppose Assumptions 1-3 hold. Then the EIF of $\tau_{\textnormal{obs}}$ at the truth $\tau_{\textnormal{obs}}^{*}$ is

$$ \addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:yang_{e}if}\tilde{\varphi}_{\textnormal{eff},\textnormal{obs}}^{(3)}(w;\tau_{\textnormal{obs}}^{*},\eta^{*})=\frac{1-s}{1-\rho^{*}}(m_{11}^{*}(x)-m_{10}^{*}(x)-\tau_{\textnormal{obs}}^{*})+\mathbb{E}\left[D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*})^{\top}\mid S=0\right]\varphi_{\beta}(w;\eta^{*}) $$

where $\varphi_{\beta}(w;\eta^{*})$ is the first $p$ components of

$$ \varphi_{\lambda}(w;\eta^{*})=\left(\mathbb{E}\left[s_{\lambda}(W;\eta^{*})s_{\lambda}(W;\eta^{*})^{\top}\right]\right)^{-1}s_{\lambda}(w;\eta^{*}) $$

for

$$ \displaystyle s_{\lambda}(w;\eta^{*}) \displaystyle=(Z-\mathbb{E}[Z\omega^{*}(R)\mid S,X]\mathbb{E}[\omega^{*}(R)\mid S,X]^{-1})\omega^{*}(R)(Y-m^{*}(R))\begin{bmatrix}D_{\mu}(x;\beta^{*})\\
D_{\phi}(x;\theta^{*})\end{bmatrix}, \displaystyle\omega^{*}(r) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{V^{*}(r)} $$

the efficient score for $\lambda=(\beta,\theta)$ , as given explicitly by Theorem 1 of Yang et al. (2024).

Showing that $\varphi_{\textnormal{eff},\textnormal{obs}}^{(3)}=\tilde{\varphi}_{\textnormal{eff},\textnormal{obs}}^{(3)}$ requires some algebra which we outline below. First we compute

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\omega^{*}(R)\mid S,X] \displaystyle=S\left(\frac{e^{*}(X)}{V_{11}^{*}(X)}+\frac{1-e^{*}(X)}{V_{10}^{*}(X)}\right)+(1-S)\left(\frac{q^{*}(X)}{V_{01}^{*}(X)}+\frac{1-q^{*}(X)}{V_{00}^{*}(X)}\right),\quad\text{ and } \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[Z\omega^{*}(R)\mid S,X] \displaystyle=S\left(\frac{e^{*}(X)}{V_{11}^{*}(X)}\right)+(1-S)\left(\frac{q^{*}(X)}{V_{01}^{*}(X)}\right). $$

Then

$$ \displaystyle\Omega^{*}(R) \displaystyle:=(Z-\mathbb{E}[Z\omega^{*}(R)\mid S,X]\mathbb{E}[\omega^{*}(R)\mid S,X]^{-1})\omega^{*}(R) \displaystyle\quad=S\frac{Z(1-e^{*}(X))-(1-Z)e^{*}(X)}{V_{10}^{*}(X)e^{*}(X)+V_{11}^{*}(X)(1-e^{*}(X))}+(1-S)\frac{Z(1-q^{*}(X))-(1-Z)q^{*}(X)}{V_{00}^{*}(X)q^{*}(X)+V_{01}^{*}(X)(1-q^{*}(X))}. $$

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[s_{\lambda}(W;\eta^{*})s_{\lambda}(W;\eta^{*})^{\top}] \displaystyle\quad=\mathbb{E}\left(\mathbb{E}[(\Omega^{*}(R))^{2}(Y-m^{*}(R))^{2}\mid X]\begin{bmatrix}D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*})D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*})^{\top}&D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*})D_{\phi}(X;\theta^{*})^{\top}\\
D_{\phi}(X;\theta^{*})D_{\mu}(X;\beta^{*})^{\top}&D_{\phi}(X;\theta^{*})D_{\phi}(X;\theta^{*})^{\top}\end{bmatrix}\right) $$

with

$$ \mathbb{E}[(\Omega^{*}(R))^{2}(Y-m^{*}(R))^{2}\mid X]=\frac{p^{*}(X)e^{*}(X)(1-e^{*}(X))}{V_{10}^{*}(X)e^{*}(X)+V_{11}^{*}(X)(1-e^{*}(X))}+\frac{(1-p^{*}(X))q^{*}(X)(1-q^{*}(X))}{(V_{00}^{*}(X)q^{*}(X)+V_{01}^{*}(X)(1-q^{*}(X))}. $$

$$ \mathbb{E}[s_{\lambda}(W;\eta^{*})s_{\lambda}(W;\eta^{*})^{\top}]=\begin{bmatrix}A_{\mu\mu}&A_{\mu\phi}\\
A_{\mu\phi}^{\top}&A_{\phi\phi}\end{bmatrix} $$

where $A_{\mu\mu}$ , $A_{\mu\phi}$ , and $A_{\phi\phi}$ are as in (58), (59), and (60). So

$$ \varphi_{\lambda}(w;\eta^{*})=\begin{bmatrix}A_{\mu\mu}&A_{\mu\phi}\\
A_{\mu\phi}^{\top}&A_{\phi\phi}\end{bmatrix}^{-1}s_{\lambda}(w;\eta^{*}) $$

and by block matrix inversion formulas

$$ \varphi_{\beta}(w;\eta^{*})=\begin{bmatrix}(A_{\mu\mu}-A_{\mu\phi}A_{\phi\phi}^{-1}A_{\mu\phi}^{\top})^{-1}&-(A_{\mu\mu}-A_{\mu\phi}A_{\phi\phi}^{-1}A_{\mu\phi}^{\top})^{-1}A_{\mu\phi}A_{\phi\phi}^{-1}\end{bmatrix}s_{\lambda}(w;\eta^{*}). $$

where the last equality follows by (67) and (68). Plugging into (74) verifies that indeed, $\varphi_{\textnormal{eff},\textnormal{obs}}^{(3)}=\tilde{\varphi}_{\textnormal{eff},\textnormal{obs}}^{(3)}$ .

### B.4 Linear confounding bias

Here we derive the EIF for an arbitrary scalar estimand $\tau$ , which can be estimated by an RAL estimator with influence function $\varphi_{0}$ , in the linear confounding bias model $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}_{4}}$ .

As argued in the main text, $\mathcal{M}_{4}$ is a linear space so $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{4}}=\mathcal{M}_{4}$ by Proposition 2. The remainder of the EIF derivation closely follows the outcome-mediated selection bias example in Section 2.3. As in that example, we note $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{4}}^{\perp}$ is precisely set of all functions $f\in\mathcal{H}_{R}$ for which the projection $g=\Pi(f;\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{4}})$ is zero. Given $f$ , by the form of $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{4}}=\mathcal{M}_{4}$ we can write

$$ g(r)=s(1-z)g_{1}(x)+(1-s)zg_{2}(x)+(1-s)(1-z)g_{3}(x)+sz\kappa(x;\beta,g_{1},g_{2},g_{3}) $$

where $g_{1},g_{2},g_{3}$ in $\mathcal{H}_{X}$ and $\beta\in\real^{q}$ minimize the objective

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{O}(g_{1},g_{2},g_{3},\beta) \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\left(f(R)-S(1-Z)g_{1}(X)-(1-S)Zg_{2}(X)-(1-S)(1-Z)g_{3}(X)-SZ\kappa(X;\beta,g_{1},g_{2},g_{3})\right)^{2}\right] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[p^{*}(X)e^{*}(X)(f_{11}(X)-\kappa(X;\beta,g_{1},g_{2},g_{3}))^{2}+p^{*}(X)(1-e^{*}(X))(f_{10}(X)-g_{1}(X))^{2}] \displaystyle\quad+\mathbb{E}[(1-p^{*}(X))r^{*}(X)(f_{01}(X)-g_{2}(X))^{2}+(1-p^{*}(X))(1-r^{*}(X))(f_{00}(X)-g_{3}(X))^{2}] $$

over $\mathcal{H}_{X}^{3}\times\real^{q}$ , for

$$ \kappa(x;\beta,g_{1},g_{2},g_{3})=g_{1}(x)+g_{2}(x)-g_{3}(x)+\psi(x)^{\top}\beta. $$

The second equality follows from writing

$$ f(R)=SZf_{11}(X)+S(1-Z)f_{10}(X)+(1-S)Zf_{01}(X)+(1-S)(1-Z)f_{00}(X) $$

and conditioning on $X$ . With the objective now an expectation of a function of $X$ , for fixed $\beta$ we can minimize over $g_{1}$ , $g_{2}$ , and $g_{3}$ pointwise to obtain the first-order conditions

$$ \displaystyle 0 \displaystyle=-p^{*}(x)e^{*}(x)(f_{11}(x)-\kappa(x;\beta,g_{1},g_{2},g_{3}))-p^{*}(x)(1-e^{*}(x))(f_{10}(x)-g_{1}(x)) \displaystyle 0 \displaystyle=-p^{*}(x)e^{*}(x)(f_{11}(x)-\kappa(x;\beta,g_{1},g_{2},g_{3}))-(1-p^{*}(x))r^{*}(x)(f_{01}(x)-g_{2}(x)) \displaystyle 0 \displaystyle=p^{*}(x)e^{*}(x)(f_{11}(x)-\kappa(x;\beta,g_{1},g_{2},g_{3}))-(1-p^{*}(x))(1-r^{*}(x))(f_{00}(x)-g_{3}(x)) $$

for all $x\in\mathcal{X}$ . Further, setting the partial derivative of the objective with respect to $\beta$ equal to zero yields the additional first-order condition

$$ \mathbb{E}[p^{*}(X)e^{*}(X)(f_{11}(X)-\kappa(X;\beta,g_{1},g_{2},g_{3}))\psi(X)]=0. $$

Rearranging, we see these first-order conditions are satisfied by $g=0$ (i.e. $g_{1}=g_{2}=g_{3}=0$ , $\beta=0$ ) if and only if

$$ \displaystyle(1-e^{*}(x))f_{10}(x) \displaystyle=-e^{*}(x)f_{11}(x) \displaystyle(1-p^{*}(x))r^{*}(x)f_{01}(x) \displaystyle=-p^{*}(x)e^{*}(x)f_{11}(x) \displaystyle(1-p^{*}(x))(1-r^{*}(x))f_{00}(x) \displaystyle=p^{*}(x)e^{*}(x)f_{11}(x) \displaystyle 0 \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[p^{*}(X)e^{*}(X)f_{11}(X)\psi(X)\right] $$

for all $x\in\mathcal{X}$ . So $\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{4}}$ is the set of all functions $f\in\mathcal{H}_{R}$ satisfying these equations, and by Theorem 2

$$ \mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{M}_{4}}^{\perp}=\{w\mapsto f(r)(y-m^{*}(r))\mid f\in\mathcal{H}_{R}\text{ satisfies~\eqref{eq:T_M_perp_1},~\eqref{eq:T_M_perp_2},~\eqref{eq:T_M_perp_3}, and \eqref{eq:T_M_perp_4}}. $$

Noting that (75), (76), and (77) determine $f_{10}$ , $f_{01}$ , and $f_{00}$ in terms of $f_{11}$ and letting $\nu(x)=p^{*}(x)e^{*}(x)f_{11}(x)$ , we can write this succinctly as

$$ \addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:T_{M}{}_{1}{}_{p}erp}\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{M}_{4}}^{\perp}=\{w\mapsto h(r;\eta^{*})\nu(x)(y-m^{*}(r))\mid\nu\in\mathcal{H}_{X},\ \mathbb{E}[\nu(X)\psi(X)]=0\}. $$

where $h(r;\eta)$ is as in (30).

To compute the projection (7), as in the other examples we condition on $X$ to write the objective as the expectation of a function of $X$ and minimize this function pointwise. Unlike in the projection for computing $\varphi_{\textnormal{eff}}^{(5)}$ in the main text, but like the computation in Appendix B.1 for the EIF in the restricted moment model, we deal with the constraints using Lagrange multipliers. By (8), an arbitrary element $g\in\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{M}_{4}}^{\perp}$ takes the form

$$ g(w)=h(r;\eta^{*})\nu(x)(y-m^{*}(r)) $$

for some $\nu\in\mathcal{H}_{X}$ with $\mathbb{E}[\nu(X)\psi(X)]=0$ . Then the EIF is $\varphi_{\textnormal{eff}}^{(4)}=\varphi_{0}-g_{\textnormal{eff}}^{(4)}$ where

$$ g_{\textnormal{eff}}^{(4)}(w)=h(r;\eta^{*})\nu^{*}(x;\varphi_{0})(y-m^{*}(r)) $$

for $\nu^{*}(\cdot;\varphi_{0})$ solving the optimization problem

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\varphi_{0}(W;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})-h(R;\eta^{*})\nu(X)(Y-m^{*}(R))\right)^{2}\right]\mbox{over $\nu\in\mathcal{H}_{X}$} \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\nu(X)\psi(X)]=0 $$

We eliminate the constraint by introducing Lagrange multipliers $\lambda\in\real^{q}$ , and then rewrite the Lagrangian by conditioning on $X$ :

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\tilde{g}(X;\nu)]\mbox{ over $\nu\in\mathcal{H}_{X}$}\mbox{ where } \displaystyle\tilde{g}(X;\nu) \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\varphi_{0}(W;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})-h(R;\eta^{*})\nu(X)(Y-m^{*}(R))\right)^{2}\mid X\right] \displaystyle=\nu(X)^{2}\mathbb{E}[h^{2}(R;\eta^{*})(Y-m^{*}(R))^{2}\mid X]-2\nu(X)I(X;\eta^{*},\tau^{*},\varphi_{0})-2\nu(X)\lambda^{\top}\psi(X)\  $$

Since $\tilde{g}(x;\nu)$ is quadratic in $\nu$ , the minimizer is

$$ \nu^{*}(x)=\frac{I(x;\eta^{*},\tau^{*},\varphi_{0})+\lambda^{\top}\psi(x)}{\Sigma(x;\eta^{*})} $$

where $I(x;\eta,\tau,\varphi_{0})$ is given by (31). This matches the formula for $\nu(x;\eta^{*},\tau^{*},\varphi_{0})$ in (32), upon noting that

$$ p^{*}(x)e^{*}(x)\mathbb{E}[h^{2}(R;\eta^{*})(Y-m^{*}(R))^{2}\mid X=x]=\Sigma(x;\eta^{*}) $$

for $\Sigma(x;\eta)$ as in (33). We solve for the Lagrange multiplier $\lambda$ using the constraint

$$ \mathbb{E}[\nu^{*}(X;\nu_{0})\psi(X)]=0 $$

which gives $\lambda=\lambda(\eta^{*},\tau^{*},\eta_{0})$ as in (34). Thus

$$ g_{\textnormal{eff}}^{(4)}(w)=h(r;\eta)\nu(x;\eta^{*},\tau^{*},\varphi_{0})(y-m^{*}(r)) $$

which shows (29).

### B.5 Known RCT propensity scores

We characterize the EIF $\tilde{\varphi}_{\textnormal{eff}}$ for any pathwise differentiable estimand $\tau\in\real$ in the model $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}_{\mathcal{M}}$ in terms of the EIF $\varphi_{\textnormal{eff}}$ for the analogous model $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}}$ where the RCT propensity score $e^{*}$ is unknown. Our result will work for any mean function collection $\mathcal{M}$ satisfying the conditions of Corollary 1.

It is easy to see that the space

$$ \tilde{\mathcal{U}}=\{w\mapsto sh(x)(z-e^{*}(x))\mid h\in\mathcal{H}_{X}\} $$

is orthogonal to $\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\perp}$ . Hence

$$ \tilde{\varphi}_{\textnormal{eff}}=\varphi_{0}-\Pi(\varphi_{0};\tilde{\mathcal{T}}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\perp})=\varphi_{0}-\Pi(\varphi_{0};\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\perp})-\Pi(\varphi_{0};\tilde{\mathcal{U}})=\varphi_{\textnormal{eff}}-\Pi(\varphi_{0};\tilde{\mathcal{U}}) $$

where as in the main text, $\varphi_{0}$ is the influence function of any initial RAL estimator. Thus it suffices to compute $\Pi(\varphi_{0};\tilde{\mathcal{U}})$ . By definition

$$ \Pi(\varphi_{0};\tilde{\mathcal{U}})(w)=s\nu^{*}(x)(z-e^{*}(x)) $$

where

$$ \nu^{*}=\argmin_{h\in\mathcal{H}_{X}}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\varphi_{0}(W)-Sh(X)(Z-e^{*}(X))\right)^{2}\right]. $$

As usual, we expand the right-hand side and condition on $X$ :

$$ \displaystyle\argmin_{h\in\mathcal{H}_{X}}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\varphi_{0}(W)-Sh(X)(Z-e^{*}(X))\right)^{2}\right] \displaystyle\quad=\argmin_{h\in\mathcal{H}_{X}}\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbb{E}[S(Z-e^{*}(X))^{2}\mid X]h(X)^{2}-2\mathbb{E}[S(Z-e^{*}(X))\varphi_{0}(W)\mid X]h(X)\right] $$

We compute

$$ \mathbb{E}[S(Z-e^{*}(X))^{2}\mid X]=p^{*}(X)e^{*}(X)(1-e^{*}(X)) $$

and so by minimizing pointwise we conclude

$$ \nu^{*}(x)=\frac{\mathbb{E}[S(Z-e^{*}(X))\varphi_{0}(W)\mid X=x]}{p^{*}(x)e^{*}(x)(1-e^{*}(x))}. $$

For $\varphi_{0}\in\{\varphi_{0,\textnormal{rct}},\varphi_{0,\textnormal{obs}},\varphi_{0,\textnormal{tgt}}\}$ we have

$$ \mathbb{E}[S(Z-e^{*}(X))\varphi_{0}(W)\mid X]=0 $$

and hence $\nu^{*}(x)=0$ . Thus, knowing the RCT propensity score does not improve the semiparametric efficiency bound for estimating $\tau_{\textnormal{rct}}$ , $\tau_{\textnormal{obs}}$ , or $\tau_{\textnormal{tgt}}$ in any semiparametric model restricting the outcome mean function. In particular, the EIF’s $\varphi_{\textnormal{eff}}^{(k)},k=1,2,3,4,5$ in the models $\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{M}_{k}}$ for these estimands are also the EIF’s in the corresponding models $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}_{\mathcal{M}_{k}}$ .

## Appendix C Conditions for efficiency

In this section, we provide specific primitive conditions under which the cross-fit one-step estimators $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{eff}}^{(4)}$ and $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{eff}}^{(5)}$ defined in Section 4 indeed attain the efficiency bound, by proving that these conditions imply those of the generalized Lemma in Section A.5. One condition is the following overlap assumption; a version of overlap is needed to even identify causal estimands in the nonparametric model.

#### Assumption 3 (Overlap).

There exists $\delta>0$ such that $e^{*}(x)\in[\delta,1-\delta]$ whenever $p^{*}(x)>0$ , $r^{*}(x)\in[\delta,1-\delta]$ , and $p^{*}(x)\in\{0\}\cup[\delta,1-\delta]$ for all $x\in\mathcal{X}$ .

#### Remark 1.

The condition on $p^{*}(x)$ in Assumption 3 presumes that the support of the covariates in the RCT is contained within the support of the covariates of the observational dataset. Unlike typical analyses, we allow this inclusion to be strict since assumptions like linear confounding bias or outcome mediated selection permit extrapolation of the CATE beyond the support of the covariates in the RCT.

We also need the nuisance estimates to satisfy a similar overlap condition, as well as $o_{p}(N^{-1/4})$ root-mean-square convergence rates, typical in the double machine learning literature.

#### Assumption 4.

Cross-fit estimates of the nuisance functions $e^{*}$ , $m_{10}^{*}$ , $m_{01}^{*}$ , $m_{00}^{*}$ , $r^{*}$ , and $p^{*}$ satisfy Assumption 3 along with the following for each $k=1,\ldots,K$ :

- • (Convergence of infinite-dimensional nuisance estimates) $\displaystyle\|\hat{e}^{(-k)}-e^{*}\|_{2,P^{*}}+\|\hat{m}_{sz}^{(-k)}-m_{sz}^{*}\|_{2,P^{*}}+\|\hat{r}^{(-k)}-r^{*}\|_{2,P^{*}}+\|\hat{p}^{(-k)}-p^{*}\|_{2,P^{*}}$ (80) $\displaystyle\quad=o_{p}(N^{-1/4}),\quad(s,z)\neq(1,1)$ (81)

- • (Overlap in infinite-dimensional nuisance estimates) With probability tending to 1 as $N\rightarrow\infty$ , the statement of Assumption 3 holds with $e^{*}$ , $r^{*}$ , and $p^{*}$ replaced by their estimates $\hat{e}^{(-k)}$ , $\hat{r}^{(-k)}$ , and $\hat{p}^{(-k)}$ , respectively.

### C.1 Linear confounding bias

#### Proposition.

Suppose Assumption 3 holds and $m^{*}\in\mathcal{M}_{4}$ . Consider a function

$$ g(w;\eta)=h(r;\eta)\zeta(x;\eta)(y-m(r))+s(z-e^{*}(x))h_{2}(x;\eta) $$

where $\eta$ includes $(p(\cdot),e(\cdot),m(\cdot),q(\cdot),V(\cdot))$ , $h(r;\eta)$ is as in (30), $h_{2}(\cdot;\eta^{*})\in\mathcal{H}_{X}$ , and $\zeta^{*}(x)=\zeta(x;\eta^{*})$ satisfies $\mathbb{E}[\zeta^{*}(X)\psi(X)]=0$ so that $g^{*}(\cdot)=g(\cdot;\eta^{*})\in\tilde{\mathcal{T}}_{\mathcal{M}_{4}}^{\perp}$ by (79) and Corollary 1. $$ \addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:m_{h}at_{r}espect}\hat{m}_{11}^{(-k)}(x)=\hat{m}_{10}^{(-k)}(x)+\hat{m}_{01}^{(-k)}(x)-\hat{m}_{00}^{(-k)}(x)+\psi(x)^{\top}\hat{\theta}^{(-k)},\quad k=1,\ldots,K $$

### C.2 Outcome-mediated selection bias

#### Proposition.

Suppose Assumption 3 holds and $m^{*}\in\mathcal{M}_{5}$ . Consider a function

$$ g(w;\eta)=f(r;\eta)\zeta(x;\eta)(y-m(r))+s(z-e^{*}(x))h_{2}(x;\eta) $$

where $\eta$ includes $(p(\cdot),e(\cdot),m(\cdot),q(\cdot))$ , $f(r;\eta)$ is as in (20), $h_{2}(\cdot;\eta^{*})\in\mathcal{H}_{X}$ , and $\zeta^{*}(\cdot)=\zeta(\cdot;\eta^{*})\in\mathcal{H}_{X}$ so that $g^{*}(\cdot)=g(\cdot;\eta^{*})\in\tilde{\mathcal{T}}_{\mathcal{M}_{5}}^{\perp}$ by (21) and Corollary 1. Further suppose that there are cross-fit estimates $\hat{\eta}^{(-k)}$ of $\eta^{*}$ satisfying Assumption 4 with

$$ \addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:m_{h}at_{r}espect_{s}election}\hat{m}_{11}^{(-k)}(x)=\ell^{-1}\left(\ell\left(\hat{m}_{10}^{(-k)}(x)\right)+\ell\left(\hat{m}_{01}^{(-k)}(x)\right)-\ell\left(\hat{m}_{00}^{(-k)}(x)\right)\right),\quad k=1,\ldots,K. $$

Finally, assume that the rate conditions $\|\zeta(\cdot;\hat{\eta}^{(-k)})-\zeta(\cdot;\eta^{*})\|_{2,P^{*}}=o_{p}(N^{-1/4})$ and $\|h_{2}\left(\cdot;\hat{\eta}^{(-k)}\right)-h_{2}\left(\cdot;\eta^{*}\right)\|_{2,P^{*}}=o_{p}(1)$ hold, and additionally that $\max(|\zeta(x;\eta^{*})|,|\zeta(x,\hat{\eta}^{(-k)})|)\leqslant C$ for all $(s,z)\in\{0,1\}^{2}$ , $x\in\mathcal{X}$ , and folds $k=1,\ldots,K$ . Then the Lemma in Section A.5 holds with $\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{M}_{5}$ , $g(\cdot;\tau^{*},\eta^{*})=g(\cdot;\eta^{*})$ , and $g\left(\cdot;\hat{\tau}^{(-k)},\hat{\eta}^{(-k)}\right)=g\left(\cdot;\hat{\eta}^{(-k)}\right)$ .

#### Proof.

The proof is similar in structure to the argument in Appendix C.1. We must show the boundedness, approximate tangency, and rate conditions in the Lemma of Appendix A.5 with

$$ \displaystyle h_{1}^{*}(r) \displaystyle=f(r;\eta^{*})\zeta(x;\eta^{*}),\quad\hat{h}_{1}^{(-k)}(r)=f\left(r;\hat{\eta}^{(-k)}\right)\zeta\left(x;\hat{\eta}^{(-k)}\right) \displaystyle h_{2}^{*}(x) \displaystyle=h_{2}(x;\eta^{*}),\quad\hat{h}_{2}^{(-k)}(x)=h_{2}\left(x;\hat{\eta}^{(-k)}\right). $$

Boundedness: We have $V^{*}(s,z,x)\leqslant 1$ trivially since $Y\in[0,1]$ . Furthermore by the overlap condition (Assumption 3) it is clear that $f(r;\eta^{*})$ is uniformly upper bounded for $P^{*}$ -almost all $r$ , a qualifier we omit hereafter in all inequalities and equalities in this proof, in absolute value by $C\delta^{-2}$ . Similarly, by the overlap in infinite-dimensional nuisance estimates condition in Assumption 4, we have $f\left(r;\hat{\eta}^{(-k)}\right)$ is uniformly upper bounded in absolute value by $C\delta^{-2}$ for all $k=1,\ldots,K$ . With $\max\left(|\zeta(x;\eta^{*})|,\Big|\zeta\left(x;\hat{\eta}^{(-k)}\right)\Big|\right)\leqslant C$ for all $k$ , we conclude that $\max\left(\|h_{1}^{*}\|_{\infty,P^{*}},\left\|\hat{h}_{1}^{(-k)}\right\|_{\infty,P^{*}}\right)\leqslant C^{2}\delta^{-2}$ . ∎

Approximate tangency: Fix $k\in\{1,\ldots,K\}$ and consider the one-dimensional outcome mean function parametric submodel

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{m}(s,z,x;t) \displaystyle=m^{*}(s,z,x)+t\left(\hat{m}^{(-k)}(s,z,x)-m^{*}(s,z,x)\right),\quad(s,z)\neq(1,1) \displaystyle\tilde{m}(1,1,x;t) \displaystyle=\ell^{-1}(\ell(\tilde{m}(1,0,x;t))+\ell(\tilde{m}(0,1,x;t))-\ell(\tilde{m}(0,0,x;t))) $$

indexed by $t$ in an open subset of containing $[0,1]$ , where we note that $\tilde{m}(s,z,x;1)=\hat{m}^{(-k)}(s,z,x)$ for all $(s,z)$ (including for $(s,z)=(1,1)$ by (84)). The overlap and nuisance in overlap conditions ensure that this is a well-defined submodel in the sense that it does not violate the restriction $\epsilon<m<1-\epsilon$ in the definition of $\mathcal{M}_{5}$ in (5).

By Taylor’s theorem, for each $x$ there exists $\tilde{t}=\tilde{t}(x)\in[0,1]$ for which

$$ \displaystyle\hat{m}^{(-k)}(1,1,x)-m^{*}(1,1,x) \displaystyle=\tilde{m}(1,1,x;1)-\tilde{m}(1,1,x;0) \displaystyle=\frac{\partial\tilde{m}(1,1,x;t)}{\partial t}\Big|_{t=0}+\frac{1}{2}\frac{\partial^{2}\tilde{m}(1,1,x;t)}{\partial t^{2}}\Big|_{t=\tilde{t}(x)} $$

which implies that for all $(s,z,x)$ we have

$$ \hat{m}^{(-k)}(s,z,x)-m^{*}(s,z,x)-\hat{R}^{(-k)}(s,z,x)=\frac{\partial\tilde{m}(s,z,x;t)}{\partial t}\Big|_{t=0} $$

for

$$ \hat{R}^{(-k)}(s,z,x)=\frac{sz}{2}\frac{\partial^{2}\tilde{m}(1,1,x;t)}{\partial t^{2}}\Big|_{t=\tilde{t}(x)}. $$

since evidently

$$ \frac{\partial\tilde{m}(s,z,x;t)}{\partial t}=m^{(-k)}(s,z,x)-m^{*}(s,z,x) $$

for $(s,z)\neq(1,1)$ . Hence $\hat{m}^{(-k)}-m^{*}-\hat{R}^{(-k)}\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathcal{M}_{1}}$ and it remains to show the necessary rate conditions on $\hat{R}^{(-k)}$ .

By the chain rule

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\partial\tilde{m}(1,1,x;t)}{\partial t} \displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{(s,z)\neq(1,1)}\ell^{\prime}(\tilde{m}(s,z,x;t))\left(\hat{m}^{(-k)}_{sz}(x)-m^{*}_{sz}(x)\right)}{\ell^{\prime}(\tilde{m}(1,1,x;t))}. $$

and then by the quotient rule

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\partial^{2}\tilde{m}(1,1,x;t)}{\partial t^{2}} \displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{(s,z)\neq(1,1)}\ell^{\prime\prime}(\tilde{m}(s,z,x;t))\left(\hat{m}^{(-k)}_{sz}(x)-m^{*}_{sz}(x)\right)^{2}-\ell^{\prime\prime}(\tilde{m}(1,1,x;t))\left(\frac{\partial\tilde{m}(1,1,x;t)}{\partial t}\right)^{2}}{\ell^{\prime}(\tilde{m}(1,1,x;t))}. $$

We also note that for each $(s,z),(s^{\prime},z^{\prime})\in\{0,1\}^{2}$ , we have

$$ \addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:m_{e}rror_{p}roduct}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}S_{i}Z_{i}\left|\hat{m}_{sz}^{(-k)}(X_{i})-m_{sz}^{*}(X_{i})\right|\left|\hat{m}_{s^{\prime}z^{\prime}}^{(-k)}(X_{i})-m_{s^{\prime}z^{\prime}}^{*}(X_{i})\right|=o_{p}(N^{-1/2}) $$

by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, the rate condition $\left\|\hat{m}^{(-k)}-m^{*}\right\|_{2,P^{*}}=o_{p}(N^{-1/4})$ , and Lemma 4.

Note $\ell^{\prime}$ and $\ell^{\prime\prime}$ are uniformly bounded, i.e. there exist $0<c<C<\infty$ for which

$$ \displaystyle c\leqslant\ell^{\prime}(\tilde{m}(s,z,x;t))\leqslant C,\quad|\ell^{\prime\prime}(\tilde{m}(s,z,x;t))|\leqslant C $$

for all $(s,z,x)$ , $t\in[0,1]$ . Hence

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\Big|\hat{R}^{(-k)}(R_{i})\Big| \displaystyle\quad\leqslant\frac{C}{2c|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}S_{i}Z_{i}\left[\sup_{t\in[0,1]}\left(\frac{\partial\tilde{m}(1,1,X_{i};t)}{\partial t}\right)^{2}+\sum_{(s,z)\neq(1,1)}\left(\hat{m}_{sz}^{(-k)}(X_{i})-m^{*}_{sz}(X_{i})\right)^{2}\right]. $$

But

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}S_{i}Z_{i}\sup_{t\in[0,1]}\left(\frac{\partial\tilde{m}(1,1,X_{i};t)}{\partial t}\right)^{2} \displaystyle\quad\leqslant\frac{1}{c^{2}|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}S_{i}Z_{i}\sup_{t\in[0,1]}\left(\sum_{(s,z)\neq(1,1)}\ell^{\prime}(\tilde{m}(s,z,X_{i};t))\left(\hat{m}_{sz}^{(-k)}(X_{i})-m_{sz}^{*}(X_{i})\right)\right)^{2} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{c^{2}|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}S_{i}Z_{i}\sup_{t\in[0,1]}\sum_{(s,z)\neq(1,1)}\sum_{(s^{\prime},z^{\prime})\neq(1,1)}\ell^{\prime}(\tilde{m}(s,z,X_{i};t))\ell^{\prime}(\tilde{m}(s^{\prime},z^{\prime},X_{i};t))\left(\hat{m}_{sz}^{(-k)}(X_{i})-m_{sz}^{*}(X_{i})\right)\times \displaystyle\qquad\left(\hat{m}_{s^{\prime}z^{\prime}}^{(-k)}(X_{i})-m_{s^{\prime}z^{\prime}}^{*}(X_{i})\right) \displaystyle\leqslant\frac{C^{2}}{c^{2}|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\sum_{(s,z)\neq(1,1)}\sum_{(s^{\prime},z^{\prime})\neq(1,1)}S_{i}Z_{i}|\hat{m}_{sz}^{(-k)}(X_{i})-m_{sz}^{*}(X_{i})||\hat{m}_{s^{\prime}z^{\prime}}^{(-k)}(X_{i})-m_{s^{\prime}z^{\prime}}^{*}(X_{i})| \displaystyle=o_{p}(N^{-1/2})\text{ by~\eqref{eq:m_error_product}} $$

while

$$ \frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\sum_{(s,z)\neq(1,1)}S_{i}Z_{i}\left(\hat{m}_{sz}^{(-k)}(X_{i})-m_{sz}^{*}(X_{i})\right)^{2}=o_{p}(N^{-1/2})\text{ by~\eqref{eq:m_error_product}.} $$

This completes the proof of the required rate conditions on $\hat{R}^{(-k)}$ .

Rate conditions: Fixing $k\in\{1,\ldots,K\}$ , we have $\|\hat{m}^{(-k)}-m^{*}\|_{2,P^{*}}=o_{p}(N^{-1/4})$ by (80) and (84). With $\|\hat{h}_{2}^{(-k)}-h_{2}^{*}\|_{2,P^{*}}=o_{p}(1)$ by assumption, to show the rate conditions it suffices to show that $\|\hat{h}_{1}^{(-k)}-h_{1}^{*}\|_{2,P^{*}}=o_{p}(N^{-1/4})$ . To that end, we write

$$ \hat{h}_{1}^{(-k)}(r)-h_{1}^{*}(r)=f\left(r;\hat{\eta}^{(-k)}\right)\zeta\left(x;\hat{\eta}^{(-k)}\right)-f(r;\eta^{*})\zeta(x;\eta^{*}) $$

and note that since $|f(r;\eta^{*})|\leqslant C$ as shown above and we have $\max\left(|\zeta(x;\eta^{*})|,\Big|\zeta\left(x;\hat{\eta}^{(-k)}\right)\Big|\right)\leqslant C$ and $\|\zeta(x;\hat{\eta}^{(-k)})-\zeta(x;\eta^{*})\|_{2,P^{*}}=o_{p}(N^{-1/4})$ by assumption, it suffices by Lemma 3 to show that

$$ \addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:f_{r}ate}\int\left(f\left(r;\hat{\eta}^{(-k)}\right)-f(r;\eta^{*})\right)^{2}dP^{*}(w)=o_{p}(N^{-1/2}). $$

We compute

$$ \displaystyle\left(f\left(s,z,x;\hat{\eta}^{(-k)}\right)-f(s,z,x;\eta^{*})\right)^{2} \displaystyle=sz\left(\ell\left(\hat{m}_{11}^{(-k)}(x)\right)-\ell(m_{11}^{*}(x))\right)^{2} \displaystyle\quad+s(1-z)\left(\frac{\hat{e}^{(-k)}(x)\ell^{\prime}\left(\hat{m}_{10}^{(-k)}(x)\right)}{1-\hat{e}^{(-k)}(x)}-\frac{e^{*}(x)\ell^{\prime}(m_{10}^{*}(x))}{1-e^{*}(x)}\right)^{2} \displaystyle\quad+(1-s)z\left(\frac{\hat{p}^{(-k)}(x)\hat{e}^{(-k)}(x)\ell^{\prime}\left(\hat{m}_{01}^{(-k)}(x)\right)}{(1-\hat{p}^{(-k)}(x))\hat{q}^{(-k)}(x)}-\frac{p^{*}(x)e^{*}(x)\ell^{\prime}(m_{01}^{*}(x))}{(1-p^{*}(x))q^{*}(x)}\right)^{2} \displaystyle\quad+(1-s)(1-z)\left(\frac{\hat{p}^{(-k)}(x)\hat{e}^{(-k)}(x)\ell^{\prime}\left(\hat{m}_{00}^{(-k)}(x)\right)}{(1-\hat{p}^{(-k)}(x))(1-\hat{q}^{(-k)}(x))}-\frac{p^{*}(x)e^{*}(x)\ell^{\prime}(m_{00}^{*}(x))}{(1-p^{*}(x))(1-q^{*}(x))}\right)^{2}. $$

By (80) and (86)

$$ \addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:l_{p}rime_{r}ates}\|\ell^{\prime}\circ\hat{m}_{sz}^{(-k)}-\ell^{\prime}\circ m^{*}\|_{2,P^{*}}=o_{p}(N^{-1/4}),\quad\forall(s,z)\in\{0,1\}^{2} $$

Taking $(s,z)=(1,1)$ above shows

$$ \int sz\left(\ell\left(\hat{m}_{11}^{(-k)}(x)\right)-\ell(m_{11}^{*}(x))\right)^{2}dP^{*}(w)=o_{p}(N^{-1/2}). $$

For the remaining three terms, by Assumption 3, overlap in infinite-dimensional nuisance estimates, and (80), we know by Lemma 3 that

$$ \int\left(\frac{\hat{e}^{(-k)}(x)}{1-\hat{e}^{(-k)}(x)}-\frac{e^{*}(x)}{1-e^{*}(x)}\right)^{2}dP^{*}(w)=\int\left(\frac{\hat{e}^{(-k)}(x)-e^{*}(x)}{(1-e^{*}(x))(1-\hat{e}^{(-k)}(x))}\right)^{2}=o_{p}(N^{-1/2}). $$

Similarly

$$ \int\left(\frac{\hat{p}^{(-k)}(x)}{1-\hat{p}^{(-k)}(x)}-\frac{p^{*}(x)}{1-p^{*}(x)}\right)^{2}dP^{*}(w)=\int\left(\frac{\hat{p}^{(-k)}(x)-p^{*}(x)}{(1-p^{*}(x))(1-\hat{p}^{(-k)}(x))}\right)^{2}dP^{*}(w)=o_{p}(N^{-1/2}). $$

and

$$ \int\left(\frac{1}{1-\hat{r}^{(-k)}(x)}-\frac{1}{1-r^{*}(x)}\right)^{2}dP^{*}(w)+\int\left(\frac{1}{\hat{r}^{(-k)}(x)}-\frac{1}{r^{*}(x)}\right)^{2}dP^{*}(w)=o_{p}(N^{-1/2}). $$

Then applying Lemma 3 recursively we conclude

$$ \displaystyle\int s(1-z)\left(\frac{\hat{e}^{(-k)}(x)\ell^{\prime}\left(\hat{m}_{10}^{(-k)}(x)\right)}{1-\hat{e}^{(-k)}(x)}-\frac{e^{*}(x)\ell^{\prime}(m_{10}^{*}(x))}{1-e^{*}(x)}\right)^{2}dP^{*}(w) \displaystyle=o_{p}(N^{-1/2}) \displaystyle\int(1-s)z\left(\frac{\hat{p}^{(-k)}(x)\hat{e}^{(-k)}(x)\ell^{\prime}\left(\hat{m}_{01}^{(-k)}(x)\right)}{(1-\hat{p}^{(-k)}(x))\hat{r}^{(-k)}(x)}-\frac{p^{*}(x)e^{*}(x)\ell^{\prime}(m_{01}^{*}(x))}{(1-p^{*}(x))r^{*}(x)}\right)^{2}dP^{*}(w) \displaystyle=o_{p}(N^{-1/2}),\quad\text{ and} \displaystyle\int(1-s)(1-z)\left(\frac{\hat{p}^{(-k)}(x)\hat{e}^{(-k)}(x)\ell^{\prime}\left(\hat{m}_{00}^{(-k)}(x)\right)}{(1-\hat{p}^{(-k)}(x))(1-\hat{r}^{(-k)}(x))}-\frac{p^{*}(x)e^{*}(x)\ell^{\prime}(m_{00}^{*}(x))}{(1-p^{*}(x))(1-r^{*}(x))}\right)^{2}dP^{*}(w) \displaystyle=o_{p}(N^{-1/2}) $$

as desired.

## Appendix D Details of numerical simulations in Section 5

Here we specify the full data generating processes for the numerical simulations in Section 5.

For the simulations in Section 5, in the discrete scenario, we emulate the data generating process in Section 5 of Guo et al. (2022):

$$ \displaystyle X=(X_{1},X_{2}) \displaystyle\sim\textnormal{Bern}(0.5)\times\textnormal{Bern}(0.5) \displaystyle Z\mid X \displaystyle\sim\textnormal{Bern}(X_{1}-X_{2}) \displaystyle Y\mid X,Z \displaystyle\sim\textnormal{Bern}\left(\textnormal{expit}\left(-0.5+Z+(1-2Z)(X_{1}-X_{2})\right)\right). $$

For the continuous scenario, we have

$$ \displaystyle X=(X_{1},X_{2}) \displaystyle\sim\mathcal{\mathbb{U}}(-1,1)\times\mathcal{\mathbb{U}}(-1,1) \displaystyle Z\mid X \displaystyle\sim\textnormal{Bern}(X_{1}-X_{2}) \displaystyle Y\mid X,Z \displaystyle\sim\textnormal{Bern}\left(\textnormal{expit}\left(-0.5+Z+(1-2Z)(X_{1}-X_{2})+(1.5Z-1)X_{1}X_{2}\right)\right). $$

To generate the simulated observational dataset, we draw observations from these DGP’s with the selection process described in Section 5 until 3000 selected observations are obtained. Then additional observations from the above DGP’s are generated without selection to form the RCT.

## Appendix E Implementation detail for control variate estimator

As indicated in the main text, our implementation of the control variate estimator $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{cv}}$ follows the guidance of Guo et al. (2022). In the discrete scenario simulation, the differences $\{OR_{1}(x)-OR_{0}(x)\mid x\in\{0,1\}^{2}\}$ are used as four control variates. In the continuous scenario simulation and the Spambase data example, we use the average of $\log(OR_{1}(x))-\log(OR_{0}(x))$ over 50 randomly chosen distinct values of the covariates $x$ in the combined RCT and observational datasets as a single control variate. As the odds ratios are determinstic transformations of the outcome mean function $m$ , we can estimate all of these control variates via deterministic transformations of an outcome mean function estimator $\hat{m}$ . We use the same model for $\hat{m}$ as the cross-fit outcome mean function estimates $\hat{m}^{(-k)}$ used for computing the baseline estimator $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{ba}}$ (i.e. the +1/+2 estimator in the discrete simulation scenario, MARS in the continuous simulation scenario ) except that we refit the model to the entire dataset (i.e. avoiding cross-fitting) as cross-fitting is not known to improve estimation of mean functions at a single point.

We can write

$$ \hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{cv}}=\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{ba}}-\hat{\Gamma}\hat{\lambda} $$

where $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{ba}}$ is the initial baseline estimator (AIPW or AIPSW in all simulations and the data example), $\hat{\lambda}$ is the estimate of the control variate(s) viewed as a vector, and $\hat{\Gamma}$ is an estimate of the optimal adjustment factor $\textnormal{cov}(\hat{\lambda},\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{ba}})\textnormal{cov}(\hat{\lambda})^{-1}$ . The same adjustment $\hat{\Gamma}$ is used for all Monte Carlo simulations in each simulation scenario. This adjustment is computed by calculating $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{ba}}$ and $\hat{\lambda}$ in each of $B=1000$ Monte Carlo replicates of the data-generating process of the scenario, independent of the Monte Carlo replicates from which we report results, and then extracting the appropriate components of the sample covariance matrix. Similarly, for the Spambase data example, we compute $\hat{\Gamma}$ using the sample covariance matrix of estimates $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{ba}}$ and $\hat{\lambda}$ computed on $B=1000$ bootstrapped replications of the dataset, independent of the bootstrap replications on which we report results. This is exactly what is done by Guo et al. (2022). We remark that in practice, an investigator will not have access to additional, independent data on which to compute a regression adjustment independently of the data, and even if they did, they would want to use it for causal estimation to gain full efficiency. Thus, we believe a more accurate estimate of the performance of $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{cv}}$ would be reflected by computing a different adjustment factor $\hat{\Gamma}$ each time $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{cv}}$ is computed. We presume this is not done in Guo et al. (2022) due to the computation time required (each computation of $\hat{\tau}_{\textnormal{ba}}$ requires estimating nuisance functions, so estimating separate adjustments $\hat{\Gamma}$ would require fitting $B$ times as many nuisance function estimates).

# Scalable Vision-Guided Crop Yield Estimation

**Authors:** Harrison H. Li Medhanie Irgau Nabil Janmohamed Karen Solveig Rieckmann David B. Lobell

## Abstract

Precise estimation and uncertainty quantification for average crop yields are critical for agricultural monitoring and decision making. Existing data collection methods, such as crop cuts in randomly sampled fields at harvest time, are relatively time-consuming. Thus, we propose an approach based on prediction-powered inference (PPI) to supplement these crop cuts with less time-consuming field photos. After training a computer vision model to predict the ground truth crop cut yields from the photos, we learn a “control function” that recalibrates these predictions with the spatial coordinates of each field. This enables fields with photos but not crop cuts to be leveraged to improve the precision of zone-wide average yield estimates. Our control function is learned by training on a dataset of nearly 20,000 real crop cuts and photos of rice and maize fields in sub-Saharan Africa. To improve precision, we pool training observations across different zones within the same first-level subdivision of each country. Our final PPI-based point estimates of the average yield are provably asymptotically unbiased and cannot increase the asymptotic variance beyond that of the natural baseline estimator — the sample average of the crop cuts —– as the number of fields grows. We also propose a novel bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) bootstrap to construct accompanying confidence intervals. Even in zones with as few as 20 fields, the point estimates show significant empirical improvement over the baseline, increasing the effective sample size by as much as 73% for rice and by 12-23% for maize. The confidence intervals are accordingly shorter at minimal cost to empirical finite-sample coverage. This demonstrates the potential for relatively low-cost images to make area-based crop insurance more affordable and thus spur investment into sustainable agricultural practices.

## 1 Introduction

Improved agricultural productivity is critical to achieve greater food security and economic growth worldwide. A significant impediment to progress in many countries has been the lack of reliable data on cropping outcomes such as yield, which can impede many forms of investments. A prime example is that farmers often lack access to affordable and effective crop insurance, which would enable higher levels of investment and risk-taking needed to raise productivity. Effective insurance, in turn, relies on the ability to accurately assess cropping conditions and yields across large and heterogeneous cropping regions. Historically, this information has proven to be difficult and costly to obtain.

Recent progress has been made by conducting systematic large-scale crop cutting measurements during the harvest season. These crop cuts are then averaged over pre-defined regions called zones to provide an objective measure of average yields that forms the basis for area-based insurance products.

The motivation for the present work comes from the promise of photographs or aerial imagery as more affordable and scalable approaches to yield estimation (Khaki et al. 2021; Li et al. 2022). While they have commonly been promoted as potential alternatives to ground-based measures like crop cuts, they often explain only half or less of true yield variability in complex smallholder farming settings (Darra et al. 2023) and can be biased (Lobell et al. 2020). This makes using such yield proxies in the place of ground measurements inadequate for insurance and re-insurance providers. We thus seek to instead supplement ground measurements with images — specifically, photos of fields taken at harvest time — to increase the effective sample size without introducing bias.

To do so, we propose leveraging recent statistical methods to efficiently combine small amounts of expensive, error-free data with larger amounts of cheaper but less accurate measures. After training a computer vision model to predict yields from photos, we post-process these predictions by adopting ideas from the framework of prediction-powered inference (PPI). Importantly, we are able to guarantee that in large samples, our zone-level average yield estimates remain unbiased and cannot have larger variance than using the crop cuts alone, regardless of the performance of the computer vision model. However, a better computer vision model enables a lower asymptotic variance for the final estimator, to a degree that we can quantify. We empirically validate these theoretical guarantees under relatively small sample sizes using an extensive dataset from Pula, a provider of area-based crop insurance products in sub-Saharan Africa.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes the dataset and preprocessing steps. Section 3 reviews the prediction-powered inference framework and introduces our estimation approach. Section 4 details the photo-based yield prediction models underlying our methodology, and Section 5 presents some innovations that leverage the nature of area-based insurance data to improve learning of the control function that underpins PPI. Section 6 reports empirical findings and Section 7 concludes.

## 2 Data

Our dataset contains field-level observations from four (country, harvest year) pairs: rice fields from (Nigeria, 2022) and maize (corn) fields from (Zambia, 2023), (Zambia, 2024), and (Zimbabwe, 2024). For each field, two random crop cuts were taken at harvest time. Their average is treated as the ground truth yield, in units of $\texttt{mt ha}^{-1}$ . Photographs were also manually captured for each field. Some examples are provided in Fig. 1. The data from Zambia are commercially sensitive; however, we provide the complete data from Nigeria and Zimbabwe in the link following the abstract of this paper. Currently, we do not have access to photos from additional fields; in our evaluations we use bootstrapping to simulate the desired future setting where there are additional “unlabeled” fields with photos but not crop cuts (Section 6).
