## Appendix A Proofs

### A.1 Proof of Theorem 1

Throughout the proof we write

$$ \displaystyle\psi_{i} \displaystyle\equiv\psi(\Delta(X_{i})),\quad i=1,\ldots,n+N \displaystyle\hat{\psi}_{i} \displaystyle\equiv\psi(\hat{\Delta}(X_{i})),\quad i=1,\ldots,n \displaystyle\hat{\psi}^{(-k)}_{i} \displaystyle\equiv\psi(\hat{\Delta}^{(-k)}(X_{i})),\quad i\in\mathcal{I}_{k},\quad k=1,\ldots,K $$

for brevity. We note that

$$ \sqrt{n}(\hat{\bar{\tau}}-\bar{\tau})=\frac{\sqrt{n}}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\left(\hat{\bar{\beta}}^{\top}\hat{\psi}_{i}^{(-k)}-\bar{\beta}^{\top}\psi_{i}\right)+\frac{\sqrt{n}}{N}\sum_{i=n+1}^{n+N}\left(\bar{\mu}(X_{i})-\bar{\tau}\right) $$

where $\bar{\beta}$ is given by (2) since $\mathbb{E}_{\textnormal{rct}}[\psi(\Delta(X))\psi(\Delta(X))^{\top}]$ is invertible. The rate conditions (8) imply $\mathbb{E}_{\textnormal{obs}}[\|\psi(\Delta(X))\|_{2}^{2}]<\infty$ and hence $\mathbb{E}_{\textnormal{obs}}[\bar{\mu}(X)^{2}]<\infty$ , so

$$ \frac{\sqrt{n}}{N}\sum_{i=n+1}^{n+N}(\bar{\mu}(X_{i})-\bar{\tau})=\sqrt{n}\cdot\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=n+1}^{n+N}(\bar{\mu}(X_{i})-\bar{\tau})=\sqrt{n}\cdot O_{p}(N^{-1/2})=o_{p}(1) $$

and it suffices to show that

$$ \frac{\sqrt{n}}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\left(\hat{\bar{\beta}}^{\top}\hat{\psi}^{(-k)}_{i}-\bar{\beta}^{\top}\psi_{i}\right)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma). $$

To that end, we write

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\sqrt{n}}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\left(\hat{\bar{\beta}}^{\top}\hat{\psi}_{i}^{(-k)}-\bar{\beta}^{\top}\psi_{i}\right)=\sqrt{n}(\hat{\bar{\beta}}-\bar{\beta})^{\top}\cdot\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\hat{\psi}^{(-k)}_{i}+\frac{\sqrt{n}}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\bar{\beta}^{\top}\left(\hat{\psi}^{(-k)}_{i}-\psi_{i}\right). $$

First, we examine the behavior of $\sqrt{n}(\hat{\bar{\beta}}-\bar{\beta})$ . We have that

$$ \hat{\bar{\beta}}=\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{\psi}_{i}\hat{\psi}_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}D_{i}\hat{\psi}_{i}\right). $$

and so

$$ \sqrt{n}(\hat{\bar{\beta}}-\bar{\beta})=\underbrace{\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{\psi}_{i}\hat{\psi}_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}}_{\hat{A}_{n,N}}\times\underbrace{\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(D_{i}-\hat{\psi}_{i}^{\top}\bar{\beta}\right)\hat{\psi}_{i}\right)}_{\hat{b}_{n,N}}. $$

We can split the RHS into several terms:

$$ \displaystyle\sqrt{n}(\hat{\bar{\beta}}-\bar{\beta})=\underbrace{\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\psi_{i}\psi_{i}^{\top}\right)^{-1}}_{A_{n}}\times\underbrace{\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(D_{i}-\psi_{i}^{\top}\bar{\beta}\right)\psi_{i}\right)}_{b_{n}}+(\hat{A}_{n,N}-A_{n})b_{n}+\hat{A}_{n,N}(\hat{b}_{n,N}-b_{n}). $$

By the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem

$$ \displaystyle A_{n} \displaystyle=\left(\mathbb{E}_{\textnormal{rct}}[\psi(\Delta(X))\psi(\Delta(X))^{\top}]\right)^{-1}+o_{p}(1) \displaystyle b_{n} \displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathcal{N}\left(0,\mathbb{E}_{\textnormal{rct}}[(D-\bar{\mu}(X))^{2}\psi(\Delta(X))\psi(\Delta(X))^{\top}]\right) $$

(note that $\mathbb{E}_{\textnormal{rct}}[(D-\psi(\Delta(X))^{\top}\bar{\beta})\psi(\Delta(X))]=\mathbb{E}_{\textnormal{rct}}[(D-\bar{\mu}(X))\psi(\Delta(X))]=0$ by the first-order conditions defining $\bar{\mu}(\cdot)=\psi(\Delta(\cdot))^{\top}\bar{\beta}$ ). We conclude

$$ \begin{split}A_{n}b_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\rightarrow}}&\mathcal{N}\left(0,\left(\mathbb{E}_{\textnormal{rct}}[\psi(\Delta(X))\psi(\Delta(X))^{\top}]\right)^{-1}\mathbb{E}_{\textnormal{rct}}[(D-\bar{\mu}(X))^{2}\psi(\Delta(X))\psi(\Delta(X))^{\top}]\right.\\
&\qquad\left.\left(\mathbb{E}_{\textnormal{rct}}[\psi(\Delta(X))\psi(\Delta(X))^{\top}]\right)^{-1}\right).\end{split} $$

Next, we note that

$$ \hat{A}_{n,N}^{-1}-A_{n}^{-1}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{\psi}_{i}\left[\hat{\psi}_{i}-\psi_{i}\right]^{\top}+\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[\hat{\psi}_{i}-\psi_{i}\right]\psi_{i}^{\top} $$

Letting $\psi_{i,j}$ denote the $j$ -th component of $\psi_{i}$ (and similarly defining $\hat{\psi}_{i,j})$ as the $j$ -th component of $\hat{\psi}_{i}$ ), for each $1\leqslant j,j^{\prime}\leqslant p$ we have

$$ \displaystyle\left|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\psi_{i,j}\left[\hat{\psi}_{i,j^{\prime}}-\psi_{i,j^{\prime}}\right]\right| \displaystyle\leqslant\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\psi_{i,j}^{2}}\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[\hat{\psi}_{i,j^{\prime}}-\psi_{i,j^{\prime}}\right]^{2}} \displaystyle=O_{p}(1)\cdot o_{p}(n^{-1/2})=o_{p}(1) $$

where the inequality above follows by Cauchy-Schwarz, and the $o_{p}(n^{-1/2})$ estimate follows from the rate condition (8) and Lemma 4 of Li (2024) (which applies since $\hat{\Delta}(\cdot)$ is independent of all of the experimental observations). By an identical argument

$$ \addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:psi_{C}S}\left|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{\psi}_{i,j}\left[\hat{\psi}_{i,j^{\prime}}-\psi_{i,j^{\prime}}\right]\right|=o_{p}(n^{-1/2})=o_{p}(1) $$

as well. We conclude $\hat{A}_{n,N}^{-1}-A_{n}^{-1}=o_{p}(1)$ and hence $\hat{A}_{n,N}-A_{n}=o_{p}(1)$ and $(\hat{A}_{n,N}-A_{n})b_{n}=o_{p}(1)$ . Finally, we write

$$ \hat{b}_{n,N}-b_{n}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}[\psi_{i}-\hat{\psi}_{i}]^{\top}\bar{\beta}\cdot\hat{\psi}_{i}+(D_{i}-\psi_{i}^{\top}\bar{\beta})(\hat{\psi}_{i}-\psi_{i}). $$

By (23) we know that

$$ \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{\psi}_{i}[\psi_{i}-\hat{\psi}_{i}]^{\top}\bar{\beta}=o_{p}(1). $$

Additionally

$$ d_{n,j}:=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(D_{i}-\psi_{i}^{\top}\bar{\beta}\right)\left(\hat{\psi}_{i,j}-\psi_{i,j}\right) $$

satisfies

$$ |d_{n,j}|\leqslant\sqrt{n}\cdot\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(D_{i}-\psi_{i}^{\top}\bar{\beta}\right)^{2}}\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\hat{\psi}_{i,j}-\psi_{i,j}\right)^{2}}=o_{p}(1) $$

for all $j=1,\ldots,p$ by Cauchy-Schwarz, the rate condition (8), and Lemma 4 of Li (2024) once again. Hence we can conclude $\hat{b}_{n,N}-b_{n}=o_{p}(1)$ and so

$$ \hat{A}_{n,N}(\hat{b}_{n,N}-b_{n})=(A_{n}+o_{p}(1))(\hat{b}_{n,N}-b_{n})=o_{p}(1) $$

as well. This shows that

$$ \addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:beta_{h}at_{e}xpansion}\begin{split}\sqrt{n}(\hat{\bar{\beta}}-\bar{\beta})&=A_{n}b_{n}+o_{p}(1)\\
&\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathcal{N}\left(0,\left(\mathbb{E}_{\textnormal{rct}}[\psi(\Delta(X))\psi(\Delta(X))^{\top}]\right)^{-1}\right.\\
&\qquad\left.\mathbb{E}_{\textnormal{rct}}[(D-\bar{\mu}(X))^{2}\psi(\Delta(X))\psi(\Delta(X))^{\top}]\left(\mathbb{E}_{\textnormal{rct}}[\psi(\Delta(X))\psi(\Delta(X))^{\top}]\right)^{-1}\right).\end{split} $$

Next, we note that for each $k=1,\ldots,K$ and $j=1,\ldots,p$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\left|\hat{\psi}_{i,j}^{(-k)}-\psi_{i,j}\right| \displaystyle\leqslant\sqrt{\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\left(\hat{\psi}_{i,j}^{(-k)}-\psi_{i,j}\right)^{2}}\text{ by Jensen's inequality} \displaystyle=o_{p}(n^{-1/2})\text{ by Lemma 4 of~\cite[citet]{\@@bibref{Authors Phrase1YearPhrase2}{li2024efficient}{\@@citephrase{(}}{\@@citephrase{)}}}} $$

and hence

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\bar{\beta}^{\top}\left(\hat{\psi}_{i,j}^{(-k)}-\psi_{i,j}\right)=o_{p}(n^{-1/2}) $$

as well. With $|\mathcal{I}_{k}|=O(N)$ for each fold $k=1,\ldots,K$ we conclude that

$$ \frac{\sqrt{n}}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\bar{\beta}^{\top}\left(\hat{\psi}_{i,j}^{(-k)}-\psi_{i,j}\right)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}{N}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{n}}{|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\bar{\beta}^{\top}\left(\hat{\psi}_{i,j}^{(-k)}-\psi_{i,j}\right)=o_{p}(1) $$

and so in fact

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\sqrt{n}}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\left(\hat{\bar{\beta}}^{\top}\hat{\psi}_{i}^{(-k)}-\bar{\beta}^{\top}\psi_{i}\right) \displaystyle=\sqrt{n}(\hat{\bar{\beta}}-\bar{\beta})^{\top}\cdot\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\hat{\psi}^{(-k)}_{i}+o_{p}(1) \displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\rightarrow}}\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma) $$

where the final convergence uses (24) along with the fact that

$$ \addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:avg_{p}si_{h}at_{o}bs}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\hat{\psi}_{i}^{(-k)}=\mathbb{E}_{\textnormal{obs}}[\psi(\Delta(X))]+o_{p}(1) $$

by the law of large numbers and (25).

To prove asymptotic validity of the confidence interval, it suffices to show that

$$ n\hat{V}_{n,N}=\Sigma+o_{p}(1). $$

To that end, we first show that

$$ \addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:ci_{m}eat}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{r}_{i}\hat{r}_{i}^{\top}=\mathbb{E}_{\textnormal{rct}}\left[(D-\bar{\mu}(X))^{2}\psi(\Delta(X))\psi(\Delta(X))^{\top}\right]+o_{p}(1). $$

Since

$$ \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(D_{i}-\bar{\mu}(X_{i}))^{2}\psi_{i}\psi_{i}^{\top}=\mathbb{E}_{\textnormal{rct}}\left[(D-\bar{\mu}(X))^{2}\psi(\Delta(X))\psi(\Delta(X))^{\top}\right]+o_{p}(1) $$

by the law of large numbers, it suffices to show that

$$ \addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:ri_{h}at}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{r}_{i}\hat{r}_{i}^{\top}-(D_{i}-\bar{\mu}(X_{i}))^{2}\psi_{i}\psi_{i}^{\top}=o_{p}(1). $$

To do so, we fix $1\leqslant j,j^{\prime}\leqslant p$ and write

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(D_{i}-\hat{\bar{\mu}}(X_{i})\right)^{2}\hat{\psi}_{i,j}\hat{\psi}_{i,j^{\prime}}-(D_{i}-\bar{\mu}(X_{i}))^{2}\psi_{i,j}\psi_{i,j^{\prime}}=t_{n}+u_{n} $$

where

$$ \displaystyle t_{n} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(2D_{i}-\bar{\mu}(X_{i})-\hat{\bar{\mu}}(X_{i})\right)\left(\bar{\mu}(X_{i})-\hat{\bar{\mu}}(X_{i})\right)\psi_{i,j}\psi_{i,j^{\prime}} \displaystyle=2\cdot\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(D_{i}-\bar{\mu}(X_{i})\right)\left(\bar{\mu}(X_{i})-\hat{\bar{\mu}}(X_{i})\right)\psi_{i,j}\psi_{i,j^{\prime}}+\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\bar{\mu}(X_{i})-\hat{\bar{\mu}}(X_{i})\right)^{2}\psi_{i,j}\psi_{i,j^{\prime}} \displaystyle u_{n} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(D_{i}-\hat{\bar{\mu}}(X_{i})\right)^{2}\left(\hat{\psi}_{i,j}\hat{\psi}_{i,j^{\prime}}-\psi_{i,j}\psi_{i,j^{\prime}}\right) $$

and show that $t_{n}+u_{n}=o_{p}(1)$ .

To bound the first term of $t_{n}$ , we apply Cauchy-Schwarz and then Hölder’s inequality:

$$ \displaystyle\left|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(D_{i}-\bar{\mu}(X_{i})\right)\left(\bar{\mu}(X_{i})-\hat{\bar{\mu}}(X_{i})\right)\psi_{i,j}\psi_{i,j^{\prime}}\right| \displaystyle\quad\leqslant\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(D_{i}-\bar{\mu}(X_{i}))^{2}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\times\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\bar{\mu}(X_{i})-\hat{\bar{\mu}}(X_{i})\right)^{2}\psi_{i,j}^{2}\psi_{i,j^{\prime}}^{2}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}} \displaystyle\quad\leqslant\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(D_{i}-\bar{\mu}(X_{i}))^{2}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\times\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left|\hat{\bar{\mu}}(X_{i})-\bar{\mu}(X_{i})\right|^{2+\epsilon}\right)^{\frac{1}{2+\epsilon}}\times\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}|\psi_{i,j}|^{2q}||\psi_{i,j^{\prime}}|^{2q}\right)^{\frac{1}{2q}} $$

where $q:=1+2/\epsilon$ satisfies

$$ \frac{2}{2+\epsilon}+\frac{1}{q}=1. $$

Evidently

$$ \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(D_{i}-\bar{\mu}(X_{i}))^{2}=O_{p}(1) $$

since $D_{i}$ and $\bar{\mu}(X_{i})$ are both square integrable while

$$ \addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:all_{m}oments}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}|\psi_{i,j}|^{k}||\psi_{i,j^{\prime}}|^{k}=O_{p}(1),\quad\forall k<\infty $$

by the assumption that $\psi_{j}(\Delta(X))$ and $\psi_{j^{\prime}}(\Delta(X))$ have finite moments of all orders in the RCT. Thus,

$$ \displaystyle\left|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(D_{i}-\bar{\mu}(X_{i})\right)\left(\bar{\mu}(X_{i})-\hat{\bar{\mu}}(X_{i})\right)\psi_{i,j}\psi_{i,j^{\prime}}\right|=O_{p}(1)\times\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left|\hat{\bar{\mu}}(X_{i})-\bar{\mu}(X_{i})\right|^{2+\epsilon}\right)^{\frac{1}{2+\epsilon}} $$

We bound

$$ \displaystyle\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left|\hat{\psi}_{i}^{\top}\hat{\bar{\beta}}-\psi_{i}^{\top}\bar{\beta}\right|^{2+\epsilon}\right)^{\frac{1}{2+\epsilon}} \displaystyle\leqslant\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left|(\hat{\psi}_{i}-\psi_{i})^{\top}\hat{\bar{\beta}}\right|^{2+\epsilon}\right)^{\frac{1}{2+\epsilon}}+\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left|(\hat{\bar{\beta}}-\bar{\beta})^{\top}\psi_{i}\right|^{2+\epsilon}\right)^{\frac{1}{2+\epsilon}} \displaystyle\leqslant\sum_{\tilde{j}=1}^{p}\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left|(\hat{\psi}_{i,\tilde{j}}-\psi_{i,\tilde{j}})\hat{\bar{\beta}}_{\tilde{j}}\right|^{2+\epsilon}\right)^{\frac{1}{2+\epsilon}}+\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left|(\hat{\bar{\beta}}_{\tilde{j}}-\bar{\beta}_{\tilde{j}})\psi_{i,\tilde{j}}\right|^{2+\epsilon}\right)^{\frac{1}{2+\epsilon}} $$

by Minkowski’s inequality. Evidently for each $\tilde{j}=1,\ldots,p$ we have

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left|(\hat{\psi}_{i,\tilde{j}}-\psi_{i,\tilde{j}})\hat{\bar{\beta}}_{\tilde{j}}\right|^{2+\epsilon}=|\hat{\bar{\beta}}_{\tilde{j}}|^{2+\epsilon}\cdot\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left|\hat{\psi}_{i,\tilde{j}}-\psi_{i,\tilde{j}}\right|^{2+\epsilon}=O_{p}(1)\cdot o_{p}(1)=o_{p}(1) $$

since $\|\psi_{\tilde{j}}\circ\hat{\Delta}-\psi_{\tilde{j}}\circ\Delta\|_{2+\epsilon,\textnormal{rct}}=o_{p}(1)$ , and similarly

$$ \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left|(\hat{\bar{\beta}}_{\tilde{j}}-\bar{\beta}_{\tilde{j}})\psi_{i,\tilde{j}}\right|^{2+\epsilon}=\left|\hat{\bar{\beta}}_{\tilde{j}}-\bar{\beta}_{\tilde{j}}\right|^{2+\epsilon}\cdot\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left|\psi_{i,\tilde{j}}\right|^{2+\epsilon}=O_{p}(n^{-\frac{1}{2}\cdot(2+\epsilon)})\cdot O_{p}(1)=o_{p}(1) $$

by (24). We conclude that

$$ \addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:mu_{h}at_{v}s_{m}u_{r}ct}\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left|\hat{\bar{\mu}}(X_{i})-\bar{\mu}(X_{i})\right|^{2+\epsilon}\right)^{\frac{1}{2+\epsilon}}=\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left|\hat{\psi}_{i}^{\top}\hat{\bar{\beta}}-\psi_{i}^{\top}\bar{\beta}\right|^{2+\epsilon}\right)^{\frac{1}{2+\epsilon}}=o_{p}(1) $$

and so in fact

$$ \left|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(D_{i}-\bar{\mu}(X_{i})\right)\left(\bar{\mu}(X_{i})-\hat{\bar{\mu}}(X_{i})\right)\psi_{i,\tilde{j}}\psi_{i,\tilde{j}^{\prime}}\right|=O_{p}(1)\times o_{p}(1)=o_{p}(1). $$

For the second term of $t_{n}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\left|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\bar{\mu}(X_{i})-\hat{\bar{\mu}}(X_{i}))^{2}\psi_{i,j}\psi_{i,j^{\prime}}\right| \displaystyle\leqslant\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left|\hat{\bar{\mu}}(X_{i})-\bar{\mu}(X_{i})\right|^{2+\epsilon}\right)^{\frac{2}{2+\epsilon}}\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}|\psi_{i,j}|^{q}|\psi_{i,j^{\prime}}|^{q}\right)^{\frac{1}{q}} \displaystyle=o_{p}(1)\cdot O_{p}(1)=o_{p}(1) $$

by Hölder’s inequality, (29), and (30). Thus, we have shown $t_{n}=o_{p}(1)$ .

To show $u_{n}=o_{p}(1)$ , by Cauchy-Schwarz

$$ \displaystyle|u_{n}| \displaystyle\leqslant\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}|D_{i}-\hat{\bar{\mu}}(X_{i})|^{4}\right)^{1/2}\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left|\hat{\psi}_{i,j}\hat{\psi}_{i,j^{\prime}}-\psi_{i,j}\psi_{i,j^{\prime}}\right|^{2}\right)^{1/2}. $$

By Minkowski

$$ \displaystyle\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}|D_{i}-\hat{\bar{\mu}}(X_{i})|^{4}\right)^{1/4} \displaystyle\leqslant\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}D_{i}^{4}\right)^{1/4}+\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left|\psi(\hat{\Delta}(X_{i}))^{\top}\hat{\bar{\beta}}\right|^{4}\right)^{1/4} \displaystyle\leqslant O_{p}(1)+\|\hat{\bar{\beta}}\|_{2}\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left\|\psi(\hat{\Delta}(X_{i}))\right\|_{2}^{4}\right)^{1/4} \displaystyle=O_{p}(1) $$

using the fact that $\mathbb{E}_{\textnormal{rct}}[|D|^{4}]<\infty$ and that (9) holds with $k=4$ . Another application of Minkowski shows that

$$ \displaystyle\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left|\hat{\psi}_{i,j}\hat{\psi}_{i,j^{\prime}}-\psi_{i,j}\psi_{i,j^{\prime}}\right|^{2}\right)^{1/2} \displaystyle\leqslant\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left|(\hat{\psi}_{i,j}-\psi_{i,j})\hat{\psi}_{i,j^{\prime}}\right|^{2}\right)^{1/2}+\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left|\psi_{i,j}(\hat{\psi}_{i,j^{\prime}}-\psi_{i,j^{\prime}})\right|^{2}\right)^{1/2} $$

Then we use Hölder’s inequality to bound

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left|\psi_{i,j}(\hat{\psi}_{i,j^{\prime}}-\psi_{i,j^{\prime}})\right|^{2} \displaystyle\leqslant\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left|\hat{\psi}_{i,j^{\prime}}-\psi_{i,j^{\prime}}\right|^{2+\epsilon}\right)^{\frac{2}{2+\epsilon}}\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left|\psi_{i,j}\right|^{2q}\right)^{\frac{1}{q}} \displaystyle=o_{p}(1)\cdot O_{p}(1)=o_{p}(1) $$

where the rate estimates hold by the assumptions that

$$ \|\psi_{j^{\prime}}\circ\hat{\Delta}-\psi_{j^{\prime}}\circ\Delta\|_{2+\epsilon,\textnormal{rct}}=o_{p}(1) $$

and $\mathbb{E}_{\textnormal{rct}}[\|\psi(\Delta(X))\|^{2q}]<\infty$ . By an identical argument, except using (9) with $k=2q$ in place of the assumption $\mathbb{E}_{\textnormal{rct}}[\|\psi(\Delta(X))\|^{2q}]<\infty$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left|(\hat{\psi}_{i,j}-\psi_{i,j})\hat{\psi}_{i,j^{\prime}}\right|^{2} \displaystyle\leqslant\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left|\hat{\psi}_{i,j}-\psi_{i,j}\right|^{2+\epsilon}\right)^{\frac{2}{2+\epsilon}}\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left|\hat{\psi}_{i,j^{\prime}}\right|^{2q}\right)^{\frac{1}{q}} \displaystyle=o_{p}(1)\cdot O_{p}(1)=o_{p}(1). $$

We conclude that in fact $u_{n}=o_{p}(1)$ , and so we have shown (28) and thus (27).

Now we write

$$ n\hat{V}_{n,N}=\hat{a}_{n,N}^{\top}\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{r}_{i}\hat{r}_{i}^{\top}\right)\hat{a}_{n,N}+\frac{n}{N}\cdot\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\left(\hat{\bar{\mu}}^{(-k)}(X_{i})-\hat{\bar{\tau}}\right)^{2} $$

to see that in light of (27), to conclude the proof it suffices to show that

$$ \displaystyle\hat{a}_{n,N}=\bar{\alpha}+o_{p}(1)\qquad\text{and}\qquad\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\left(\hat{\bar{\mu}}^{(-k)}(X_{i})-\hat{\bar{\tau}}\right)^{2}=O_{p}(1). $$

But the statement that $\hat{a}_{n,N}=\bar{\alpha}+o_{p}(1)$ follows immediately from (26) and the fact that

$$ \hat{A}_{n,N}=A_{n}+o_{p}(1)=\left(\mathbb{E}_{\textnormal{rct}}\left[\psi(\Delta(X))\psi(\Delta(X))^{\top}\right]\right)^{-1}+o_{p}(1) $$

as shown in the first part of this proof. Finally, the assertion

$$ \frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\left(\hat{\bar{\mu}}^{(-k)}(X_{i})-\hat{\bar{\tau}}\right)^{2}=O_{p}(1) $$

is apparent since

$$ \frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{k}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{k}}\left(\hat{\mu}^{(-k)}(X_{i})\right)^{2} $$

has finite expectation for all $k=1,\ldots,K$ by assumption.

### A.2 Proof of Theorem 2

In the setting of Theorem 2, there are no structural restrictions on the distribution of $W_{i}=(Q_{i},X_{i},Y_{i})$ , i.e., we have a fully nonparametric model. Then the corresponding semiparametric tangent space is equal to $\mathcal{H}_{W}^{0}$ , the set of all mean zero, square-integrable functions of $W=(Q,X,Y)$ under the true data generating distribution $P^{*}$ (Bickel et al., 1993; Kennedy, 2024). Hence, for the proof of the efficiency bound it suffices to show that

$$ \addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:pathwise_{d}erivative}\frac{\partial\bar{\tau}(0)}{\partial\theta}=\mathbb{E}\left[\psi(W;\bar{\tau},\eta)s(W;0)\right] $$

for all smooth parametric submodels $\{P_{\theta}\mid\theta\in\Theta\}$ with corresponding score $s(w;\theta)$ , where for each $\theta\in\Theta$ , $\bar{\tau}(\theta)$ denotes the value of the parameter $\bar{\tau}$ under the distribution $P_{\theta}$ . Following standard texts on semiparametric theory (Bickel et al., 1993; van der Vaart, 2000), a parametric submodel $\{P_{\theta}\mid\theta\in\Theta\}$ is a collection of distributions $P_{\theta}$ indexed by $\theta$ in an open interval $\Theta$ containing 0 such that $P_{0}=P^{*}$ , the true data-generating process. Above and throughout this proof, for brevity we use the notation

$$ \frac{\partial F(a)}{\partial\theta}\equiv\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}F(\theta)\Big|_{\theta=a}. $$

for any function $F$ .

We fix an arbitrary parametric submodel, which contains densities of the form

$$ p(w;\theta)=f(q;\theta)g(x\mid q;\theta)h(y\mid x,q;\theta) $$

where $w=(q,x,y)$ and $f$ , $g$ , and $h$ are the density of $Q$ , the conditional density of $X$ given $Q$ , and the conditional density of $Y$ given $(X,Q)$ , respectively with respect to measures $\lambda_{Q}$ , $\lambda_{X\mid Q}$ , and $\lambda_{Y\mid QX}$ , respectively. Then

$$ \displaystyle\bar{\tau}(\theta) \displaystyle=\left[\frac{\int\bm{1}(q\neq 2)\psi(\Delta(x;\theta))f(q;\theta)g(x\mid q;\theta)d(\lambda_{Q}\times\lambda_{X\mid Q})(q,x)}{1-f(2;\theta)}\right]^{\top}\bar{\beta}(\theta),\quad \displaystyle\Delta(x;\theta) \displaystyle=\int y\left[h(y\mid x,1;\theta)-h(y\mid x,0;\theta)\right]d\lambda_{Y\mid QX}(y),\quad \displaystyle\bar{\beta}(\theta) \displaystyle=\left[\int g(x\mid 2;\theta)\psi(\Delta(x;\theta))\psi(\Delta(x;\theta))^{\top}d\lambda_{X\mid Q}(x)\right]^{-1}\times \displaystyle\left[\int g(x\mid 2;\theta)h(y\mid x,2;\theta)y\psi(\Delta(x;\theta))d(\lambda_{X\mid Q}\times\lambda_{Y\mid QX})(x,y)\right]. $$

It follows by the product rule that

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\partial\bar{\tau}(0)}{\partial\theta} \displaystyle=\left(\mathbb{E}[\psi(\Delta(X))\mid Q\neq 2]\right)^{\top}\frac{\partial\bar{\beta}(0)}{\partial\theta} \displaystyle+\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\left(\frac{\int\bm{1}(q\neq 2)f(q;0)g(x\mid q;0)\psi(\Delta(x;0))d(\lambda_{Q}\times\lambda_{X\mid Q})(q,x)}{1-f(2;0)}\right)\right]^{\top}\bar{\beta} $$

where above and hereafter in this proof, all expectations are with respect to the true data-generating distribution $P_{0}$ .

Differentiating under the integral sign, we get

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\partial\bar{\beta}(0)}{\partial\theta} \displaystyle=\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\psi(\Delta(X))\psi(\Delta(X))^{\top}\mid Q=2\right]\right)^{-1}\left(B_{1}+B_{2}-B_{3}-B_{4}\right) $$

for

$$ \displaystyle B_{1} \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[YD_{gh}(X,Y\mid 2)\psi(\Delta(X))\Big|Q=2\right] \displaystyle B_{2} \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[Y\frac{\partial\Delta(X;0)}{\partial\theta}\dot{\psi}(\Delta(X))\Big|Q=2\right] \displaystyle B_{3} \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\partial\log g(X\mid 2;0)}{\partial\theta}\psi(\Delta(X))\psi(\Delta(X))^{\top}\bar{\beta}\Big|Q=2\right] \displaystyle B_{4} \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\partial\Delta(X;0)}{\partial\theta}\left(\psi(\Delta(X))\dot{\psi}(\Delta(X))^{\top}+\dot{\psi}(\Delta(X))\psi(\Delta(X))^{\top}\right)\bar{\beta}\Big|Q=2\right] $$

where we let

$$ D_{gh}(X,Y\mid q)=\frac{\partial\log g(X\mid q;0)}{\partial\theta}+\frac{\partial\log h(Y\mid X,q;0)}{\partial\theta},\quad q=0,1,2. $$

On the other hand,

$$ \frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\left(\frac{\int\bm{1}(q\neq 2)f(q;0)g(x\mid q;0)\psi(\Delta(x;0))d(\lambda_{Q}\times\lambda_{X\mid Q})(q,x)}{1-f(2;0)}\right)=A_{1}+A_{2}+A_{3} $$

for

$$ \displaystyle A_{1} \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\frac{\partial\log f(Q;0)}{\partial\theta}+\frac{\partial\log g(X\mid Q;0)}{\partial\theta}\right)\psi(\Delta(X))\Big|Q\neq 2\right] \displaystyle A_{2} \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\partial\Delta(X;0)}{\partial\theta}\dot{\psi}(\Delta(X))\Big|Q\neq 2\right] \displaystyle A_{3} \displaystyle=\frac{\rho_{2}}{1-\rho_{2}}\frac{\partial\log f(2;0)}{\partial\theta}\mathbb{E}\left[\psi(\Delta(X))\Big|Q\neq 2\right]. $$

Thus, to show (31) it suffices to prove that

$$ \mathbb{E}[\psi(W;\bar{\tau},\eta)s(W;0)]=\bar{\alpha}^{\top}(B_{1}+B_{2}-B_{3}-B_{4})+(A_{1}+A_{2}+A_{3})^{\top}\bar{\beta}. $$

where

$$ s(w;0)=\frac{\partial\log f(q;0)}{\partial\theta}+D_{gh}(x,y\mid q). $$

is the score function corresponding to the parametric submodel at $\theta=0$ .

To that end, we write $\psi(w;\bar{\tau},\eta)=\psi_{1}(w;\bar{\tau},\eta)+\psi_{2}(w;\bar{\tau},\eta)$ where

$$ \displaystyle\psi_{1}(w;\bar{\tau},\eta) \displaystyle=\frac{\bm{1}(q\neq 2)}{1-\rho_{2}}\left(\bar{\mu}(x)-\bar{\tau}+\iota(w;\eta)\kappa(x;\eta)\right),\quad\text{and} \displaystyle\psi_{2}(w;\bar{\tau},\eta) \displaystyle=\frac{\bm{1}(q=2)}{\rho_{2}}(y-\bar{\mu}(x))\bar{\alpha}^{\top}\psi(\Delta(x)). $$

The first-order conditions for $\bar{\mu}$ imply that

$$ \mathbb{E}[\psi_{2}(W;\bar{\tau},\eta)]=0 $$

and so

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[\psi_{2}(W;\bar{\tau},\eta)\frac{\partial\log f(q;0)}{\partial\theta}\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\psi_{2}(W;\bar{\tau},\eta)\frac{\partial\log f(2;0)}{\partial\theta}\right]=\frac{\partial\log f(2;0)}{\partial\theta}\mathbb{E}\left[\psi_{2}(W;\bar{\tau},\eta)\right]=0. $$

Thus

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\psi_{2}(W;\bar{\tau},\eta)s(W;0)\right] \displaystyle\quad=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\bm{1}(Q=2)}{\rho_{2}}(Y-\bar{\mu}(X))\bar{\alpha}^{\top}\psi(\Delta(X))D_{gh}(X,Y\mid 2)\right] \displaystyle\quad=\bar{\alpha}^{\top}\left(\mathbb{E}\left[YD_{gh}(X,Y\mid 2)\psi(\Delta(X))\mid Q=2\right]-\mathbb{E}\left[\bar{\mu}(X)D_{gh}(X,Y\mid 2)\psi(\Delta(X))\mid Q=2\right]\right) \displaystyle\quad=\bar{\alpha}^{\top}(B_{1}-B_{3}) $$

and the final equality uses the fact that

$$ \addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:h_{0}}\mathbb{E}\left[F(X,Q)\frac{\partial\log h(Y\mid X,Q;0)}{\partial\theta}\right]=0 $$

for any square integrable function $F$ , applied to $F(x,q)=\bm{1}(q=2)\bar{\mu}(x)\psi(\Delta(x))$ .

Next, we have

$$ \mathbb{E}[\psi_{1}(W;\bar{\tau},\eta)s(W;0)]=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\bm{1}(Q\neq 2)}{1-\rho_{2}}(\bar{\mu}(X)-\bar{\tau})D_{fg}(Q,X)\right]+\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\iota(W;\eta)\kappa(X;\eta)}{1-\rho_{2}}\frac{\partial\log h(Y\mid X,Q;0)}{\partial\theta}\right]\\
 $$

where some terms cancel by (32) and observing by conditioning on $(X,Q)$ that both

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\iota(W;\eta)\kappa(X;\eta)}{1-\rho_{2}}\frac{\partial\log f(Q;0)}{\partial\theta}\right] \displaystyle=\sum_{q=0}^{1}\frac{\partial\log f(q;0)}{\partial\theta}\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\kappa(X;\eta)\bm{1}(Q=q)}{(r(X)-(1-q))(1-\rho_{2})}(Y-m_{q}(X))\right] \displaystyle=0+0=0 $$

and

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\iota(W;\eta)\kappa(X;\eta)}{1-\rho_{2}}\frac{\partial\log g(X\mid Q;0)}{\partial\theta}\right] \displaystyle=\sum_{q=0}^{1}\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\kappa(X;\eta)\bm{1}(Q=q)}{(r(X)-(1-q))(1-\rho_{2})}\frac{\partial\log g(X\mid Q;0)}{\partial\theta}(Y-m_{q}(X))\right] \displaystyle=0+0=0. $$

We further compute

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\bm{1}(Q\neq 2)}{1-\rho_{2}}(\bar{\mu}(X)-\bar{\tau})D_{fg}(Q,X)\right] \displaystyle\quad=\left(\mathbb{E}[D_{fg}(Q,X)\psi(\Delta(X))\mid Q\neq 2]\right)^{\top}\bar{\beta}-\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\partial\log f(Q;0)}{\partial\theta}\Big|Q\neq 2\right]\left(\mathbb{E}[\psi(\Delta(X))\mid Q\neq 2]\right)^{\top}\bar{\beta} \displaystyle\quad=\left(\mathbb{E}[D_{fg}(Q,X)\psi(\Delta(X))\mid Q\neq 2]\right)^{\top}\bar{\beta}+\frac{\rho_{2}}{1-\rho_{2}}\frac{\partial\log f(2;0)}{\partial\theta}\left(\mathbb{E}[\psi(\Delta(X))\mid Q\neq 2]\right)^{\top}\bar{\beta} \displaystyle\quad=(A_{1}+A_{3})^{\top}\bar{\beta} $$

where the second equality follows by the law of total expectation since

$$ \displaystyle 0=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\partial\log f(Q;0)}{\partial\theta}\right]=(1-\rho_{2})\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\partial\log f(Q;0)}{\partial\theta}\Big|Q\neq 2\right]+\rho_{2}\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\log f(2;0). $$

Finally,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\iota(W;\eta)\kappa(X;\eta)}{1-\rho_{2}}\frac{\partial\log h(Y\mid X,Q;0)}{\partial\theta}\right] \displaystyle\quad=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{Y}{1-\rho_{2}}\left(\frac{\bm{1}(Q=1)}{r(X)}-\frac{\bm{1}(Q=0)}{1-r(X)}\right)\kappa(X;\eta)\frac{\partial\log h(Y\mid X,Q;0)}{\partial\theta}\right] \displaystyle\quad=\mathbb{E}\left[(1-\rho_{2})^{-1}\left(\frac{\bm{1}(Q=1)}{r(X)}-\frac{\bm{1}(Q=0)}{1-r(X)}\right)\kappa(X;\eta)\mathbb{E}\left[Y\frac{\partial\log h(Y\mid X,Q,0)}{\partial\theta}\Big|X,Q\right]\right] \displaystyle\quad=(1-\rho_{2})^{-1}\sum_{q=0}^{1}\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\textnormal{Pr}(Q=q\mid X)}{r(X)-(1-q)}\kappa(X;\eta)\frac{\partial\int yh(y\mid X,q;0)d\lambda_{Y\mid QX}(y)}{\partial\theta}\right] \displaystyle\quad=(1-\rho_{2})^{-1}\mathbb{E}\left[\textnormal{Pr}(Q\neq 2\mid X)\kappa(X;\eta)\frac{\partial\Delta(X;0)}{\partial\theta}\right] \displaystyle\quad=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\partial\Delta(X;0)}{\partial\theta}\left(\dot{\psi}(\Delta(X))^{\top}\bar{\beta}+\Lambda(X)m_{2}(X)\bar{\alpha}^{\top}\dot{\psi}(\Delta(X))\right)\Big|Q\neq 2\right] \displaystyle\quad-\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\partial\Delta(X;0)}{\partial\theta}\Lambda(X)\bar{\alpha}^{\top}\left[\psi(\Delta(X))\dot{\psi}(\Delta(X))^{\top}+\dot{\psi}(\Delta(X))\psi(\Delta(X))^{\top}\right]\bar{\beta}\Big|Q\neq 2\right] \displaystyle\quad=A_{2}^{\top}\bar{\beta}+\bar{\alpha}^{\top}(B_{2}-B_{4}) $$

where the first equality follows from (32) applied to the functions $F(x,q)=\frac{m_{r}(x)\bm{1}(Q=r)\kappa(x;\eta)}{(r(x)-q)(1-\rho_{2})}$ for $r=0,1$ , and the fourth equality follows from observing that

$$ \textnormal{Pr}(Q=q\mid X)=\textnormal{Pr}(Q=q\mid X,Q\neq 2)P(Q\neq 2\mid X)=(r(X)-(1-q))P(Q\neq 2\mid X)(-1)^{q+1}. $$

We conclude that indeed

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\psi(W;\bar{\tau},\eta)s(W;0)] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\psi_{1}(W;\bar{\tau},\eta)s(W,0)]+\mathbb{E}[\psi_{2}(W;\bar{\tau},\eta)s(W,0)] \displaystyle=\bar{\alpha}^{\top}(B_{1}+B_{2}-B_{3}-B_{4})+(A_{1}+A_{2}+A_{3})^{\top}\bar{\beta} $$

which concludes the proof of (31).

It remains to show that whenever the efficiency bound $V_{\textnormal{eff}}$ is finite, $\rho_{2}V_{\textnormal{eff}}\rightarrow\Sigma$ as $M\rightarrow\infty$ with $\rho_{2}\rightarrow 0$ while the conditional distribution of $W=(Q,X,Y)$ given $\bm{1}(Q=2)$ remains constant. To see this, we write

$$ \displaystyle V_{\textnormal{eff}} \displaystyle=(1-\rho_{2})^{-1}\mathbb{E}\left[(\bar{\mu}(X)-\bar{\tau}\iota(W;\eta)\kappa(X;\eta))^{2}\mid Q\neq 2\right] \displaystyle\quad+\rho_{2}^{-1}\mathbb{E}\left[(Y-\bar{\mu}(X))^{2}\bar{\alpha}^{\top}\psi(\Delta(X))\psi(\Delta(X))^{\top}\bar{\alpha}\mid Q=2\right] $$

The assumption $V_{\textnormal{eff}}<\infty$ implies $0<\rho_{2}<1$ and both conditional expectations

$$ \displaystyle E_{1} \displaystyle\equiv\mathbb{E}\left[(\bar{\mu}(X)-\bar{\tau}\iota(W;\eta)\kappa(X;\eta))^{2}\mid Q\neq 2\right]\quad\text{ and } \displaystyle E_{2} \displaystyle\equiv\mathbb{E}\left[(Y-\bar{\mu}(X))^{2}\bar{\alpha}^{\top}\psi(\Delta(X))\psi(\Delta(X))^{\top}\bar{\alpha}\mid Q=2\right] $$

are finite. These conditional expectations $E_{1}$ and $E_{2}$ remain fixed in our asymptotics. Then as desired, evidently

$$ \rho_{2}V_{\textnormal{eff}}=\frac{\rho_{2}}{1-\rho_{2}}E_{1}+E_{2}\rightarrow E_{2}=\Sigma $$

as $M\rightarrow\infty$ and $\rho_{2}\rightarrow 0$ .

## Appendix B Efficiency bound for $\bar{\tau}$ when $\Delta(\cdot)$ is known

Here we present the semiparametric efficiency bound (under the nested formulation of our setting introduced in Section 4) for our estimand $\bar{\tau}$ when the treatment-control contrast $\Delta(\cdot)$ is known. As discussed in Section 4, prior work on efficient estimation of projection estimands gives the semiparametric efficiency bound for the estimand $\bar{\theta}=(1-\rho_{2})\bar{\tau}=\mathbb{E}[\bm{1}(Q\neq 2)\bar{\tau}]$ when $\Delta(\cdot)$ is known as a special case. In particular, from Proposition 4 of Newey (1994), we see that the efficient influence function (EIF) for $\bar{\theta}$ , evaluated at a generic observation $w=(q,x,y)$ , is

$$ \psi_{\bar{\theta}}(w)=\bm{1}(q\neq 2)\bar{\mu}(x)-\bar{\theta}+\frac{\bm{1}(q=2)(1-\rho_{2})\bar{\alpha}^{\top}\psi(\Delta(x)))(y-\bar{\mu}(x))}{\rho_{2}} $$

when $\Delta(\cdot)$ is known, where $\bar{\alpha}$ is given by (12). Then to get the EIF $\psi_{\bar{\tau}}(\cdot)$ of $\bar{\tau}=(1-\rho_{2})^{-1}\bar{\theta}$ with $\Delta(\cdot)$ known, we recall that the EIF for $1-\rho_{2}=\mathbb{E}[\bm{1}(Q\neq 2)]$ is simply

$$ \psi_{1-\rho_{2}}(w)=\bm{1}(q\neq 2)-(1-\rho_{2})=\rho_{2}-\bm{1}(q=2). $$

Then using the properties of influence functions as derivatives (e.g., Theorems 20.8 and 20.9 of van der Vaart (2000) or Kennedy (2024)), we can apply the quotient rule to conclude

$$ \addcontentsline{lla}{section}{\numberline q:eif_{D}elta_{k}nown}\psi_{\bar{\tau}}(w)=\frac{(1-\rho_{2})\psi_{\bar{\theta}}(w)-\bar{\theta}\psi_{1-\rho_{2}}(w)}{(1-\rho_{2})^{2}}=\frac{\bm{1}(q\neq 2)}{1-\rho_{2}}(\bar{\mu}(x)-\bar{\tau})+\frac{\bm{1}(q=2)}{\rho_{2}}(y-\bar{\mu}(x))\bar{\alpha}^{\top}\psi(\Delta(x)). $$

Note that this differs from the EIF in the case $\Delta$ must be estimated (Theorem 2) by the omission of the term

$$ \frac{\bm{1}(q\neq 2)}{1-\rho_{2}}\iota(w;\eta)\kappa(x;\eta). $$

From (33), the efficiency bound (when $\Delta$ is known) is

$$ \mathbb{E}[\psi_{\bar{\tau}}(W)^{2}]=\frac{\mathbb{E}[(\bar{\mu}(X)-\bar{\tau})^{2}\mid Q\neq 2]}{(1-\rho_{2})}+\frac{\mathbb{E}[(Y-\bar{\mu}(X))^{2}\bar{\alpha}^{\top}\psi(\Delta(X))\psi(\Delta(X))^{\top}\bar{\alpha}\mid Q=2]}{\rho_{2}}. $$

Assuming this is finite, we observe that as $M\rightarrow\infty$ with $\rho_{2}\rightarrow 0$ and the distribution of $(Q,X,Y)$ given $\bm{1}(Q=2)$ remaining constant, we have

$$ \rho_{2}\mathbb{E}[\psi_{\bar{\tau}}(W)^{2}]\rightarrow\mathbb{E}[(Y-\bar{\mu}(X))^{2}\bar{\alpha}^{\top}\psi(\Delta(X))\psi(\Delta(X))^{\top}\bar{\alpha}\mid Q=2]=\Sigma. $$

In conjunction with Theorem 2, this shows the claim at the end of Section 4 that in this asymptotic regime, the need to estimate $\Delta(\cdot)$ does not affect the efficiency bound.

## Appendix C Nuisance function estimation for numerical studies

For the simulation study in Section 5.1 with a one-dimensional covariate, we estimate the observational treatment-control contrast $\Delta(\cdot)$ by applying the DR-learner (Kennedy, 2023) to the observational dataset, with generalized additive models (GAMs) as implemented by the gam function in the mgcv package in R (Wood, 2017) as base learners and the observational propensity score

$$ r(x)=\textnormal{Pr}_{\textnormal{obs}}(Z=1\mid X=x) $$

estimated using a GAM with logit link. For all of our GAM fits, we use the default behavior for a “smooth” term s() in the gam function (thin-plate regression splines with degrees of freedom chosen automatically via restricted maximum likelihood). For the AIPSW and collaborative estimators, we estimate the CATE $\mu(\cdot)$ using the super learner (Polley et al., 2024) with $L_{1}$ -penalized linear regression (Tibshirani, 1996), multivariate adaptive regression splines (Friedman, 1991), random forests (Breiman, 2001), and support vector machines (Cortes and Vapnik, 1995) as the component learners, with the observations $\{D_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}$ as the response. We incorporate the prognostic adjustment idea of Liao et al. (2025) to improve learning of the CATE $\mu(\cdot)$ from the small experimental dataset by including both $X$ and our estimates $\hat{\Delta}(X)$ of the treatment contrast $\Delta(X)$ as predictors in the super learner. The odds ratio $q_{n,N}$ for the AIPSW estimator is estimated by fitting a GAM with logit link to the combined experimental and observational dataset, with the response variable being the binary indicator of whether the observation is in the experimental dataset. The odds ratio $g_{n,N}$ for the collaborative estimator is estimated in the same way, except with $\hat{\mu}(X_{i})$ as the single predictor (instead of $X_{i}$ ). Finally, the nuisance function $k_{n,N}(\cdot)$ for the collaborative estimator is estimated by fitting a GAM (with identity link) to predict $\hat{\mu}(X_{i})$ from the estimates $\hat{g}_{n,N}(X_{i})$ . Since $X$ is univariate, we do not use cross-fitting for any of our nuisance function estimates for the simulations in Section 5.1. In particular, we set $K=1$ in the algorithm described at the start of Section 3.

For the simulations with ten covariates in Section 5.2, we learn $\Delta(\cdot)$ using a causal forest, as implemented by the causal_forest function with default hyperparameters in the grf package in R (Tibshirani et al., 2026). To compute the estimates $\hat{\Delta}(X_{i})$ in the observational dataset (observations $i=n+1,\ldots,n+N$ ), we use the out-of-bag predictions in lieu of cross-fit predictions. The odds ratio $q_{n,N}(\cdot)$ for the AIPSW estimator is estimated using logistic regression (with additive terms for all 10 covariates), as advocated in the semi-supervised learning literature (Zhang et al., 2023). The remaining nuisance functions $\mu(\cdot)$ , $g_{n,N}(\cdot)$ , and $k_{n,N}(\cdot)$ for the AIPSW and collaborative estimators are estimated in the same way as for the univariate simulations in Section 5.1, except that for $\mu(\cdot)$ we now implement cross-fitting with $K=5$ folds due to the dimensionality of the covariate space relative to the experimental dataset size $n=100$ .

Finally, for the simulations based on the crop rotation data in Section 5.3, we also estimate $\Delta(\cdot)$ using a causal forest (though with only 200 trees to speed up the computation time). We estimate the odds ratio $q_{n,N}$ for the AIPSW estimator using $L_{1}$ -penalized logistic regression with potential predictors including linear terms for all covariates as well as interactions up to order two between latitude and longitude. The remaining nuisance functions are estimated in the same way as for the multivariate simulations, as described in the preceding paragraph.

# A Human Skeletal Muscle Atlas Identifies the Trajectories of Stem and Progenitor Cells across Development and from Human Pluripotent Stem Cells

**Authors:** Haibin Xi; Justin Langerman; Shan Sabri; Peggie Chien; Courtney S. Young; Shahab Younesi; Michael Hicks; Karen Gonzalez; Wakana Fujiwara; Julia Marzi; Simone Liebscher; Melissa Spencer; Ben Van Handel; Denis Evseenko; Katja Schenke-Layland; Kathrin Plath; April D. Pyle
